The Chairperson and members are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a Selection Committee consisting of the Prime Minister, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha, the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, the Chief Justice of India or a judge nominated by the Chief Justice, and an eminent jurist. They hold office for five years or until the age of seventy, whichever is earlier.

Complaints against the Prime Minister are subject to special safeguards: the Lokpal may inquire only if the full bench so decides by a two-thirds majority, and the inquiry is to be held in camera. For other public servants, the Lokpal may conduct a preliminary inquiry, refer the matter to the Central Vigilance Commission or another agency, and, where a prima facie case is made out, direct investigation and prosecution. The Lokpal also has a prosecution wing and may direct the filing of cases in special courts.

The first Lokpal was constituted only in March 2019, when Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose was appointed Chairperson, more than five years after the Act came into force. That delay illustrates a recurring governance problem: an institution created by law does not function until its members are appointed, its staff are in place and its procedures are notified. The Lokpal's record since then is debated, but its design remains instructive: independence is built through appointment, composition and tenure, not through the name of the body alone.
takeaways: The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, in force from January 2014, creates a Union ombudsman and requires state Lokayuktas.
The Lokpal has a Chairperson and up to eight members, half judicial, with selection by a committee including the Prime Minister, Speaker, Leader of Opposition and Chief Justice.
The first Lokpal was constituted in March 2019 under Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose, more than five years after the Act came into force.
relevance: The Lokpal shows that creating an institution by law is only half the task: appointment, staffing and procedure decide whether it ever functions.
question: Should complaints against a Prime Minister be heard by the Lokpal at all, or does that risk turning an anti-corruption body into a political weapon?

title: The National Human Rights Commission: a statutory watchdog with recommendatory powers
syllabus: GS II — Important aspects of governance, transparency and accountability, e-governance, citizens' charters; statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies; role of civil services in a democracy.
paragraphs: The National Human Rights Commission, or NHRC, was established under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. It is a statutory body, not a constitutional body, and its mandate is to protect and promote human rights, defined in the Act as rights relating to life, liberty, equality and dignity guaranteed by the Constitution or embodied in international covenants and enforceable by courts in India. The Commission may inquire into complaints of human rights violations or negligence in preventing them by a public servant.

The Commission's composition reflects its intended independence. It is headed by a Chairperson who, after the 2019 amendment, may be a former Chief Justice of India or a former judge of the Supreme Court, together with members including former judges and persons with knowledge of human rights. State Human Rights Commissions perform a similar role at state level. The NHRC may visit jails and other institutions under state control, review safeguards in law, study treaties, and promote research and awareness on human rights.

The NHRC's powers are recommendatory. It may recommend compensation, prosecution or other action, but it cannot itself punish an official or enforce its recommendations. It may also intervene in court proceedings involving human rights and may approach the Supreme Court or a High Court for directions. Its annual reports are laid before Parliament. This design gives the Commission moral and public authority, but leaves enforcement to governments and courts.

Critics argue that recommendatory powers, delays in appointments and dependence on government staff limit the Commission's effectiveness, especially in cases involving security forces, for which the Act provides a special procedure. Supporters reply that a watchdog that can investigate, publish and recommend is still valuable, because it creates a record that courts, Parliament and the press can use. For civil studies, the NHRC is a useful contrast with a court: it can inquire widely, but it cannot decide a case.
takeaways: The NHRC was established under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, as a statutory body to inquire into human rights violations by public servants.
It is headed by a former Chief Justice or, after the 2019 amendment, a former Supreme Court judge, with members drawn from the judiciary and human rights expertise.
Its recommendations on compensation or prosecution are not binding; enforcement rests with governments and courts.
relevance: The NHRC tests the value of a watchdog without enforcement power: its influence comes from investigation, publication and recommendation.
question: Should a human rights commission be able to enforce its orders, or would that turn it into another court?

title: The Central Vigilance Commission: vigilance over corruption in central administration
syllabus: GS II — Important aspects of governance, transparency and accountability, e-governance, citizens' charters; statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies; role of civil services in a democracy.
paragraphs: The Central Vigilance Commission, or CVC, is the apex vigilance institution for the Central Government. It was set up in 1964 on the recommendation of the Committee on Prevention of Corruption, known as the Santhanam Committee, and was given statutory status by the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003. Its mandate is to inquire into offences alleged to have been committed under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 by central public servants, and to exercise superintendence over the vigilance work of central departments and the Central Bureau of Investigation in corruption cases.

The Commission consists of a Central Vigilance Commissioner and up to two Vigilance Commissioners, appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee consisting of the Prime Minister, the Minister of Home Affairs and the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha. They hold office for four years or until the age of sixty-five, whichever is earlier. The Commission is not an investigating agency in the ordinary sense: it advises, supervises and reviews, and it refers cases for investigation and for departmental or criminal action.

The CVC's advice is a central part of disciplinary proceedings against central officers. Departments consult the Commission at stages such as the decision to initiate proceedings and the final penalty, and the Commission's advice is ordinarily followed, although the department remains responsible for the final decision. The Commission also promotes preventive vigilance, including transparency in procurement, e-governance and the identification of corruption-prone areas, and it receives complaints under the Public Interest Disclosure and Protection of Informers framework.

The CVC's limits are structural. It depends on departments for action, it does not control the police or the courts, and its jurisdiction is confined to central administration. Its value lies in creating an independent check inside the executive: an officer facing a corruption allegation knows that a body outside the department will examine the record. For students, the CVC illustrates the difference between vigilance, investigation and prosecution, which are often confused but are performed by different institutions.
takeaways: The CVC was set up in 1964 on the Santhanam Committee's recommendation and given statutory status by the Act of 2003.
It exercises superintendence over vigilance in central departments and over the CBI in corruption cases, and advises departments on disciplinary action.
Its Commissioners are appointed on the recommendation of a committee including the Prime Minister, Home Minister and Leader of Opposition.
relevance: The CVC separates vigilance from prosecution: it supervises and advises, while investigation and punishment remain with other bodies.
question: Should a vigilance body be able to direct prosecution itself, or does that concentration of power create a greater risk?

title: NITI Aayog: from central planning to cooperative federalism
syllabus: GS II — Important aspects of governance, transparency and accountability, e-governance, citizens' charters; statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies; role of civil services in a democracy.
paragraphs: NITI Aayog, the National Institution for Transforming India, was established by a Union Cabinet resolution on 1 January 2015, replacing the Planning Commission, which had been set up in 1950. Like the Planning Commission, NITI Aayog is neither a constitutional nor a statutory body. Its chairperson is the Prime Minister, and its Governing Council comprises chief ministers of all states, chief ministers of union territories with legislatures, and lieutenant governors of other union territories, together with the Aayog's vice-chairperson and members.

The change was presented as a move from a top-down, plan-allocation model to cooperative federalism. The Planning Commission prepared Five Year Plans and allocated central plan assistance to states; the Twelfth Five Year Plan, covering 2012 to 2017, was the last. NITI Aayog does not allocate funds. Its work is advisory and convening: it provides policy inputs, monitors programmes, ranks states and districts on indicators, and brings the Union and states together to discuss national priorities.

NITI Aayog's programmes illustrate this role. The Aspirational Districts Programme, launched in 2018, tracks progress in districts that lag on health, education, agriculture, infrastructure and financial inclusion, using a dashboard and ranking to encourage competition and attention. The Aayog also produces indices and reports on subjects such as health, water and innovation, and advises on the Sustainable Development Goals. Its influence therefore depends on the quality of its data and on whether governments act on its rankings.

Critics argue that without fund-allocation power, the Aayog is a think tank with limited leverage, and that rankings can reward states that already perform well rather than those facing the hardest conditions. Supporters reply that persuasion, data and a forum for chief ministers are valuable in a federal system where the Union cannot simply direct states. The contrast with the Planning Commission remains the key lesson: the same Prime Minister chairs both bodies, but the power to allocate money has been separated from the power to advise.
takeaways: NITI Aayog was established on 1 January 2015 by Cabinet resolution, replacing the Planning Commission set up in 1950; neither body is constitutional or statutory.
Its Governing Council, chaired by the Prime Minister, includes all chief ministers and lieutenant governors of union territories.
Unlike the Planning Commission, NITI Aayog does not allocate funds; it advises, monitors, ranks and convenes, including through the Aspirational Districts Programme.
relevance: NITI Aayog shows how an institution's power can change without changing its chair: removing fund allocation turns a planner into an adviser.
question: Is persuasion through rankings enough to change state performance, or does a federal think tank need control over money to matter?

title: Citizen's Charters and grievance redress: promising a standard of service
syllabus: GS II — Important aspects of governance, transparency and accountability, e-governance, citizens' charters; statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies; role of civil services in a democracy.
paragraphs: A Citizen's Charter is a public commitment by a government department or agency about the services it provides, the standards it promises, the time within which a service will be delivered, and the remedy available if the standard is not met. The idea came to India in the late 1990s, following the British Citizen's Charter model, and the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances has promoted charters across central ministries and departments. A charter is meant to turn a citizen from a supplicant into a holder of a stated expectation.

The Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System, known as CPGRAMS, is the online platform through which citizens may lodge grievances against central ministries and departments, and, through state portals, against many state governments. A grievance is forwarded to the concerned department, which is expected to examine it and reply within a prescribed period. The platform allows a citizen to track the grievance and to appeal if the reply is unsatisfactory. It does not itself decide a legal claim or award compensation.

The limits of charters and grievance systems are important. A charter is generally not a legally enforceable contract, and a grievance reply may close a complaint without solving the underlying problem, for example where a pension is delayed by a missing document that the citizen cannot easily obtain. The quality of redress therefore depends on whether departments treat grievances as feedback for reform, rather than as cases to be closed quickly to improve statistics.

For civil studies, charters and grievance platforms illustrate a shift from grievance as petition to grievance as service management. The useful questions are practical: is the standard measurable, is the time limit realistic, is the remedy stated, and is there an appeal that is genuinely independent of the office that failed? A charter that answers those questions is a governance tool; one that does not is a poster on a wall.
takeaways: A Citizen's Charter states the services, standards, time limits and remedies promised by a department, an idea adopted in India in the late 1990s.
CPGRAMS is the central online grievance platform, allowing citizens to lodge, track and appeal grievances against ministries and departments.
Charters are generally not legally enforceable contracts, and grievance closure does not always mean the underlying problem is solved.
relevance: Citizen's Charters turn administration into a promise with a deadline — but a promise that is not enforceable needs an appeal that is independent.
question: What makes a grievance system trustworthy: a fast reply, a correct outcome, or a public record of how many complaints were actually resolved?

title: E-governance and Digital India: services online, and the access question
syllabus: GS II — Important aspects of governance, transparency and accountability, e-governance, citizens' charters; statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies; role of civil services in a democracy.
paragraphs: E-governance means the use of information technology to deliver government services, to share information and to allow citizens to interact with the state without repeated visits to offices. The Digital India programme, launched on 1 July 2015, set out three visions: digital infrastructure as a core utility, governance and services on demand, and digital empowerment of citizens. Its pillars include broadband connectivity, universal mobile access, public internet access, e-governance, electronic delivery of services, and information for all.

Several platforms illustrate the model. DigiLocker allows citizens to store and share verified digital documents, such as driving licences and education certificates, without carrying physical copies. UMANG provides access to services of central and state governments through a single application. The Unified Payments Interface, developed by the National Payments Corporation of India, allows instant payments between bank accounts through a mobile phone, and has become a central part of digital payments in India, although it is a payments system rather than a government service portal.

E-governance can reduce discretion and delay, because an application leaves a digital trail and a service may be delivered without an intermediary. It can also create new barriers. Citizens without smartphones, connectivity, digital literacy or reliable identity documents may find an online-only service harder to use than an office, and errors in digital records can be difficult to correct. The design question is therefore not whether a service is online, but whether an offline alternative, help desk and correction mechanism remain available.

For civil studies, e-governance should be judged by outcomes for the least connected citizen, not by the number of services listed online. A service that is fast for a city resident with broadband and impossible for a rural resident without connectivity has not become more accessible; it has changed who can access it. Inclusion, language, grievance redress and data protection are part of e-governance, not additions to it.
takeaways: Digital India, launched on 1 July 2015, aims at digital infrastructure as a utility, governance and services on demand, and digital empowerment.
DigiLocker stores verified digital documents and UMANG brings central and state services into a single application.
Online delivery can reduce discretion but can exclude citizens without connectivity, devices, literacy or reliable records.
relevance: E-governance is judged not by how many services are online, but by whether the least connected citizen can still reach the state.
question: Should every government service have an offline alternative, or does keeping one slow the move to a fully digital state?

title: The National Commission for Scheduled Castes: a constitutional watchdog
syllabus: GS II — Important aspects of governance, transparency and accountability, e-governance, citizens' charters; statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies; role of civil services in a democracy.
paragraphs: The National Commission for Scheduled Castes, or NCSC, is established under Article 338 of the Constitution. It consists of a Chairperson, a Vice-Chairperson and three other members, appointed by the President. Its duties include investigating and monitoring matters relating to safeguards for Scheduled Castes, inquiring into specific complaints about deprivation of their rights, advising on socio-economic development planning, and evaluating the progress of their development under the Union and states.

The Commission's reports are laid before Parliament and state legislatures, and governments are expected to explain action taken on its recommendations. The NCSC may, while investigating a matter, exercise the powers of a civil court, including summoning persons, requiring documents and receiving evidence on affidavit. It is a constitutional body, which gives it a standing that a purely executive committee would not have, and its recommendations carry weight even though they are not binding orders.

The National Commission for Scheduled Tribes was separated from the NCSC by the 89th Amendment in 2003, which inserted Article 338A. Before that amendment, a single commission dealt with both Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The separation recognised that the two groups face distinct issues, including, for Scheduled Tribes, questions of forest rights, displacement and the special provisions of the Fifth and Sixth Schedules.

The Commission's effectiveness depends on the follow-up to its reports. A recommendation that is noted but not acted on does not change a school admission, a land dispute or a case of discrimination. Its value lies in investigation, publicity and persistence: a constitutional body that repeatedly records the same failure, names the department concerned and returns to the issue in later reports makes it harder for governments to claim that the failure is unknown or merely an isolated lapse. For students, the NCSC is a case study in constitutional watchdogs that advise rather than decide.
takeaways: The NCSC is established under Article 338, with a Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and three members appointed by the President.
It investigates safeguards and complaints, advises on development planning, and may exercise civil court powers while investigating.
The National Commission for Scheduled Tribes was separated by the 89th Amendment in 2003, inserting Article 338A.
relevance: A constitutional commission that advises rather than orders still matters if its reports are laid before Parliament and cannot be ignored quietly.
question: Should a commission like the NCSC be able to enforce its recommendations, or would binding powers blur the line between watchdog and court?

title: Administrative Tribunals: speedy justice for service disputes, outside the ordinary courts
syllabus: GS II — Important aspects of governance, transparency and accountability, e-governance, citizens' charters; statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies; role of civil services in a democracy.
paragraphs: Article 323A allows Parliament to establish administrative tribunals for adjudication of disputes relating to recruitment and conditions of service of public servants. The Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 gave effect to that provision and established the Central Administrative Tribunal, or CAT, in 1985, together with state administrative tribunals where states so decide. The CAT deals with service matters of central government employees and of employees of bodies notified by the government.

Tribunals are designed to be faster and more specialised than ordinary courts. They are not bound by the strict rules of evidence in the Indian Evidence Act, but must follow principles of natural justice. They may be headed by a judicial member and include administrative members with experience in public administration. Appeals from the CAT lie to the concerned High Court, and from there to the Supreme Court, following the Supreme Court's decision in L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India in 1997, which held that tribunal decisions are subject to judicial review by High Courts under Articles 226 and 227.

The tribunal model has spread beyond service matters. Article 323B allows tribunals for tax, foreign exchange, industrial and labour disputes, land reforms, elections and other specified matters, and Parliament and state legislatures have created tribunals in several of these areas. The National Green Tribunal, the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal and consumer commissions are examples of specialised forums, although they rest on different constitutional and statutory bases.

Tribunals raise a recurring question about independence. A forum that is speedy but dependent on the executive for appointments, tenure and infrastructure may not inspire confidence, especially when the government is a party to the dispute. The Supreme Court has therefore emphasised that tribunals must have judicial independence, including security of tenure and conditions for members. Speed without independence is not a substitute for justice.
takeaways: Article 323A allows Parliament to create administrative tribunals for public service disputes; the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 established the CAT in 1985.
Tribunals follow natural justice rather than strict evidence rules, and their decisions are subject to High Court review after L. Chandra Kumar in 1997.
Article 323B extends the tribunal model to tax, labour, land, election and other specified matters.
relevance: Tribunals trade the generality of courts for speed and specialisation — but only if their independence is protected as carefully as a court's.
question: Should service disputes go to a specialised tribunal at all, or should they stay in the High Courts that can review them anyway?

title: Whistle-blower protection: disclosure without retaliation
syllabus: GS II — Important aspects of governance, transparency and accountability, e-governance, citizens' charters; statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies; role of civil services in a democracy.
paragraphs: The Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 was enacted to provide a mechanism for receiving complaints about corruption, wilful misuse of power or discretion, and criminal offences by public servants, and to protect persons who make such disclosures from victimisation. It is distinct from the general right to information: a whistle-blower does not ask for a document, but reports wrongdoing inside an organisation, often at personal risk, and seeks protection for doing so.

Under the Act, a disclosure may be made to a competent authority, and the identity of the complainant is to be protected. The competent authority is to conceal the complainant's identity unless the complainant has revealed it or unless disclosure is necessary for inquiry, and is to take action on the disclosure, including inquiry and recommendation for action against the public servant concerned. The Act also provides for penalties for revealing a complainant's identity and for making false or frivolous complaints.

The Act's scope is limited in important ways. It does not apply to disclosures relating to matters that would prejudicially affect the sovereignty, integrity, security or economic interests of India, or relations with a foreign state, and it excludes the armed forces and certain other categories. Amendments proposed in 2015, which would have aligned the Act's exemptions more closely with the Right to Information Act, were passed by the Lok Sabha but were not enacted into law in the form proposed, and the operational framework for the Act has remained a subject of debate.

Whistle-blower protection therefore depends on trust in the receiving authority. A law can promise confidentiality, but a potential complainant will judge whether that promise is credible by looking at past cases, at the independence of the authority, and at whether complainants who came forward were protected or punished. For civil studies, the Act is a reminder that accountability depends on safe channels for insiders, not only on information for outsiders.
takeaways: The Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 provides for complaints about corruption, misuse of power and criminal offences by public servants, with protection from victimisation.
Disclosures go to a competent authority, which is to protect the complainant's identity and act on the disclosure.
The Act excludes matters affecting sovereignty, security and economic interests, and its operational framework has remained debated after 2015 amendment proposals.
relevance: Whistle-blower law is about credible safety: a disclosure channel works only if insiders believe they will be protected, not punished.
question: Should whistle-blower protection cover private-sector wrongdoing as well, or should it stay confined to public servants?

title: India and UN Security Council reform: the G4 case for a permanent seat
syllabus: GS II — India and its neighbourhood — relations; bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India's interests; effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India's interests, Indian Diaspora.
paragraphs: The United Nations Security Council has five permanent members — China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States — each with a veto over substantive resolutions, and ten non-permanent members elected for two-year terms. Its permanent membership reflects the power structure of 1945, when the United Nations was founded, rather than the distribution of population, economic weight and peacekeeping contribution today. India, which is not a permanent member, has argued for decades that the Council must be reformed to reflect contemporary realities.

India's case rests on several grounds: it is the world's most populous country, a large economy, a major contributor of troops to United Nations peacekeeping operations, and a country whose decisions affect climate, health, trade and development for a large share of humanity. India has served multiple terms as a non-permanent member, most recently in 2021 to 2022, but non-permanent membership does not carry a veto and does not allow a country to shape the Council's agenda in the same way as permanent membership.

India pursues reform through the G4, a grouping of Brazil, Germany, India and Japan, each of which seeks a permanent seat for itself in an expanded Council. The G4 proposal envisages expanding the Council from fifteen to around twenty-five members, adding six new permanent seats — two for Africa, two for Asia-Pacific, one for Latin America and one for Western Europe — and additional non-permanent seats. Under the proposal, new permanent members would initially not exercise a veto, with the question to be reviewed after a period.

Reform faces a high procedural bar. Amending the UN Charter requires adoption by two-thirds of the General Assembly and ratification by two-thirds of member states, including all five permanent members. The Uniting for Consensus group, including Italy, Pakistan, South Korea and Argentina, opposes new permanent seats and favours expanding only non-permanent membership. Reform therefore requires both a proposal that commands broad support and the consent of the very members whose exclusivity it would dilute.
takeaways: The Security Council has five veto-holding permanent members from 1945 and ten non-permanent members elected for two years.
India's reform case rests on population, economic weight, peacekeeping contribution and repeated non-permanent terms, most recently 2021 to 2022.
The G4 — Brazil, Germany, India and Japan — proposes expansion to around twenty-five members with six new permanent seats, initially without veto.
relevance: UNSC reform shows how procedure can block substance: even broad support for change must pass a Charter amendment requiring the consent of existing permanent members.
question: Is a permanent seat without a veto worth seeking, or does it create a second-class membership that weakens the reform case?

title: India and ASEAN: from Look East to Act East
syllabus: GS II — India and its neighbourhood — relations; bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India's interests; effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India's interests, Indian Diaspora.
paragraphs: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN, was founded in 1967 by Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand, and now has ten members, including Brunei, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and Vietnam. India became a sectoral dialogue partner of ASEAN in 1992 and a full dialogue partner in 1995, and held its first summit with ASEAN in 2002. The relationship has since grown into a strategic partnership covering political and security cooperation, trade, connectivity, culture and education.

India's Look East Policy, launched in the early 1990s after economic liberalisation, sought closer economic engagement with Southeast Asia. In 2014 it was renamed the Act East Policy, signalling a more active approach, including stronger connectivity with Northeast India, maritime cooperation, and engagement with the wider Indo-Pacific. The renaming matters because it marks a shift from trade alone to a broader agenda: roads, ports, digital links and security dialogues are treated as part of the same relationship.

Trade and connectivity are central. India and ASEAN have a free trade agreement in goods, in force from 2010, with later agreements on services and investment. Connectivity projects, including the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway, aim to link India's Northeast with Southeast Asia by road, although progress has been slower than planned. Maritime cooperation in the South China Sea region, where several ASEAN members have disputes with China, is another shared interest, with India supporting freedom of navigation and a rules-based order under international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.

The relationship also has limits. Trade between India and ASEAN remains smaller than ASEAN's trade with China, and India chose not to join the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership in 2019, citing concerns about trade deficits and the impact on domestic producers. For civil studies, ASEAN illustrates how India balances economic openness with domestic protection, and how a regional grouping can be a partner in connectivity and security even when trade negotiations stall.
takeaways: ASEAN, founded in 1967, now has ten members; India became a sectoral dialogue partner in 1992, a full dialogue partner in 1995, and held a first summit in 2002.
The Look East Policy of the early 1990s became the Act East Policy in 2014, broadening the agenda from trade to connectivity and maritime cooperation.
India-ASEAN trade in goods has operated under a free trade agreement since 2010, while India stayed out of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership in 2019.
relevance: ASEAN shows that regional policy is not only trade: connectivity, maritime rules and the Northeast's geography are part of the same relationship.
question: Should India prioritise connectivity with Southeast Asia through its Northeast, even if trade gains are slower than expected?

title: India and Africa: the Forum Summit and South-South cooperation
syllabus: GS II — India and its neighbourhood — relations; bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India's interests; effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India's interests, Indian Diaspora.
paragraphs: India's engagement with Africa draws on a shared history of decolonisation, the Non-Aligned Movement and support for liberation movements, and on contemporary interests in trade, energy, health, education and peacekeeping. The India-Africa Forum Summit, or IAFS, is the official platform for that relationship. The first summit was held in New Delhi in April 2008, with leaders of fourteen African countries chosen by the African Union, and it adopted the Delhi Declaration and the Africa-India Framework for Cooperation.

Subsequent summits were held in Addis Ababa in 2011 and in New Delhi in 2015, the third summit being the first to invite all African countries rather than a limited group under the earlier Banjul formula. The summits have covered agriculture and food security, health, education, science and technology, infrastructure, trade and investment, and peace and security. Capacity building is a recurring theme: India offers training, scholarships and technical assistance, including through the Indian Technical and Economic Cooperation programme, which predates the summit format.

Health and pharmaceuticals illustrate the practical content of the partnership. Indian generic medicines supply a large share of affordable drugs in many African countries, and Indian training and hospital partnerships support health systems. Trade and investment have grown, with Indian companies active in sectors such as telecommunications, agriculture and manufacturing, while African exports to India include oil, minerals and agricultural products. The partnership is often described as South-South cooperation, meaning cooperation between developing countries on more equal terms than traditional aid relationships.

The relationship is not without tensions. African partners have at times criticised the pace of project delivery, the terms of lines of credit and the treatment of African students in India, while India has sought greater African support for its positions in multilateral forums, including United Nations reform. For civil studies, India-Africa relations are a test of whether South-South cooperation can be genuinely mutual, or whether it reproduces the asymmetries it claims to avoid.
takeaways: The first India-Africa Forum Summit was held in New Delhi in April 2008, with fourteen African countries chosen by the African Union.
Summits followed in Addis Ababa in 2011 and New Delhi in 2015, when all African countries were invited for the first time.
Capacity building, health, education and training are central to the partnership, alongside trade, energy and infrastructure.
relevance: India-Africa relations test the idea of South-South cooperation: partnership is judged by delivery, terms and treatment, not by summit declarations alone.
question: Should South-South cooperation be judged by the same standards as traditional aid, or by different standards of mutual benefit?

title: India and the European Union: a strategic partnership still negotiating trade
syllabus: GS II — India and its neighbourhood — relations; bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India's interests; effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India's interests, Indian Diaspora.
paragraphs: The European Union is India's largest trading partner as a bloc, and the relationship covers trade, investment, technology, climate, research and foreign policy dialogue. India and the European Union established a strategic partnership in 2004, and hold regular summits, ministerial meetings and dialogues on subjects ranging from counter-terrorism to maritime security. The European Union is also a major source of foreign investment in India and a destination for Indian exports, students and professionals.

Trade negotiations have been the most difficult part of the relationship. Talks on a broad-based trade and investment agreement began in 2007, stalled in 2013, and were relaunched in 2022, with separate negotiations on investment protection and geographical indications. Differences remain over market access for agriculture and services, government procurement, labour and environmental standards, and data protection. The European Union's carbon border adjustment mechanism, which imposes charges on imports of certain carbon-intensive goods, has added a new source of friction, with India arguing that it penalises developing-country exporters.

Beyond trade, the partnership includes cooperation on climate and clean energy, digital regulation, research under programmes such as Horizon Europe, and connectivity in the Indo-Pacific. The European Union's Indo-Pacific strategy, adopted in 2021, emphasises a rules-based order, freedom of navigation and partnerships with countries including India, Japan and ASEAN members. India and the European Union also cooperate on maritime security, including in the western Indian Ocean, where piracy and trafficking affect shipping.

The relationship illustrates a wider pattern in India's foreign policy: partnerships with large economies bring technology, investment and market access, but also regulatory demands that India must weigh against domestic priorities. A trade agreement with the European Union would be judged not only by tariff cuts, but by its effects on farmers, small manufacturers, data governance, climate policy, and the ability of Indian regulators to set standards for their own market in future.
takeaways: India and the European Union established a strategic partnership in 2004 and hold regular summits and dialogues on trade, security and climate.
Trade talks begun in 2007 stalled in 2013 and were relaunched in 2022, alongside separate investment and geographical indications negotiations.
The EU carbon border adjustment mechanism and differences over agriculture, services, procurement and data remain sources of friction.
relevance: India-EU relations show that a strategic partnership can be broad in dialogue and narrow in agreement, especially when trade meets regulation.
question: Should India accept European labour and environmental standards in a trade deal in return for market access, or keep those standards out of trade talks?

title: India and West Asia: energy, workers and a changing Gulf
syllabus: GS II — India and its neighbourhood — relations; bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India's interests; effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India's interests, Indian Diaspora.
paragraphs: West Asia, often called the Middle East, is central to India's energy security, trade and diaspora. The region supplies a large share of India's crude oil and liquefied natural gas imports, and Gulf countries host millions of Indian workers, whose remittances support households across India, particularly in Kerala and other coastal and southern states. India's relationships in the region therefore combine foreign policy with the welfare of citizens abroad, including evacuation operations when conflict erupts.

India's approach has been to maintain relations with all major actors in the region, including Israel, Palestine, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, rather than aligning exclusively with one side. India recognised Israel in 1950 and established full diplomatic relations in 1992, while continuing to support a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine. Relations with Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have deepened through strategic partnership agreements, defence cooperation, investment and energy deals, including long-term supply arrangements.

The Abraham Accords of 2020, under which the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain normalised relations with Israel, changed the region's diplomacy and created new possibilities for cooperation, including through the I2U2 grouping of India, Israel, the United Arab Emirates and the United States, which focuses on food security, water, energy, transport and space. India has also sought connectivity through the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor, announced in 2023, linking India with the Gulf and Europe by sea and rail, although its implementation depends on regional stability.

West Asia tests India's ability to balance competing interests: energy imports, worker welfare, defence ties, and positions on conflicts in which partners disagree. A policy that works for one relationship may strain another, and the test of the approach is whether India can protect its citizens abroad, secure energy supplies at affordable prices, and maintain credibility with all sides at once.
takeaways: West Asia supplies a large share of India's oil and gas imports and hosts millions of Indian workers whose remittances support households in India.
India recognised Israel in 1950, established full diplomatic relations in 1992, and continues to support a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine.
The I2U2 grouping of India, Israel, the UAE and the US, and the India-Middle East-Europe Corridor announced in 2023, reflect new regional cooperation.
relevance: West Asia combines foreign policy with citizen welfare: energy, remittances and evacuations make it a domestic issue as well as a diplomatic one.
question: Can India maintain relations with all sides in West Asia indefinitely, or will a future conflict force it to choose?

title: BIMSTEC: India's Bay of Bengal grouping beyond SAARC
syllabus: GS II — India and its neighbourhood — relations; bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India's interests; effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India's interests, Indian Diaspora.
paragraphs: The Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation, or BIMSTEC, brings together Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Thailand. It was founded in 1997 in Bangkok and takes its name from the Bay of Bengal that connects most of its members. Its sectors include trade, transport, energy, tourism, agriculture, environment, disaster management, public health, counter-terrorism and people-to-people contact, reflecting a broad agenda rather than a single trade deal.

BIMSTEC gained importance for India as the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation, or SAARC, stalled after its last summit in 2014, with the next summit cancelled amid tensions between India and Pakistan. BIMSTEC excludes Pakistan and Afghanistan and includes Thailand and Myanmar, linking South Asia with Southeast Asia. For India, it offers a regional forum that can discuss connectivity, coastal shipping, power trade and disaster response without the India-Pakistan deadlock that has affected SAARC.

The grouping adopted its Charter in 2022, giving it a formal institutional structure, including a secretariat in Dhaka, a rotating chairmanship and a mechanism for summits and ministerial meetings. A framework agreement on a free trade area has been under negotiation for many years, with agreements on goods, services and investment discussed separately, but a comprehensive free trade agreement has not been concluded. Progress has been faster on subjects such as disaster management, counter-terrorism cooperation and transport connectivity.

BIMSTEC's limits are also clear. Myanmar's internal crisis since 2021 has complicated meetings and projects, member economies differ greatly in size, and the grouping lacks the enforcement mechanisms of a trade bloc. Its value may therefore lie less in a single agreement than in practical cooperation: a road, a power line, a disaster warning system or a joint exercise that would not happen through bilateral talks alone, and that directly benefits coastal communities and border regions.
takeaways: BIMSTEC, founded in 1997 in Bangkok, brings together Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Thailand.
It gained importance as SAARC stalled after its last summit in 2014, offering India a forum linking South and Southeast Asia without Pakistan.
BIMSTEC adopted its Charter in 2022, with a secretariat in Dhaka, but a comprehensive free trade agreement has not been concluded.
relevance: BIMSTEC shows that regional cooperation can be rebuilt around a different map when an older grouping stalls — but a new map alone does not guarantee results.
question: Should India invest more in BIMSTEC or try to revive SAARC, and what does each choice cost in relations with neighbours?

title: SAARC: why South Asia's regional organisation stalled
syllabus: GS II — India and its neighbourhood — relations; bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India's interests; effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India's interests, Indian Diaspora.
paragraphs: The South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation, or SAARC, was founded in Dhaka in 1985 by Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, with Afghanistan joining in 2007. Its Charter commits members to promoting welfare, economic growth, social progress and cultural development in the region, and to cooperation in areas such as agriculture, health, education, science and technology. Decisions are taken by unanimity, which means any member can block a decision.

SAARC created several institutions and agreements, including the SAARC Development Fund, the South Asian University in New Delhi, and the South Asian Free Trade Area, or SAFTA, which came into force in 2006. SAFTA aimed to reduce tariffs among members, with longer timelines and sensitive lists for less developed members. Intra-regional trade in South Asia remains low compared with other regions, however, partly because of political tensions, non-tariff barriers, poor connectivity and the size difference between India and its neighbours.

The organisation's summits have been the clearest sign of its difficulties. The nineteenth SAARC summit, scheduled for Islamabad in 2016, was cancelled after India, Bangladesh, Bhutan and Afghanistan declined to attend following a terrorist attack in Uri. No SAARC summit has been held since the eighteenth summit in Kathmandu in 2014. Working-level cooperation has continued in some areas, including through the SAARC Disaster Management Centre and health cooperation during the COVID-19 pandemic, but the leaders' forum has not met.

SAARC's experience raises a question for regionalism in South Asia: can an organisation based on unanimity work when its two largest members are in a prolonged confrontation? Some argue that sub-regional cooperation, through BIMSTEC or bilateral projects, is more practical. Others argue that abandoning SAARC removes the only forum where all South Asian leaders meet, and that its social and technical cooperation still has value even when political summits stall.
takeaways: SAARC was founded in Dhaka in 1985 with seven members; Afghanistan joined in 2007, and decisions require unanimity.
The South Asian Free Trade Area came into force in 2006, but intra-regional trade remains low compared with other regions.
No SAARC summit has been held since Kathmandu in 2014; the 2016 Islamabad summit was cancelled after India and others declined to attend.
relevance: SAARC shows the limits of unanimity: a regional organisation cannot move faster than the trust between its most divided members.
question: Is a stalled SAARC still worth keeping for technical cooperation, or should South Asia build new forums and let SAARC lapse?

title: India and Russia: a longstanding partnership in a changing world
syllabus: GS II — India and its neighbourhood — relations; bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India's interests; effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India's interests, Indian Diaspora.
paragraphs: India's relationship with Russia dates to the Soviet period. The Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation between India and the Soviet Union was signed in 1971, and the Soviet Union supported India on industrialisation, defence and space during the Cold War. After the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, India and Russia signed a Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation in 1993 and declared a strategic partnership in 2000, later raised to a special and privileged strategic partnership. Defence, energy, science and space remain central pillars.

Defence cooperation is the most visible pillar. Russia has supplied a large share of India's military equipment over decades, including aircraft, submarines, tanks and air defence systems, and the two countries have jointly developed systems such as the BrahMos cruise missile with Russia. India has diversified its defence suppliers in recent years, buying equipment from the United States, France and Israel as well, but Russian-origin platforms still form a large part of India's inventory and require spares, maintenance and upgrades.

Energy cooperation has grown, including oil and gas supplies and nuclear power. Russia is building nuclear reactors at Kudankulam in Tamil Nadu, and India has invested in Russian oil and gas projects. Since 2022, India's purchases of discounted Russian oil have increased sharply, a choice India has defended as necessary for energy security and for protecting consumers from high prices, while Western countries have criticised it in the context of Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

The relationship faces a structural tension. Russia's growing closeness to China, India's main strategic rival, sits uneasily with India's partnerships with the United States, Japan and Australia in the Indo-Pacific. India has sought to keep the Russia relationship on its own terms, abstaining on several United Nations resolutions on Ukraine while calling for dialogue and diplomacy. The question for the future is whether a partnership built in the Cold War can be sustained when its partners' other alliances pull in opposite directions.
takeaways: India and the Soviet Union signed a Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation in 1971; India and Russia declared a strategic partnership in 2000.
Defence, energy, science and space are central pillars, including joint development of the BrahMos missile and Russian reactors at Kudankulam.
Since 2022 India's purchases of Russian oil have increased, defended by India on energy security grounds amid Western criticism over Ukraine.
relevance: India-Russia relations show how a Cold War partnership adapts: defence and energy ties persist even as both countries' other alliances change.
question: Can India keep a privileged partnership with Russia while deepening security ties with the United States, or will it eventually have to choose?

title: India and the United States: the civil nuclear deal that changed the relationship
syllabus: GS II — India and its neighbourhood — relations; bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India's interests; effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India's interests, Indian Diaspora.
paragraphs: For much of the Cold War, India and the United States were, in the phrase often used by scholars, estranged democracies: they shared democratic systems but differed on non-alignment, nuclear policy and relations with the Soviet Union and Pakistan. The civil nuclear agreement of 2008 changed that pattern. It began with a joint statement by Prime Minister Manmohan Singh and President George W. Bush on 18 July 2005, under which India agreed to separate its civil and military nuclear facilities and place its civil facilities under International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards, while the United States agreed to work toward full civil nuclear cooperation.

The agreement required several steps. India produced a separation plan, concluded a safeguards agreement with the IAEA, and obtained a waiver from the Nuclear Suppliers Group on 6 September 2008, allowing civilian nuclear trade despite India not being a party to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. The United States Congress passed enabling legislation, and the bilateral agreement, known as the 123 Agreement after Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act, was signed on 10 October 2008 and entered into force on 6 December 2008.

The deal's significance went beyond nuclear energy. It ended a long period in which India was largely excluded from civilian nuclear commerce after its 1974 nuclear test, and it signalled American acceptance of India as a responsible nuclear power outside the Non-Proliferation Treaty framework. It also opened the way for closer defence, technology and strategic cooperation, including later agreements on logistics, communications and geospatial cooperation, and the elevation of the relationship to a comprehensive global strategic partnership.

The deal also had domestic costs. It was debated intensely in India, including over the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act of 2010, which suppliers argued made them liable in ways that discouraged investment, and over whether the agreement constrained India's strategic programme. For civil studies, the nuclear deal is a case study in how a single agreement can reset a bilateral relationship, while leaving implementation questions that last for years.
takeaways: The 2005 joint statement by Prime Minister Manmohan Singh and President George W. Bush set out separation of civil and military facilities under IAEA safeguards.
The Nuclear Suppliers Group granted India a waiver on 6 September 2008, and the 123 Agreement was signed on 10 October 2008 and entered into force on 6 December 2008.
The deal ended India's exclusion from civilian nuclear commerce after the 1974 test, despite India remaining outside the Non-Proliferation Treaty.
relevance: The civil nuclear deal shows how an exception can become a turning point: a single agreement reset a relationship that decades of diplomacy had not.
question: Was the nuclear deal primarily about energy, about strategic partnership, or about India's status in the global order?

title: The International Solar Alliance: India as founder of a solar institution
syllabus: GS II — India and its neighbourhood — relations; bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India's interests; effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India's interests, Indian Diaspora.
paragraphs: The International Solar Alliance, or ISA, was launched by India and France on 30 November 2015, alongside the Paris climate conference, known as COP21. Its original idea was to bring together sunshine countries, lying wholly or partly between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, to promote solar energy, reduce dependence on fossil fuels and mobilise finance and technology for solar deployment. Membership was later opened to all member states of the United Nations, following an amendment to its framework agreement.

The ISA is a treaty-based intergovernmental organisation, and its headquarters are at the National Institute of Solar Energy campus in Gwal Pahari, Gurugram, Haryana. It is described by the Government of India as the first treaty-based intergovernmental organisation headquartered in India. Its work includes aggregating demand for solar equipment, supporting solar applications such as solar pumps and mini-grids, building capacity and helping member countries develop solar policies and projects, with a focus on least developed countries and small island developing states.

The ISA has also promoted initiatives such as One Sun One World One Grid, which envisages connecting solar power across regions so that sunshine in one part of the world can meet demand in another, and a World Solar Bank concept for financing solar projects. These ideas illustrate a distinctive approach to climate diplomacy: rather than only negotiating emission targets, India has sought to create institutions that pool demand, lower costs and share technology, with India as host and co-founder.

The ISA's record is still being written. Its membership is large, but translating membership into financed projects, installed capacity and lower costs depends on finance, grid infrastructure and national policies that the ISA does not control. For civil studies, the ISA is useful as an example of institutional diplomacy: a country can shape global governance not only by joining existing bodies, but by founding a new one and hosting it.
takeaways: The ISA was launched by India and France on 30 November 2015 alongside the Paris climate conference, COP21, for sunshine countries between the Tropics.
Its headquarters are at the National Institute of Solar Energy campus in Gwal Pahari, Gurugram, Haryana, the first treaty-based intergovernmental organisation headquartered in India.
Membership was later opened to all UN member states, and the ISA promotes demand aggregation, capacity building and initiatives such as One Sun One World One Grid.
relevance: The ISA shows a different kind of climate leadership: founding and hosting an institution that pools demand and finance, rather than only negotiating targets.
question: Should climate diplomacy be judged by the institutions a country founds, or only by the emissions its own economy cuts?

title: The structure of the Indian economy: farm, factory and services
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilisation of resources, growth, development and employment.
paragraphs: India's economy is usually described in three sectors: agriculture and allied activities, industry, and services. The balance between them has changed sharply since independence. In 1950-51 agriculture produced more than half of national output, while services produced about a third. By 2023-24, according to the Economic Survey 2023-24, the shares of gross value added at current prices were 17.7 per cent for agriculture, 27.6 per cent for industry and 54.7 per cent for services. India therefore looks, on output, like a services-led economy.

Employment tells a different story. The Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) for 2023-24 found agriculture still employing about 46 per cent of workers, up from about 44 per cent in 2017-18. So nearly half the workforce produces less than a fifth of output, which means labour productivity in farming is far below the rest of the economy. This gap between output shares and employment shares is the single most important structural fact about the Indian economy: it explains low farm incomes, disguised unemployment in villages, and the pressure to create non-farm jobs.

Within services, the picture is also uneven. Trade, hotels, transport and communication employ large numbers, while finance, real estate, professional services and information technology produce much of the value but employ relatively few highly skilled workers. Industry includes manufacturing, mining, construction and utilities; construction has been a major absorber of rural workers moving out of farming, though often in informal, insecure jobs.

Economists describe this pattern as a partial structural transformation. Unlike the classic path, where workers moved from farms to factories and then to services, India moved from farms directly to services in output terms, while factory employment stayed modest. The policy question that follows is not whether services matter — they plainly do — but how manufacturing, agro-processing and labour-intensive services can absorb workers at better wages.
takeaways: Output has shifted decisively to services, but employment has not: agriculture still employs about 46 per cent of workers.
The gap between agriculture's output share (17.7 per cent) and its employment share is the core structural problem.
India's transformation skipped the usual factory stage, leaving job creation as the central challenge.
relevance: Sector shares link growth, employment, farm incomes and regional inequality in one frame.
question: Should India aim to raise manufacturing employment even if services grow faster, and what would that cost?

title: Five-Year Plans: how India planned its economy
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilisation of resources, growth, development and employment.
paragraphs: From 1951 to 2017 India ran its development effort through Five-Year Plans drawn up by the Planning Commission. The First Plan (1951-56) used a simple Harrod-Domar framework and gave priority to agriculture, irrigation and power after the food shortages of the late 1940s. The Second Plan (1956-61), built around the Mahalanobis model, shifted priority to heavy industry — steel, machinery and mining — on the argument that a poor country had to build its own capital goods base rather than depend on imports.

The Third Plan (1961-66) aimed at self-reliance and food self-sufficiency but was hit by droughts in 1965 and 1966 and by wars, and the plan system broke down. There followed a three-year Plan Holiday (1966-69) of annual plans, then a return to five-year planning. The Fifth Plan (1974-79) adopted the slogan of Garibi Hatao, removal of poverty, and the Sixth Plan (1980-85) pushed employment and poverty programmes. The Eighth Plan (1992-97) was the first framed after the 1991 economic reforms and accepted a larger role for markets and private investment.

Planning was never just a technical exercise. Plans set investment targets, allocated scarce foreign exchange and public funds, and licensed private industry through the industrial licensing system. Critics argue this produced shortages, inefficiency and corruption, and that targets were often missed. Supporters reply that planning built the steel plants, dams, universities and scientific institutions that later growth rested on, and that in a capital-scarce economy some coordination was unavoidable.

The Twelfth Plan (2012-17) was the last. The government decided to discontinue Five-Year Plans beyond March 2017, replacing the system with shorter strategy documents and a new institution, NITI Aayog. The planning era thus closed after twelve plans, leaving a debate that still shapes policy: how much should the state direct investment, and how much should it leave to markets?
takeaways: The First Plan prioritised food and agriculture; the Second shifted to heavy industry under the Mahalanobis model.
Plans allocated capital and foreign exchange, but licensing also bred inefficiency and shortages.
Five-Year Plans ended with the Twelfth Plan in March 2017.
relevance: Planning explains the origins of India's public sector, licensing system and regional investment patterns.
question: Was the Second Plan's bet on heavy industry a mistake, or a necessary foundation for later growth?

title: From Planning Commission to NITI Aayog
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilisation of resources, growth, development and employment.
paragraphs: The Planning Commission was set up by a government resolution on 15 March 1950, with the Prime Minister as chair, to formulate Five-Year Plans and allocate central assistance to states. It became the most powerful economic body in the country: its approval mattered for state plans, and its Gadgil formula governed how plan funds were shared. But it was never a constitutional body, and its top-down style — one plan, one set of targets for a diverse federation — drew growing criticism, including from chief ministers who said it treated states as supplicants.

In his Independence Day speech in 2014, Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the Commission would be replaced. It was dissolved in August 2014, and by a Cabinet Secretariat resolution dated 1 January 2015 the National Institution for Transforming India, NITI Aayog, took its place, again chaired by the Prime Minister. The change was presented as a shift from centralised planning to cooperative federalism: NITI Aayog's Governing Council includes all chief ministers and lieutenant governors, and states are meant to be partners rather than recipients of a plan handed down from Delhi.

The substantive difference is that NITI Aayog does not allocate funds. Financial transfers to states now run mainly through Finance Commission devolution and central schemes decided by ministries. NITI Aayog's work is advisory and evaluative: it publishes strategy documents, runs the Aspirational Districts programme for lagging districts, ranks states on indicators such as health and school education, and maintains an SDG India Index tracking progress on the Sustainable Development Goals.

Critics argue that without money to distribute, NITI Aayog has less leverage than the Planning Commission, and that rankings can oversimplify complex state realities. Supporters reply that advice, data and competition between states are more appropriate tools for a market economy, and that the old allocation power sat uneasily with fiscal federalism. Either way, the change marks a real institutional break: India no longer plans in five-year blocks from the Centre.
takeaways: The Planning Commission (1950-2014) made plans and allocated funds; NITI Aayog (from 1 January 2015) advises and evaluates.
NITI Aayog's Governing Council brings chief ministers into national policy-making, reflecting cooperative federalism.
Without fund allocation, NITI Aayog works through strategy, data, rankings and programmes such as Aspirational Districts.
relevance: The change from planning to a think-tank model defines how the Centre and states now negotiate development.
question: Does an advisory body without funds have enough influence to change state policy, or is that a strength?

title: The public sector and the mixed economy
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilisation of resources, growth, development and employment.
paragraphs: Independent India chose a mixed economy: private enterprise would continue, but the state would own and run the commanding heights — heavy industry, mining, banking, insurance and infrastructure. The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1948 reserved certain industries for the state, and the 1956 resolution widened that list and divided industries into three schedules: those reserved for the state, those where the state would increasingly dominate, and the rest left to private enterprise. The idea was that private capital was too scarce and too risk-averse to build steel plants, power stations and machine-building capacity on its own.

The public sector expanded rapidly. Steel plants at Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur, the oil and coal companies, heavy engineering firms and, after bank nationalisation, most of commercial banking came under state ownership. Fourteen major banks were nationalised in July 1969 and six more in 1980, with the stated aims of directing credit to agriculture and small industry and breaking the concentration of banking in a few business houses. Insurance had been nationalised earlier, life insurance in 1956 and general insurance in 1972.

By the 1980s the record was mixed. Public enterprises had built industrial capacity and technical skills, but many lost money, were overstaffed and slow to innovate, and their losses were covered from the budget. The 1991 reforms cut the list of industries reserved for the public sector to a handful — atomic energy, defence and railways among them — and opened most sectors to private and foreign investment. Disinvestment, selling part of government equity, became a regular budget tool, and better-performing firms were given greater autonomy under the Navratna and Maharatna schemes.

The debate continues. Supporters of a strong public sector point to its role in remote areas, strategic industries and counter-cyclical investment; critics point to inefficiency and the fiscal cost of loss-making units. The practical question today is less about ownership in principle than about governance: which enterprises serve a public purpose, and which would do better in private hands with regulation?
takeaways: The 1948 and 1956 policy resolutions reserved heavy industry and infrastructure for the state within a mixed economy.
Bank nationalisation in 1969 (14 banks) and 1980 (6 more) extended state control over credit.
After 1991, reservation shrank, disinvestment began, and autonomy schemes such as Navratna and Maharatna were introduced.
relevance: The public sector's rise and partial retreat explain India's industrial geography and its fiscal debates.
question: Should loss-making public enterprises be sold, reformed, or kept for strategic reasons — and who should decide?

title: 1991: the year India opened its economy
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilisation of resources, growth, development and employment.
paragraphs: By mid-1991 India faced a balance of payments crisis. Foreign exchange reserves had fallen to a level covering only a few weeks of imports, and the country was close to defaulting on external payments. The immediate causes were a high fiscal deficit, the Gulf War's effect on oil prices and remittances, and years of borrowing to sustain imports. The government of Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao, with Manmohan Singh as Finance Minister, responded with a package that changed the direction of economic policy.

In July 1991 the rupee was devalued in two steps, making exports cheaper and imports dearer. Industrial licensing was abolished for most industries, ending the system under which firms needed government permission to expand or start production. Import licensing was progressively dismantled and tariffs reduced. Foreign investment, long restricted, was welcomed in many sectors, and the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices regime was diluted. A new industrial policy, a new trade policy and a move toward a market-determined exchange rate followed in quick succession.

The results were substantial. Growth accelerated, moving above the roughly 3.5 per cent a year often called the Hindu rate of growth in earlier decades; foreign investment and trade expanded; and later shocks, such as the Asian financial crisis of 1997, were weathered without a payments collapse. Poverty, measured by the Tendulkar methodology, fell from 37.2 per cent in 2004-05 to 21.9 per cent in 2011-12, though that decline owed much to growth and to welfare programmes as well as to the reforms themselves.

The reforms also drew criticism that remains relevant. Agriculture and small industry, critics say, received too little attention; job creation in organised manufacturing stayed weak; and inequality widened. The 1991 package is best understood not as a single event but as a break: before it, the state directed industrial investment; after it, markets and private firms took the lead, with the state regulating and providing infrastructure and welfare.
takeaways: A payments crisis in 1991, with reserves covering only weeks of imports, forced a policy break under Rao and Manmohan Singh.
Devaluation, delicensing, trade liberalisation and opening to foreign investment replaced the licence regime.
Growth and trade expanded afterwards, but job creation and inequality remained contested outcomes.
relevance: 1991 is the dividing line between the planned economy and the market economy in Indian policy.
question: Were the 1991 reforms imposed by crisis, or were they a choice India would have made anyway?

title: Growth and GDP: what the headline number hides
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilisation of resources, growth, development and employment.
paragraphs: Gross domestic product, GDP, is the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year. Real GDP adjusts for inflation, so its growth rate is meant to show whether the economy produced more, not merely whether prices rose. India measures GDP at market prices and also reports gross value added, GVA, which is GDP minus indirect taxes plus subsidies, and which is the basis for the sector shares used in most analysis. The base year for the current series is 2011-12, meaning real growth is measured against prices of that year.

The headline growth figure is useful but limited. Real GDP grew by 8.2 per cent in 2023-24, according to the Economic Survey 2023-24, a strong performance by world standards. But GDP counts market production, not well-being: it does not subtract pollution or resource depletion, it values unpaid household work at zero, and it says nothing about who gains. A year of fast GDP growth can coincide with stagnant wages, falling farm incomes or rising inequality, which is why civil studies answers should pair GDP with employment, poverty and distribution data.

Per capita GDP is a better rough guide to average living standards, since it divides output by population, but it is still an average: it hides the gap between a software engineer in Bengaluru and a landless labourer in Bihar. International comparisons add another layer. At market exchange rates India is among the world's largest economies; at purchasing power parity, which adjusts for cheaper prices in India, its rank is higher still. Both measures are estimates, revised as methods improve, and rankings move with exchange rates as well as with real production.

GDP statistics in India have also been contested. The large informal sector is hard to measure, surveys are infrequent, and revisions can be large. The lesson is not to ignore GDP — it remains the best single summary of economic activity — but to treat it as one indicator among several, and to ask, for any growth claim, whose incomes grew, in which sectors, and in which states.
takeaways: GDP measures market production; real GDP growth adjusts for inflation, and GVA is the basis for sector shares.
Real GDP grew 8.2 per cent in 2023-24, but GDP ignores unpaid work, pollution and distribution.
Per capita figures and purchasing power parity comparisons change the picture, and all are estimates subject to revision.
relevance: GDP is the most quoted economic number in exams and in policy, so its limits must be understood, not just its definition.
question: If GDP rose 8 per cent while farm wages fell, would you call that a successful year — and for whom?

title: Inflation, interest rates and the Reserve Bank
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilisation of resources, growth, development and employment.
paragraphs: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, which reduces what money can buy. India tracks it mainly through the Consumer Price Index (CPI), which measures retail prices of a basket of goods and services, and the Wholesale Price Index (WPI), which measures prices at the wholesale stage. The two can move apart: food and fuel prices, which weigh heavily in household budgets, affect CPI more directly, while global commodity prices show up faster in WPI. For ordinary households, CPI inflation is the more relevant measure, and it is the one the Reserve Bank now targets.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI), set up in 1935 and nationalised in 1949, is the central bank: it issues currency, regulates banks, manages the government's borrowing and the exchange rate, and conducts monetary policy. Since 2016, monetary policy has followed a flexible inflation targeting framework, adopted by amending the RBI Act, 1934. The government and the RBI set a CPI inflation target of 4 per cent, with a tolerance band of plus or minus 2 percentage points, so inflation between 2 and 6 per cent is within the band. The target is reviewed every five years.

The policy rate is set by the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), a six-member body created in 2016 with three members from the RBI, including the Governor as chair, and three external members appointed by the government. Its main tool is the repo rate, the rate at which the RBI lends to banks. Raising the repo rate makes borrowing dearer and is meant to cool demand and prices; cutting it is meant to support growth. The trade-off is real: fighting inflation too hard can slow jobs and investment, while tolerating it too long erodes savings and hits the poor hardest, since food takes a larger share of poor households' spending.

Inflation targeting has supporters and critics. Supporters say a public target disciplines policy and anchors expectations. Critics say food price shocks, driven by monsoon and global prices, cannot be fixed by interest rates, and that the framework can put growth second. Either way, the framework changed Indian monetary policy from a discretionary, multiple-indicator approach to a transparent, target-based one — and every rate decision is now argued in public against a single number.
takeaways: CPI inflation, targeted at 4 per cent within a 2 to 6 per cent band since 2016, is the anchor of monetary policy.
The six-member Monetary Policy Committee sets the repo rate to steer inflation toward the target.
Food-driven inflation is hard for interest rates to control, which is the framework's main weakness.
relevance: Inflation links monetary policy, household budgets and the politics of interest rates.
question: Should the RBI raise rates to fight food inflation it cannot control, or accept a breach of the band?

title: The Union Budget and fiscal policy
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilisation of resources, growth, development and employment.
paragraphs: The Union Budget is the government's annual financial statement. Article 112 of the Constitution requires the President to lay an Annual Financial Statement before Parliament, showing estimated receipts and expenditure for the coming year. The Budget speech, the Finance Bill that changes taxes, and the demands for grants that Parliament votes on are the instruments through which fiscal policy — the use of taxation and spending to influence the economy — is made. State budgets follow the same pattern under Article 202.
