Fiscal policy has three broad aims: raising revenue, allocating it to priorities such as defence, infrastructure, health and welfare, and stabilising the economy across booms and busts. The key summary numbers are the revenue deficit, the gap between current receipts and current spending, and the fiscal deficit, the gap between total spending and total receipts excluding borrowing, which shows how much the government must borrow in the year. Persistent deficits add to public debt, and interest payments then consume a large share of revenue, limiting future choices.

The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003, was meant to discipline this process by setting deficit targets and requiring the government to explain deviations. Its targets have been revised and breached repeatedly — during the 2008 financial crisis, the pandemic, and at other stress points — which raises a genuine debate: should rules bind governments tightly, or should they bend when the economy needs support? The 2021 amendment path moved the framework toward a debt anchor rather than a single-year deficit number, but the tension between discipline and flexibility remains.

Two other features matter for civil studies. First, the Goods and Services Tax, launched on 1 July 2017, replaced a tangle of central and state indirect taxes with a single national framework, with a GST Council of the Centre and states deciding rates — a major experiment in shared tax sovereignty. Second, the Finance Commission, appointed every five years, recommends how central tax revenue is shared with states, which is the main channel of fiscal federalism. A budget, in short, is not only an accounts statement: it is where taxation, federalism and political priorities meet.
takeaways: Article 112 requires an Annual Financial Statement; the fiscal deficit measures borrowing needs in a year.
The FRBM Act, 2003, set deficit discipline, but its targets have been revised and breached in crises.
GST (from 1 July 2017) and Finance Commission devolution are the two great federal features of Indian public finance.
relevance: Budget numbers reveal priorities and constraints more honestly than speeches do.
question: Should deficit rules be strict even in a crisis, or should governments be free to borrow their way out of a downturn?

title: Trade, the rupee and the balance of payments
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilisation of resources, growth, development and employment.
paragraphs: The balance of payments records all transactions between India and the rest of the world. Its current account covers trade in goods and services, income from investments, and transfers such as remittances. Its capital account covers investment flows — foreign direct investment (FDI), portfolio investment, loans and banking capital. A current account deficit means India imports more goods, services and income than it exports, and it must be financed by capital inflows or by drawing on foreign exchange reserves.

India usually runs a deficit on merchandise trade — it imports more goods, especially oil, gold and electronics, than it exports — partly offset by a surplus on services, led by software and business services, and by remittances. According to World Bank estimates, India received about 129 billion dollars in remittances in 2024, the largest inflow of any country, which cushions the current account and supports millions of households. The overall balance therefore depends on several moving parts, not on goods trade alone.

The rupee's value is set mainly by the market, with the Reserve Bank intervening to curb excessive volatility rather than to fix a level — a managed float. A weaker rupee makes exports cheaper and imports dearer, which can help exporters but raises the cost of oil and other imports and can feed domestic inflation. A stronger rupee does the reverse. There is no permanently right level: exporters, importers, borrowers in foreign currency and households all prefer different outcomes, and the RBI's job is stability, not pleasing any one group.

The 1991 crisis is the cautionary tale. When reserves ran low, India had to borrow against its gold and accept an IMF programme. Since then, reserves have been built up as insurance, and the current account deficit has generally stayed within levels the economy could finance. The lesson for policy is that external balance is not about celebrating exports or fearing imports in isolation, but about whether deficits are financed by stable investment and used for productive capacity rather than consumption.
takeaways: The current account covers goods, services, income and remittances; the capital account covers investment flows.
A goods trade deficit is partly offset by services exports and by remittances of about 129 billion dollars in 2024.
The rupee follows a managed float, with the RBI smoothing volatility rather than fixing a rate.
relevance: External balance connects trade, the exchange rate, reserves and household incomes through remittances.
question: Is a current account deficit a sign of weakness, or can it be a healthy sign of investment-led growth?

title: Banks, credit and financial inclusion
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilisation of resources, growth, development and employment.
paragraphs: Banks sit at the centre of India's financial system because they take deposits from households and lend to farms, firms and governments. The Reserve Bank of India regulates them, sets key interest rates and acts as lender of last resort. Commercial banks include public sector banks, private banks and foreign banks, alongside cooperative banks and regional rural banks that serve rural areas. The State Bank of India, created in 1955 from the former Imperial Bank, is the largest bank, and the nationalisations of 1969 and 1980 put most of commercial banking in public hands.

A distinctive feature of Indian banking is priority sector lending: banks must direct a share of their lending to agriculture, small enterprises, weaker sections and other designated areas. The aim is to correct a market failure — left alone, banks prefer large, safe borrowers — but the record is mixed, since directed lending has also produced bad loans when appraisal was weak or politically influenced. Non-performing assets, loans on which borrowers have stopped paying, became a major problem in the 2010s, especially in public sector banks, and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, was created to resolve failed firms faster and recover value for creditors.

Financial inclusion means giving every household access to a bank account, payments, credit and insurance. The Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana, launched in 2014, opened basic bank accounts on a massive scale, and the spread of mobile phones and the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), launched in 2016, made digital payments cheap and instant for small transactions. The combination of Jan Dhan accounts, Aadhaar identity and mobile phones is often called the JAM trinity, and it underpins direct benefit transfers that send subsidies straight to beneficiaries' accounts.

Inclusion is not the same as usage. Accounts can lie dormant, small borrowers may still depend on moneylenders, and digital fraud is a growing risk. The deeper question is whether the financial system serves productive purposes — lending to farmers, small firms and first-time entrepreneurs at reasonable cost — rather than merely counting accounts. On that test, India has made real progress on access, while credit quality and last-mile delivery remain works in progress.
takeaways: The RBI regulates banks; nationalisation in 1969 and 1980 put most commercial banking in public hands.
Priority sector lending directs credit to agriculture and small firms, but has also contributed to bad loans.
Jan Dhan accounts (2014) and UPI (2016) expanded access and digital payments, though usage and credit quality lag.
relevance: Banking links savings, credit, subsidies and the fight against bad loans in one system.
question: Does opening an account count as inclusion if the holder still borrows from a moneylender?

title: How India counts poverty
syllabus: GS III — Inclusive growth and issues arising from it; issues relating to poverty and hunger. Also touches GS I: poverty and developmental issues.
paragraphs: Poverty is not a physical fact like height; it is measured against a line, and where the line is drawn changes who counts as poor. India has traditionally measured poverty by consumption expenditure: households are surveyed on what they spend, and those spending below a threshold are counted as poor. The threshold is the poverty line, and the share of people below it is the poverty ratio. Because the line is a judgement — what basket of goods is the minimum for a dignified life? — rival committees have produced different numbers from the same surveys.

The Tendulkar Committee, which reported in 2009, moved the line from a calorie-only basket to one covering food, education and health, and set monthly per capita lines of Rs 816 for rural areas and Rs 1,000 for urban areas at 2011-12 prices. On that basis the Planning Commission estimated poverty at 21.9 per cent in 2011-12, down from 37.2 per cent in 2004-05. The Rangarajan Committee, which reported in 2014, used a wider basket and higher lines — Rs 972 rural and Rs 1,407 urban — and estimated poverty at 29.5 per cent for the same year. The two figures describe the same country in the same year: the gap is entirely about method.

A second approach counts deprivations directly. The National Multidimensional Poverty Index, published by NITI Aayog, uses 12 indicators across health, education and living standards, and counts a household as poor if it is deprived in a weighted combination of them. Its discussion paper reported multidimensional poverty falling from 29.17 per cent in 2013-14 to 11.28 per cent in 2022-23, with about 24.82 crore people moving out of multidimensional poverty in that period. Critics note that the 2013-14 figure is an estimate built from earlier survey data and the 2022-23 figure a projection from the 2019-21 survey, so the numbers should be read as indicative, not as precise annual counts.

International comparisons add a third lens. The World Bank, using its extreme poverty line, estimated India's extreme poverty rate at 2.3 per cent in 2022-23, down from 16.2 per cent in 2011-12. No single measure settles the question of how many Indians are poor. Consumption lines miss deprivations in health and schooling; multidimensional indices involve judgement in weighting; and all measures depend on surveys that are infrequent and contested. The honest answer in civil studies is to state the measure, the year and the source — and to note that poverty has fallen on most measures, while remaining a mass phenomenon.
takeaways: The Tendulkar method put poverty at 21.9 per cent in 2011-12; Rangarajan's wider basket put it at 29.5 per cent for the same year.
The multidimensional index counts deprivations in health, education and living standards, not just spending.
The World Bank's extreme poverty estimate for India fell to 2.3 per cent in 2022-23, but all measures depend on method and survey data.
relevance: Poverty numbers drive welfare policy, so understanding how they are built is essential to judging claims about progress.
question: If two honest methods give 22 per cent and 30 per cent for the same year, which should a government use to target help?

title: Inequality: income, wealth and opportunity
syllabus: GS III — Inclusive growth and issues arising from it; issues relating to poverty and hunger. Also touches GS I: poverty and developmental issues.
paragraphs: Inequality asks a different question from poverty. Poverty asks whether people have enough; inequality asks how the total is shared. A country can reduce poverty while inequality rises, if the rich gain faster than the poor. That is why both measures matter, and why growth alone cannot answer the question of fairness. India illustrates the point: absolute poverty has fallen on most measures, while income and wealth concentration at the top has risen.

The World Inequality Report 2022, from the World Inequality Lab, estimated that in 2021 the top 10 per cent of Indians held 57 per cent of national income and the top 1 per cent held 22 per cent, while the bottom half held about 13 per cent. Wealth was more concentrated still: the report estimated the top 10 per cent owning about 65 per cent of wealth and the top 1 per cent about 33 per cent. These are estimates built from tax data, surveys and national accounts, and they are contested — India's income-tax base is narrow and surveys understate top incomes — but the direction is consistent with other evidence of rising top shares since the 1990s.

Inequality is not only about income. Opportunity gaps matter as much: children born in different states, castes, communities and families face very different schools, health care, nutrition and networks. The Human Development Report 2025 noted that inequality reduces India's human development index value by 30.7 per cent, one of the highest losses in the region, when the index is adjusted for inequality. Gender adds another dimension: the World Inequality Report estimated women's share of labour income in India at only about 18 per cent, among the lowest in the world, reflecting both low participation and low pay.

Policy responses divide along familiar lines. Progressive taxation, inheritance and wealth taxes, and better public services are favoured by those who see inequality as a brake on growth and democracy. Others argue that taxing success discourages investment and that the priority should be expanding opportunity — schooling, health and jobs — rather than compressing outcomes. The evidence for civil studies is that both matter: transfers and services can soften inequality, but without broad-based job creation and asset-building, the top-heavy pattern tends to reproduce itself.
takeaways: Income inequality is distinct from poverty: poverty can fall while the rich gain faster than the poor.
The World Inequality Report 2022 estimated the top 10 per cent holding 57 per cent of income and the bottom half 13 per cent in 2021.
Inequality of opportunity — schooling, health, gender — compounds inequality of income.
relevance: Inequality shapes politics, tax debates and the legitimacy of growth itself.
question: Should policy aim mainly at raising the bottom, or also at limiting the top — and does it matter which?

title: Unemployment and the way work is measured
syllabus: GS III — Inclusive growth and issues arising from it; issues relating to poverty and hunger. Also touches GS I: poverty and developmental issues.
paragraphs: India's official unemployment rate looks low by international standards, and that fact misleads many readers. The Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), run by the National Statistical Office, reported an unemployment rate of 3.2 per cent for people aged 15 and above in 2023-24, on the usual status basis, down from 6.0 per cent in 2017-18. The overall labour force participation rate rose from 49.8 per cent to 60.1 per cent over the same period, and the worker population ratio rose from 46.8 per cent to 58.2 per cent. These are real improvements, but they do not mean that good jobs are plentiful.

The reason is definitional. The usual status counts a person as employed if they worked for a substantial part of the year, even in low-paid, irregular or unpaid family work. Current weekly status, which asks about the previous week, and current daily status, which counts person-days, give different pictures, and since January 2025 the PLFS has also published monthly estimates on the weekly basis. Youth unemployment, at 10.2 per cent for ages 15-29 in 2023-24, was far above the overall rate, and urban youth unemployment was higher still. A low headline rate alongside high youth joblessness is the normal pattern in a labour-surplus economy.

Two other concepts matter more than the headline rate for India. Disguised unemployment means more people work on a farm or in a family shop than the work requires, so removing them would not reduce output. Underemployment means people work fewer hours or below their skills. Both are widespread in agriculture and informal services, and both explain why the employment problem feels worse than 3.2 per cent suggests: the issue is not only finding any work, but finding productive, secure, adequately paid work.

Measurement debates are therefore policy debates. If the headline rate is low, governments can claim success; if youth unemployment and informal, low-productivity work are counted, the challenge looks larger. The right approach is to read several indicators together — participation, worker ratio, youth unemployment, wages, and the share of regular salaried jobs — rather than treating any single rate as the verdict on the jobs market.
takeaways: PLFS put unemployment at 3.2 per cent in 2023-24 (usual status, age 15+), down from 6.0 per cent in 2017-18.
Youth unemployment was 10.2 per cent, far above the headline rate, and urban youth rates were higher.
Disguised unemployment and underemployment matter more than the headline rate in a labour-surplus economy.
relevance: The jobs debate turns on definitions, so a civil servant must know what each rate counts and what it misses.
question: Is a country with 3 per cent unemployment but mostly informal work a success story or a warning?

title: The informal economy: where most Indians work
syllabus: GS III — Inclusive growth and issues arising from it; issues relating to poverty and hunger. Also touches GS I: poverty and developmental issues.
paragraphs: Most Indians do not work in a registered firm with a written contract, paid leave and social security. They work on family farms, in small workshops, as street vendors, construction workers, domestic workers, drivers and shop helpers. The International Labour Organization's report on formalisation in Asia and the Pacific put informal employment in India at 88.8 per cent of total employment, close to 90 per cent, a level broadly unchanged since 2014. The informal economy is not a small fringe: it is where the great majority of Indians earn their living.

Two distinctions help. The informal sector means unregistered enterprises, typically small. Informal employment is wider: it also includes workers without social protection inside formal firms, such as contract workers in a factory or a delivery rider classified as a partner rather than an employee. That is why formalisation of firms alone does not solve the problem: a worker can be in a formal company and still lack a contract, pension or paid sick leave.

Informal work has advantages that explain its persistence. It absorbs labour quickly, needs little capital, and lets people combine farming with seasonal wage work or a small trade. But the costs are heavy: incomes are volatile, bargaining power is weak, workplace safety is poor, and shocks such as illness, a bad monsoon or a pandemic can wipe out savings. Women and young workers are disproportionately informal, and informal workers were hit hardest by the 2020 lockdown, when many lost work overnight and had to return to their villages.

Policy has tried several routes: simplifying registration, extending social security through new laws and the e-Shram database, giving street vendors credit, and recognising gig and platform workers in the Code on Social Security, 2020. Progress has been slow, and the ILO's finding that informality has stayed near 90 per cent is a warning against easy claims. The real test is not how many firms register, but how many workers gain a contract, a pension and protection against risk.
takeaways: About 90 per cent of Indian workers are informally employed, a share broadly unchanged since 2014 according to the ILO.
Informal employment is wider than the informal sector: it includes unprotected workers inside formal firms.
Informal work absorbs labour flexibly but leaves workers exposed to income shocks, illness and old age without cover.
relevance: Informality is the frame within which poverty, gender, migration and social security must all be understood.
question: Should policy formalise firms, protect workers directly, or both — and what happens to jobs if formalisation raises costs?

title: Skills and the demographic dividend
syllabus: GS III — Inclusive growth and issues arising from it; issues relating to poverty and hunger. Also touches GS I: poverty and developmental issues.
paragraphs: India is a young country. Its median age is under 30, and the share of the population in the working ages — roughly 15 to 64 — is still rising, while the share of children falls and the share of older people is still comparatively small. Economists call this a demographic dividend: when the working-age share rises, output per person can grow faster, because more people earn relative to those who depend on them. But a dividend is an opportunity, not a guarantee. It pays off only if working-age people are educated, healthy and able to find productive work; otherwise a large young population becomes a strain on jobs, services and politics.

The education and training system is the first link. India has expanded schooling sharply, but learning outcomes remain weak, as later notes in this series show, and employers frequently report that graduates lack job-ready skills. The Skill India Mission, launched in 2015, and the Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY), which funds short-term training, were designed to close this gap, alongside Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs) and apprenticeship programmes. The record is mixed: enrolments have been large, but placement and wage gains have often been modest, and training has not always matched local employer demand.

The second link is jobs. Each year millions of young people enter the labour force, and the economy must create work at a pace and quality that matches their aspirations. Manufacturing, which absorbed young workers in East Asia's demographic dividend, has grown more slowly in India, and much new work is in informal services. The result is a paradox visible in the data: rising participation alongside complaints of educated unemployment, as graduates queue for government jobs or accept work below their qualifications.

The window will not stay open forever. As fertility falls, the population will age, and the dependency ratio will rise again in the coming decades. Countries that used their dividend well — through schooling, health, women's employment and labour-intensive growth — converted it into lasting prosperity. Those that did not faced a large, frustrated youth cohort. India's dividend is therefore best read as a deadline: the next two decades are when the investments that determine whether it pays off must be made.
takeaways: India's working-age share is still rising, offering a demographic dividend — but only if young workers are skilled and employed.
Skill India (2015) and PMKVY expanded training, but placement and wage gains have often been modest.
The window is time-limited: population ageing will raise dependency again in the coming decades.
relevance: The dividend links population, education, jobs and growth in a single long-run story.
question: Is India's youth bulge an asset, a risk, or both — and what decides which?

title: Women and work in India
syllabus: GS III — Inclusive growth and issues arising from it; issues relating to poverty and hunger. Also touches GS I: poverty and developmental issues.
paragraphs: For decades, one of the most striking facts about India's labour market was how few women were counted as working. That has changed sharply in recent data. The Periodic Labour Force Survey reported female labour force participation for women aged 15 and above rising from 23.3 per cent in 2017-18 to 41.7 per cent in 2023-24, with the female worker population ratio rising from 22.0 per cent to 40.3 per cent. The increase was driven mainly by rural women, and male participation in the same year was far higher, at about 78.8 per cent, leaving a gap of more than 35 percentage points.

The headline rise needs careful reading. Analysts, including a UNFPA analysis of the same survey, note that much of the increase is concentrated in informal, self-employed and unpaid family work, particularly in agriculture, where the share of rural women working in farming rose from 71.1 per cent in 2018-19 to 76.9 per cent in 2023-24. Such work is real — it feeds families and produces output — but it is often unpaid, insecure and without social protection, and it may partly reflect distress: when household incomes are squeezed, more family members, including women, take up available work.

The barriers to better-paid, formal work for women are well documented. Unpaid care work — childcare, elder care, cooking, fetching water and fuel — falls mostly on women and limits the hours and distance they can work. Safety on transport and at workplaces, the absence of childcare, and social norms about suitable work all narrow choices, especially in towns and cities, where female participation remains much lower than in villages. Legal protections exist, including the Maternity Benefit Act, amended in 2017 to provide 26 weeks of paid maternity leave in covered establishments, but most women work outside the establishments the law reaches.

The stakes are large. Raising women's participation in quality work is not only a fairness issue: it raises household incomes, improves children's health and schooling, and adds to national output. Policy levers include childcare, safe transport, skills training, credit for women entrepreneurs, and enforcement of workplace safety. The test of progress is not only the participation rate, but the share of women in regular salaried work, in higher-paying occupations, and in decision-making roles.
takeaways: Female labour force participation rose from 23.3 per cent (2017-18) to 41.7 per cent (2023-24), driven by rural women.
Much of the rise is in informal, self-employed and unpaid family work, especially in agriculture.
Care burdens, safety, transport and norms still limit women's access to formal, better-paid work.
relevance: Women's work links growth, poverty, demography and gender equality in a single indicator.
question: Should a rise in unpaid family work count as empowerment, distress, or both — and how would you tell?

title: Self-employment, microfinance and small enterprise
syllabus: GS III — Inclusive growth and issues arising from it; issues relating to poverty and hunger. Also touches GS I: poverty and developmental issues.
paragraphs: A large share of Indians are not employees at all: they run a small farm, a shop, a repair unit, a food stall or a tailoring business, or they work as own-account workers. Self-employment is therefore not a residual category but the main form of work for much of the country, and policy for jobs is, in large part, policy for small enterprise. The micro, small and medium enterprises (MSME) sector illustrates the scale: it comprises more than 6.3 crore enterprises and, by official estimates, contributes nearly 30 per cent of GDP, roughly 45 per cent of manufacturing output and about 45 per cent of exports.

Small enterprises face three chronic constraints: credit, markets and skills. Banks prefer larger, collateral-backed borrowers, so small firms have long relied on informal lenders at high cost. Self-help groups (SHGs) — small collectives, mostly of women, who save together and lend to members — became a major answer from the 1990s, linked to banks and later supported through the National Rural Livelihoods Mission, launched in 2011. Microfinance institutions, which lend small sums without collateral, expanded access further, but also drew criticism for high interest rates and aggressive recovery in some cases.

The government has layered several schemes on this base. The Pradhan Mantri MUDRA Yojana, launched in 2015, refinances loans to small borrowers through banks and microfinance institutions, with loans classified as Shishu (up to Rs 50,000), Kishore (up to Rs 5 lakh) and Tarun (up to Rs 10 lakh). Stand-Up India, also from 2016, targets bank loans for Scheduled Caste, Scheduled Tribe and women entrepreneurs. Digital payments and e-commerce platforms have since given small sellers wider markets, though they also expose them to new competition and platform fees.

The debate is about quality, not just credit. Most micro-enterprises stay tiny, employ few people beyond the family, and pay low incomes. Turning self-employment into productive enterprise requires reliable power, transport, market linkages, timely payments from buyers, and skills — the ecosystem around the firm, not only a loan. Microfinance can relieve a cash crunch, but it cannot by itself create a growth business, and when loans fund consumption rather than investment, debt can become a trap rather than a ladder.
takeaways: More than 6.3 crore MSMEs contribute nearly 30 per cent of GDP and about 45 per cent of exports.
Self-help groups and microfinance widened credit access, but high costs and over-indebtedness are real risks.
MUDRA (2015) grades small loans as Shishu, Kishore and Tarun, but enterprise growth needs markets and infrastructure too.
relevance: Self-employment is the default form of work in India, so enterprise policy is employment policy.
question: Does microcredit create entrepreneurs, or does it mainly help people survive in work that pays too little?

title: Social security for unorganised workers
syllabus: GS III — Inclusive growth and issues arising from it; issues relating to poverty and hunger. Also touches GS I: poverty and developmental issues.
paragraphs: Social security in India was built for the organised minority: employees of government, public enterprises and larger firms are covered by the Employees' Provident Fund for retirement savings, the Employees' State Insurance for health care, gratuity on leaving service, and maternity benefits. The great majority of workers — farm labourers, construction workers, domestic workers, street vendors, gig workers — fell outside these schemes, because they have no single employer to contribute, no fixed workplace, and often no written contract.

The first step toward covering them was identification. The e-Shram portal, launched on 26 August 2021, created a national database of unorganised workers seeded with Aadhaar, giving each registered worker a Universal Account Number. By November 2025, over 31.38 crore unorganised workers had registered, including over 5 lakh gig and platform workers, and the portal was linked to schemes such as pensions, insurance and food security so that a worker could access benefits in one place. Registration, however, is not the same as coverage: being listed does not guarantee a pension or health cover.

The legal framework changed with the Code on Social Security, 2020, which consolidated nine earlier laws and, for the first time, defined gig workers and platform workers in law. The Code came into force on 21 November 2025, alongside the other three labour codes, and provides for schemes covering life and disability cover, accident insurance, health and maternity benefits and old-age protection for gig and platform workers, with contributions envisaged from aggregators. In October 2026 the government notified National Social Security Boards for unorganised workers and for gig and platform workers to recommend and monitor such schemes.

The challenges are funding, portability and enforcement. Contributions must be collected from many small employers and platforms; benefits must follow a migrant worker across states and jobs; and schemes must be simple enough for workers with low literacy and patchy connectivity to use. NITI Aayog estimated 7.7 million gig workers in 2020-21, projected to reach 23.5 million by 2029-30, which shows how fast the uncovered frontier is growing. Social security for unorganised workers is therefore one of the largest unfinished tasks of Indian welfare policy.
takeaways: Organised workers have provident fund, insurance and gratuity; most unorganised workers historically had none of these.
e-Shram (launched 26 August 2021) registered over 31.38 crore unorganised workers by November 2025.
The Code on Social Security, 2020, in force from 21 November 2025, defines gig and platform workers and provides for their schemes.
relevance: Social security determines whether illness, accident or old age means destitution for most Indian workers.
question: Who should pay for gig workers' social security — the platform, the consumer, the state, or all three?

title: Regional gaps: why some states surge ahead
syllabus: GS III — Inclusive growth and issues arising from it; issues relating to poverty and hunger. Also touches GS I: poverty and developmental issues.
paragraphs: India's states differ enormously in income, health and schooling. Southern and western states such as Goa, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Gujarat have higher per capita incomes, better infrastructure and stronger industrial bases, while large northern and eastern states such as Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Jharkhand lag on most indicators, despite faster population growth. These gaps have persisted for decades and, on some measures, widened as the richer states grew faster after 1991. Regional inequality is therefore a central fact of Indian development, not a footnote.

History explains part of the pattern. Colonial investment concentrated in port cities and their hinterlands; land tenure systems differed, with zamindari areas faring worse than ryotwari areas in later studies; and early industrial policy located large public plants in a few states. Geography matters too: coastal states trade more easily, while landlocked and flood- or drought-prone regions face higher costs. Governance adds a third layer: states that invested early in primary schooling, public health and administration — Kerala's social investments and Tamil Nadu's public health system are the classic examples — built human capital that later attracted investment.

The Constitution provides two correctives. The Finance Commission recommends transfers of central tax revenue to states, with weight given to population, income distance, area and demographic performance, so that poorer states receive more per person from the divisible pool. Centrally sponsored schemes fund health, schooling, rural roads and housing across states, and programmes such as the Aspirational Districts programme target the most lagging districts rather than whole states. Special category status, once given to hill and border states, offered higher central assistance, though the Finance Commission framework has since changed how such support is structured.

Migration is the other equaliser, and it is double-edged. Workers from poorer states build the cities and industries of richer ones and send money home, which raises household incomes in source areas. But it also drains skilled workers and leaves source states dependent on remittances rather than local jobs. Closing regional gaps requires both: transfers and investment in lagging regions, and the freedom for people to move — while ensuring that destination cities provide housing, schooling and health care to migrants rather than treating them as temporary outsiders.
takeaways: Income, health and schooling gaps between states are large and persistent, and have widened on some measures since 1991.
History, geography and early social investment explain much of the pattern; Kerala and Tamil Nadu are classic cases.
Finance Commission transfers, central schemes and migration all redistribute, but none alone closes the gap.
relevance: Regional inequality shapes federal politics, migration and the design of every national scheme.
question: Should poorer states get more central funds per person indefinitely, or should transfers reward performance?

title: Migration, remittances and the moving workforce
syllabus: GS III — Inclusive growth and issues arising from it; issues relating to poverty and hunger. Also touches GS I: poverty and developmental issues.
paragraphs: Migration is one of the largest forces shaping India, and one of the least counted. The Census of 2011 recorded 45.36 crore internal migrants by place of last residence — about 37 per cent of the population — including both inter-state and intra-state movers. Most moved within their own state, and most migrants are women, largely for marriage or family reasons; the Economic Survey estimated the migrant workforce at roughly 20 per cent of the workforce, over 10 crore people, in 2016. Circular migration — workers who move seasonally between village and city without permanently relocating — is large but poorly captured by surveys that assume a fixed home.

People move for work, education, marriage, and safety, and the flows run in many directions: from villages to towns, from poorer states such as Uttar Pradesh and Bihar to industrial and construction centres, and from small towns to metros. The 2020 lockdown made the scale visible, when millions of workers tried to return to their villages after losing urban work overnight, revealing how little protection — housing, food, health cover — migrants had in destination cities. Since then, portability measures have mattered more: One Nation One Ration Card, which lets ration card holders draw subsidised grain anywhere in the country, is the most important example.

International migration adds a second flow. Indians working abroad — in the Gulf, North America, Europe and elsewhere — send money home, and the World Bank estimated remittances to India at about 129 billion dollars in 2024, the largest of any country. Remittances raise household consumption, fund schooling and housing, and cushion the balance of payments. They also create dependence: some districts rely heavily on Gulf incomes, and return migration after oil downturns or conflicts can strand workers without savings or support.

Policy for migrants is split between governments: source states lose workers, destination states gain labour but bear service costs, and neither fully owns the migrant's welfare. Voting rights are a further gap, since migrants usually remain registered in their home constituency and cannot easily vote where they work. The core challenge is portability — of food, health cover, schooling, banking and political voice — so that moving for work does not mean losing citizenship in practice.
takeaways: Census 2011 counted 45.36 crore internal migrants, about 37 per cent of the population, mostly within states.
One Nation One Ration Card makes food entitlements portable, a key reform after the 2020 lockdown exposed migrant vulnerability.
Remittances of about 129 billion dollars in 2024 made India the world's largest recipient.
relevance: Migration connects rural and urban India, and tests whether welfare follows the worker.
question: Should migrants be able to vote where they work, and what would that change in city politics?

title: India's health system: public, private and in between
syllabus: GS II — Issues relating to development and management of Social Sector/Services relating to Health, Education, Human Resources. Also touches GS III: Indian Economy — growth, development and employment.
paragraphs: India's health system is a mix. The public system is organised in three tiers: sub-centres and primary health centres for villages and small towns, community health centres for blocks, and district hospitals and medical colleges for referrals. The National Health Mission, formed by merging the National Rural Health Mission (launched 2005) and the National Urban Health Mission under one umbrella in 2013, funds much of this network and supports a large cadre of ASHA community health workers who link villages to clinics. Health is primarily a state subject, so the quality of this network varies greatly between states.

The private sector, however, provides most outpatient care and a large share of hospital care, ranging from corporate hospitals in metros to single-doctor clinics and informal practitioners in villages. Households pay a high share of health costs out of pocket, which means a serious illness can push a family into debt — the problem economists call catastrophic health expenditure. Public spending on health has historically been low compared with other large economies, and shortages of doctors, nurses, drugs and equipment in public facilities push even poor patients toward private care.

The system also faces a double burden of disease. Infectious diseases, maternal and child conditions and undernutrition remain major problems, especially in poorer states, while non-communicable diseases — heart disease, diabetes, cancers and chronic lung disease — now cause a growing share of deaths as lifestyles, diets and life expectancy change. A health system built for infections and childbirth must now also manage lifelong conditions that need regular medicines, screening and follow-up.

Reform debates therefore focus on three questions: how much public money should go to health and to what — primary care, hospitals, or insurance; how to regulate private providers on price and quality; and how to staff rural facilities. The Ayushman Bharat programme, covered in the next note, is the largest recent attempt to answer the financing question, but the underlying structure — a thin public system alongside a large, unevenly regulated private sector — remains the defining feature of Indian health care.
takeaways: Public care runs in three tiers, funded largely through the National Health Mission (rural mission from 2005, merged in 2013).
Private providers deliver most outpatient care, and out-of-pocket payments can push families into debt.
India faces a double burden: infectious and maternal conditions plus rising non-communicable disease.
relevance: Health system design decides who gets care, who pays, and whether illness means impoverishment.
question: Should public money expand free primary care, or insure hospital treatment — and can it do both?

title: Ayushman Bharat and the push for health cover
syllabus: GS II — Issues relating to development and management of Social Sector/Services relating to Health, Education, Human Resources. Also touches GS III: Indian Economy — growth, development and employment.
paragraphs: Ayushman Bharat, launched in 2018, is India's largest health programme. It has two parts. The first is a network of Health and Wellness Centres, now called Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, which upgrade sub-centres and primary health centres to provide comprehensive primary care, including screening for common conditions, maternal and child services, and free essential medicines and diagnostics. The second, and better known, part is the Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY), a health assurance scheme for hospital care.

PM-JAY was launched on 23 September 2018 at Ranchi, Jharkhand. It provides cashless cover of up to Rs 5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary hospitalisation, for about 10.74 crore poor and vulnerable families — roughly 50 crore people — identified from the Socio-Economic Caste Census on deprivation and occupational criteria. Beneficiaries can use empanelled public and private hospitals across the country, and the cover is on a family floater basis, so any member can use it up to the limit. From 2024 the scheme was extended to all citizens aged 70 and above, regardless of income.

The design tries to solve a specific problem: hospital bills are the largest cause of catastrophic health spending. By paying hospitals directly, the scheme aims to stop families selling assets or borrowing for surgery or serious illness. Early evaluations found large numbers of hospital admissions funded, but also unevenness: empanelment and usage vary by state, some hospitals are accused of overcharging or unnecessary procedures, and the poorest and most remote households are the hardest to enrol and inform.

Ayushman Bharat does not replace the public health system, and its critics note that hospital insurance cannot fix weak primary care, staff shortages or drug supply. Its supporters reply that it is the first scheme of this scale to give poor households a portable, cashless entitlement, and that its data on admissions and costs is itself a tool for planning. For civil studies, the key point is the distinction between health cover and health care: insurance pays the bill, but only a functioning system of clinics, staff and medicines delivers the treatment.
takeaways: PM-JAY, launched 23 September 2018, gives up to Rs 5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary hospitalisation.
It originally covered about 10.74 crore poor and vulnerable families, and from 2024 all citizens aged 70 and above.
Hospital insurance reduces catastrophic bills but cannot by itself fix primary care or staffing.
relevance: Ayushman Bharat is the main test of whether insurance can protect poor households from medical costs.
question: Should health budgets prioritise hospital insurance or free primary clinics — and what evidence would settle it?

title: School education and the Right to Education
syllabus: GS II — Issues relating to development and management of Social Sector/Services relating to Health, Education, Human Resources. Also touches GS III: Indian Economy — growth, development and employment.
paragraphs: School education in India is vast: hundreds of millions of children, millions of teachers, and schools run by central and state governments, local bodies, aided institutions and private managements. The Constitution originally placed free and compulsory education for children up to 14 in the Directive Principles, as a goal rather than an enforceable right. That changed with the 86th Constitutional Amendment, 2002, which inserted Article 21A, making free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 a fundamental right, and the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009, which gave it legal shape.

The RTE Act came into force on 1 April 2010. It requires free and compulsory elementary education in a neighbourhood school, bars capitation fees and screening of children at admission, and lays down norms for pupil-teacher ratios, classrooms, toilets, drinking water and playgrounds. Its best-known provision requires private unaided schools to reserve 25 per cent of entry-level seats for children from economically weaker sections and disadvantaged groups, with the government reimbursing the cost. It also originally barred detention — no child could be failed up to Class 8 — though a 2019 amendment allowed states to reintroduce examinations and detention in Classes 5 and 8 with safeguards.

Enrolment is now near-universal at primary level, but the system faces three deeper problems. First, learning levels are low, as the ASER surveys show and a later note discusses. Second, quality varies sharply: teacher vacancies and absenteeism, multi-grade classrooms and weak early-grade teaching affect poor and rural children most. Third, the school system is stratified — government schools, low-fee private schools and elite private schools offer very different experiences, and the 25 per cent quota, while important, reaches only a fraction of children.

The National Education Policy, 2020, added a new structure — 5+3+3+4, replacing the 10+2 system — and a focus on foundational literacy and numeracy, mother tongue or local language as medium in early years, and vocational exposure. Whether these changes raise learning depends less on the structure than on teacher training, classroom materials and accountability at the school level. For civil studies, the RTE story is a case study in turning a constitutional promise into a justiciable right — and in the gap between a right on paper and a classroom that delivers.
takeaways: Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) made education for ages 6-14 a fundamental right; the RTE Act, 2009, took effect on 1 April 2010.
The Act mandates free neighbourhood schooling, infrastructure norms, and 25 per cent private-school seats for weaker sections.
Enrolment is near-universal, but learning quality and stratification between school types remain the core problems.
relevance: The RTE Act shows how a directive principle became an enforceable right — and how far rights alone can go.
question: Does reserving 25 per cent of private seats help the system, or does it let the state off the hook for its own schools?

title: Higher education: expansion and quality
syllabus: GS II — Issues relating to development and management of Social Sector/Services relating to Health, Education, Human Resources. Also touches GS III: Indian Economy — growth, development and employment.
paragraphs: India has one of the world's largest higher education systems, with more than a thousand universities and tens of thousands of colleges, enrolling tens of millions of students. Expansion has been rapid since independence, when there were only a few dozen universities, and it accelerated after 2000 with private universities and colleges. The gross enrolment ratio in higher education — the share of the 18-23 age group enrolled — is under a third, well below developed countries, and the National Education Policy, 2020, sets a target of 50 per cent by 2035.

The system is highly varied. At the top are the Indian Institutes of Technology, the Indian Institutes of Management, the All India Institute of Medical Sciences and a few central universities with strong research and global recognition. Below them are hundreds of state universities and affiliated colleges that teach most students with limited funds, large classes and little research. Regulation has been fragmented across bodies such as the University Grants Commission, set up in 1956, the All India Council for Technical Education and the Medical Council's successor, the National Medical Commission, and the NEP proposes a single umbrella regulator, the Higher Education Commission of India, which remains a proposal rather than a reality.

Three problems dominate debate. First, access is uneven: students from poorer families, rural areas and disadvantaged communities are under-represented in the best institutions, despite reservations for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes in public institutions. Second, quality is uneven: many colleges lack qualified faculty, laboratories and libraries, and degrees do not reliably signal skills to employers. Third, research output is concentrated in a few institutions, while most colleges are teaching-only.

The policy direction is toward autonomy with accountability: graded autonomy for good colleges, a four-year multidisciplinary undergraduate degree with multiple entry and exit points under NEP 2020, and more vocational and online options. The open question is whether expansion and quality can rise together. Adding seats is easy; building faculty, laboratories and academic standards is slow, and the gap between the two is where most students experience the system.
takeaways: India's higher education system is among the world's largest, but enrolment of the 18-23 age group is under a third.
The NEP 2020 targets 50 per cent enrolment by 2035 and proposes a single regulator, the Higher Education Commission of India.
Access, quality and research are concentrated unevenly, with most students in under-funded affiliated colleges.
relevance: Higher education decides who gets skilled jobs and who produces research, so its inequalities compound over a lifetime.
question: Should India expand enrolment fast, or fix quality first — and can it afford to choose?

title: Nutrition and the first thousand days
syllabus: GS II — Issues relating to development and management of Social Sector/Services relating to Health, Education, Human Resources. Also touches GS III: Indian Economy — growth, development and employment.
paragraphs: Nutrition is where health, education and poverty meet. A child who is undernourished in the first thousand days — from conception to the second birthday — suffers damage that later schooling and feeding cannot fully reverse: stunted growth, weaker immunity, and reduced learning capacity. India's numbers show how large the problem remains. The National Family Health Survey-5 (2019-21) found 35.5 per cent of children under five stunted (short for their age), 19.3 per cent wasted (thin for their height) and 32.1 per cent underweight, with about two-thirds of children aged 6-59 months anaemic.

The causes are multiple, which is why no single programme can fix them. Poor maternal nutrition and early marriage affect birth weight; exclusive breastfeeding for six months is not universal; complementary feeding after six months is often inadequate — NFHS-5 found only about 11 per cent of children aged 6-23 months receiving a minimally adequate diet; repeated infections from unsafe water and poor sanitation waste nutrients; and poverty limits dietary diversity, since pulses, eggs, milk and vegetables cost more than cereals. Stunting has fallen over decades, from 52 per cent in 1992-93 to 35.5 per cent in 2019-21, but wasting has barely improved.

India's institutional response runs through the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS), launched in 1975, which provides supplementary nutrition, preschool education, immunisation and health check-ups through Anganwadi centres across the country. POSHAN Abhiyaan, launched on 8 March 2018 as the National Nutrition Mission, set targets to reduce stunting, undernutrition, anaemia and low birth weight, and introduced technology-based monitoring of Anganwadi services. The mid-day meal programme in schools, now PM POSHAN, adds a cooked meal for schoolchildren, supporting both nutrition and attendance.

The debate is about delivery and measurement. Anganwadi coverage is wide, but food quality, worker training and regular supply vary; newer administrative data from the Poshan Tracker, which covers only Anganwadi-enrolled children, shows lower malnutrition figures than NFHS-5, and the two cannot be directly compared. The lesson for civil studies is to distinguish a survey of the whole population from a register of programme beneficiaries — and to judge nutrition policy by outcomes in children's bodies, not by meals served or centres opened.
takeaways: NFHS-5 (2019-21): 35.5 per cent of under-fives stunted, 19.3 per cent wasted, 32.1 per cent underweight.
The first thousand days are critical: damage from early undernutrition is hard to reverse later.
ICDS (1975) and POSHAN Abhiyaan (2018) are the main programmes, but delivery quality and measurement vary.
relevance: Nutrition links maternal health, sanitation, poverty and learning in a single outcome.
question: Should nutrition policy prioritise food supplements, or the sanitation and maternal health that let food work?

title: Sanitation, immunisation and disease control
syllabus: GS II — Issues relating to development and management of Social Sector/Services relating to Health, Education, Human Resources. Also touches GS III: Indian Economy — growth, development and employment.
paragraphs: Two of the cheapest ways to save lives are also the oldest public health tools: clean surroundings and vaccines. Sanitation prevents the faecal contamination that spreads diarrhoea, worms and other infections, which in turn cause malnutrition and child deaths. Immunisation protects against diseases such as measles, diphtheria, tetanus and polio before children ever fall ill. Both require the state to reach every household, repeatedly, which is why they are good tests of state capacity.

The Swachh Bharat Mission, launched on 2 October 2014, made toilet construction and open defecation free status its central goals, with a large behaviour-change campaign alongside construction. In October 2019 the government declared rural India open defecation free, though independent surveys found continued open defecation in many areas and raised questions about toilet usage, water availability and maintenance. The mission's second phase shifted focus to solid and liquid waste management and to sustaining usage — an admission that building a toilet and using it are different achievements.

On immunisation, India's Universal Immunisation Programme provides free vaccines against a schedule of childhood diseases, and Mission Indradhanush, launched in December 2014, targeted districts and children missed by routine rounds. The most celebrated success is polio: India was certified polio-free by the World Health Organization in March 2014, after the last wild poliovirus case in January 2011, achieved through repeated national immunisation days reaching hundreds of millions of children. Routine immunisation coverage has risen, but gaps remain in remote, migrant and urban slum populations.

The common lesson is that coverage figures hide usage and quality. A toilet counted as built may not be used; a vaccine dose recorded may not complete the schedule; and disease control depends on cold chains, trained workers and community trust as much as on budgets. Sanitation and immunisation are also equity issues: the households missed by both are usually the poorest, the most remote, and the least served by the health system in general.
takeaways: Swachh Bharat (from 2 October 2014) built toilets at scale; declared open defecation free status in 2019 is contested on usage.
Mission Indradhanush (December 2014) chased missed children; India was certified polio-free in March 2014.
Coverage is not use: toilets unused and incomplete vaccine schedules limit real disease control.
relevance: Sanitation and immunisation are the clearest tests of whether a state can reach every household.
question: Is a toilet that is built but not used a success, a failure, or something in between — and who should be counted?

title: Human development: beyond income
syllabus: GS II — Issues relating to development and management of Social Sector/Services relating to Health, Education, Human Resources. Also touches GS III: Indian Economy — growth, development and employment.
paragraphs: In 1990 the United Nations Development Programme published the first Human Development Report, introducing the Human Development Index (HDI). The idea, developed by Mahbub ul Haq and grounded in Amartya Sen's capability approach, was that development should be judged by what people can be and do — live a long and healthy life, be educated, and enjoy a decent standard of living — not by income alone. The HDI combines three dimensions: life expectancy at birth, education (mean and expected years of schooling), and gross national income per capita, into a single score between 0 and 1.

India's trajectory on the HDI shows real progress with clear limits. In the Human Development Report 2025, India ranked 130 out of 193 countries, up from 133 in the previous edition, with its HDI value rising from 0.676 in 2022 to 0.685 in 2023, remaining in the medium human development category and approaching the 0.700 threshold for high human development. Life expectancy rose from 58.6 years in 1990 to 72 years in 2023, and schooling and incomes also improved over the same period. These gains track the poverty and health improvements described elsewhere in this series.

The HDI has well-known limits, and the UNDP itself publishes adjustments that reveal them. When adjusted for inequality, India's HDI value falls by 30.7 per cent, one of the highest losses in the region, showing how unevenly health, education and income are shared. The index also says nothing directly about political freedom, environmental sustainability, gender violence or the quality of work — a country can raise its HDI while suppressing dissent or degrading its environment. Complementary measures exist, including the Gender Development Index and the Multidimensional Poverty Index, but none captures everything.

For civil studies, the HDI's value is as a corrective. It stops a debate that begins with GDP growth from ending there, and it forces comparison across dimensions: a state or country that grows fast but leaves life expectancy and schooling behind is developing unevenly. Used alongside poverty, employment and inequality data, it gives a fuller picture of whether growth is becoming human progress.
takeaways: The HDI combines life expectancy, schooling and income into a score from 0 to 1, first published in 1990.
India ranked 130 of 193 in the 2025 report, with HDI 0.685 in 2023, up from 0.676 in 2022; life expectancy rose from 58.6 (1990) to 72 (2023).
Inequality cuts India's HDI by 30.7 per cent, and the index ignores freedom, environment and work quality.
relevance: The HDI reframes development from income to capabilities, and exposes uneven sharing of progress.
question: Should a country's development rank ignore political freedom — and what would including it change?

title: Gender and development: gaps that persist
syllabus: GS II — Issues relating to development and management of Social Sector/Services relating to Health, Education, Human Resources. Also touches GS III: Indian Economy — growth, development and employment.
paragraphs: Development is not gender-neutral. Women and girls in India have gained on many indicators — schooling, life expectancy and political participation — yet gaps remain in survival, work, assets and safety, and these gaps shape the whole economy. The most basic indicator is the sex ratio at birth: the National Family Health Survey-5 (2019-21) put it at 929 girls per 1,000 boys, up from 919 in NFHS-4, but still below the natural level, reflecting persistent son preference and sex-selective practices despite the Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PCPNDT) Act, 1994, which bans sex determination for selection.

The Beti Bachao Beti Padhao scheme, launched on 22 January 2015, combined enforcement, awareness and support for girls' education to address the declining child sex ratio. Sex ratios at birth have improved in several states, but the national figure remains skewed, and the scheme's critics argue that awareness campaigns cannot substitute for enforcement and for changing the economic reasons families prefer sons — old-age support, dowry costs and inheritance practices. The overall sex ratio of the population, by contrast, reached 1,020 females per 1,000 males in NFHS-5, because women live longer than men at older ages.

Economic gaps are large. As an earlier note showed, female labour force participation rose to 41.7 per cent in 2023-24, but remains far below men's, and much of it is informal and unpaid. Women own less land and fewer assets, face a gender pay gap, and carry most unpaid care work. Political representation has moved further: women now vote at rates equal to or above men, lead panchayats in large numbers under the one-third reservation in local bodies, and the Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023, reserves one-third of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies, to take effect after delimitation.

Gender and development is therefore not a separate topic but a lens on every other one. Health policy that ignores maternal care, education policy that ignores girls' dropout, employment policy that ignores care work, and urban policy that ignores safe transport will all underperform. The direction of change is clear — gaps are narrowing — but the pace and the quality of change, especially in paid work and asset ownership, remain the real test.
takeaways: Sex ratio at birth was 929 girls per 1,000 boys in NFHS-5, up from 919, still below natural levels despite the PCPNDT Act, 1994.
Beti Bachao Beti Padhao (22 January 2015) targets the child sex ratio, but economic motives for son preference persist.
The 106th Amendment, 2023, reserves one-third of Lok Sabha and assembly seats for women, effective after delimitation.
relevance: Gender gaps in survival, work and assets shape every development outcome.
question: Will reserved seats in legislatures change outcomes for women, or only their presence in politics?

title: Learning outcomes: what children actually learn
syllabus: GS II — Issues relating to development and management of Social Sector/Services relating to Health, Education, Human Resources. Also touches GS III: Indian Economy — growth, development and employment.
paragraphs: Enrolment is the easiest education statistic to improve, and India has largely achieved it at primary level. Learning is harder, and the Annual Status of Education Report (ASER), a citizen-led household survey of rural India run by the NGO Pratham, has documented the gap for two decades. Its headline measure is simple: can a child in Class 3 read a Class 2 level text, and can they do basic subtraction? The answers show how far schooling and learning have diverged.

ASER 2024, which surveyed about 6.5 lakh children across 605 rural districts, found improvement after the pandemic slump. Among government-school Class 3 children, the share able to read a Class 2 level text rose from 16.3 per cent in 2022 to 23.4 per cent in 2024, above the 2018 level of 20.9 per cent. Among government-school Class 5 children, the share rose from 38.5 per cent in 2022 to 44.8 per cent in 2024. Arithmetic improved too. The recovery is real, and ASER notes that gains of this size are unusual in its history.

The levels, however, remain low: even after the recovery, roughly three in four government-school Class 3 children cannot read a Class 2 text, and more than half of Class 5 children cannot. The causes are familiar: weak foundational teaching in the early grades, multi-grade classrooms, teacher shortages, and the practice of promoting children regardless of learning, which lets gaps compound year by year. The pandemic widened the gap, since school closures hit children without devices, connectivity or literate adults at home hardest.

Policy has responded with a foundational focus. NIPUN Bharat, launched in 2021 under the National Education Policy, 2020, aims for universal foundational literacy and numeracy by the end of Class 3, with teacher training, teaching materials and regular assessment. The ASER recovery suggests that focused attention on the early grades can work, but the scale of the remaining gap means the mission's success will be judged over years, not in one survey round. For civil studies, ASER is a reminder to ask, of any education claim, not how many children are in school, but what they can do.
takeaways: ASER 2024: government-school Class 3 reading rose from 16.3 per cent (2022) to 23.4 per cent (2024); Class 5 rose to 44.8 per cent.
Even after recovery, about three in four government-school Class 3 children cannot read a Class 2 text.
NIPUN Bharat (2021) targets universal foundational literacy and numeracy by the end of Class 3.
relevance: Learning outcomes, not enrolment, are the real measure of an education system.
question: Should children be held back until they master basics, or promoted with support — and which harms learning less?

title: Ageing India: population change and care
syllabus: GS II — Issues relating to development and management of Social Sector/Services relating to Health, Education, Human Resources. Also touches GS III: Indian Economy — growth, development and employment.
paragraphs: India is still young, but it is ageing fast. Life expectancy rose from 58.6 years in 1990 to 72 years in 2023, according to the Human Development Report 2025, and fertility has fallen below replacement level in most states. The result is a slow, certain shift: the share of older people will grow steadily in the coming decades, and the number of very old people — those over 80 — will grow fastest. The demographic dividend discussed earlier is therefore the first half of a longer story, and ageing is the second half.

Ageing brings three linked challenges. The first is income: most older Indians worked informally and have no pension, and the old-age pension under the National Social Assistance Programme is small. The National Pension System, opened to all citizens in 2009 after starting for government employees in 2004, and the Atal Pension Yojana, launched in 2015 for unorganised workers, extend coverage, but enrolment and benefit levels remain limited, and many older people depend on family support. The second is health: older people need long-term, chronic and palliative care, which the health system, built around episodic treatment, is poorly equipped to provide. The third is care itself: as families shrink, urbanise and see more women in paid work, the traditional model of daughters and daughters-in-law providing full-time care is under strain.

Kerala shows the future first: it has the oldest population profile in India, with high life expectancy, low fertility and large out-migration of the young, and it has experimented with palliative care networks and community-based support. Other states will follow its path at different speeds. The policy agenda includes pension adequacy, geriatric training, home-based and community care, age-friendly housing and transport, and protection against elder abuse, which the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, addresses by requiring children to maintain their parents.

Ageing is sometimes framed as a burden, but that framing is incomplete. Older people work, care for grandchildren, volunteer and vote, and their experience is a resource. The real question is whether institutions adapt in time: pension systems designed when lives were shorter, health systems designed for acute illness, and families designed around joint households all need rethinking before the age wave arrives, not after.
takeaways: Life expectancy rose from 58.6 years (1990) to 72 (2023); fertility decline means the older share will grow steadily.
Most older Indians lack pensions, and chronic and long-term care needs are poorly met by an acute-care health system.
Kerala, India's oldest state by population profile, previews the care and pension challenges other states will face.
relevance: Ageing converts today's dividend into tomorrow's dependency, and policy made now decides how well it is handled.
question: Should the state guarantee a minimum pension for all older citizens, and what would it cost the young?

title: Partition and the making of a new nation
syllabus: GS I — Post-independence consolidation and reorganisation within the country.
paragraphs: On 14-15 August 1947, British India was divided into two dominions, India and Pakistan, and India became independent. Partition was not a single decision but the outcome of a long political failure: the Congress and the Muslim League could not agree on the constitutional future of a united India, the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946 collapsed, and communal violence in 1946-47 hardened positions. The boundary was drawn by the Radcliffe Commission, whose awards were announced on 17 August 1947, after independence, leaving millions unsure, for days, which country they lived in.

The human cost was immense. About 15 million people crossed the new borders in the largest mass migration in recorded history, and estimates of deaths in the accompanying violence range widely — from several hundred thousand to around two million — because no reliable count was ever made. Trains arrived full of corpses, cities such as Delhi, Lahore and Calcutta were overwhelmed by refugees, and women suffered abduction and sexual violence on a large scale, a history that was long silenced and has only recently been studied in full. The Indian state, barely days old, had to feed, house and resettle refugees while building its administration.

Resettlement shaped the new nation. Refugee colonies grew into towns and neighbourhoods; displaced farmers, traders and artisans rebuilt livelihoods, often with government loans and land allotments; and the experience of Partition left a lasting mark on politics — on relations with Pakistan, on debates about secularism and minority rights, and on the Constitution's promise that citizenship would rest on birth and residence, not religion. The Constituent Assembly, which had begun work in December 1946, continued through Partition and produced a Constitution that deliberately rejected the logic of religious states.

Partition is therefore not only a story of division. It is the founding trauma of independent India, and it explains much of what followed: the Kashmir dispute, the wars with Pakistan, the sensitivity of communal politics, and the determination of the new state's leaders to hold a diverse, divided society together under a democratic constitution. Any account of post-independence India that skips Partition misses the context in which every later choice was made.
takeaways: Independence and Partition came together on 14-15 August 1947; the Radcliffe awards were announced on 17 August.
About 15 million people migrated; death estimates range from several hundred thousand to around two million, with no reliable count.
Refugee resettlement and the Partition experience shaped the Constitution, secularism and relations with Pakistan.
relevance: Partition is the founding context of independent India: its politics, its borders and its constitutional choices.
question: Could Partition have been avoided by a different constitutional bargain, or had the politics of the 1940s made it inevitable?

title: Uniting the princely states
syllabus: GS I — Post-independence consolidation and reorganisation within the country.
paragraphs: At independence there were about 565 princely states, covering roughly two-fifths of the subcontinent's territory and a quarter of its people. Under British rule they were governed by princes under British paramountcy — the Crown's overriding authority. The Indian Independence Act, 1947, ended paramountcy, leaving each ruler legally free to join India, join Pakistan, or remain independent. Had many chosen independence, the new India would have been a patchwork of enclaves. Preventing that was the first great task of the new government.

The task fell to Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of States, and his secretary V. P. Menon. Their instrument was the Instrument of Accession, under which a ruler ceded only defence, external affairs and communications to the dominion, keeping internal autonomy for the time being. Most rulers signed before 15 August 1947, persuaded by a mix of diplomacy, popular pressure, the promise of privy purses, and the logic of geography. The process was largely peaceful, and it is one of the least violent large-scale unifications in modern history.

Three cases resisted. Junagadh, a coastal state in Gujarat with a Hindu-majority population and a Muslim Nawab, acceded to Pakistan in September 1947; after protests, a blockade and the Nawab's flight, a plebiscite in February 1948 voted overwhelmingly for India. Hyderabad, the largest princely state, ruled by the Nizam, sought independence; after a standstill agreement and deteriorating order, Indian forces launched Operation Polo in September 1948 and integrated the state within days. Jammu and Kashmir, ruled by Maharaja Hari Singh, sought to stay independent until tribal invaders backed by Pakistan attacked in October 1947; the Maharaja signed the Instrument of Accession on 26 October 1947, and Indian troops were airlifted to Srinagar.

Integration did not end with accession. The states were then merged into larger units, their administrations unified, and their rulers' privy purses and privileges eventually abolished by the 26th Constitutional Amendment in 1971. Kashmir alone retained a special constitutional position, discussed in a later note. The achievement mattered because it gave India a single territory, a single citizenship and a single market — the preconditions for everything the republic then tried to build.
takeaways: About 565 princely states existed in 1947; paramountcy lapsed with the Indian Independence Act.
Patel and V. P. Menon used the Instrument of Accession (defence, external affairs, communications) to unite most states before 15 August 1947.
Junagadh (plebiscite, February 1948), Hyderabad (Operation Polo, September 1948) and Kashmir (accession, 26 October 1947) were the hard cases.
relevance: Territorial integration was the precondition for a single constitution, citizenship and market.
question: Was Patel's use of force in Hyderabad justified, or did it set a precedent for the Centre overriding states?

title: Redrawing the map: linguistic states
syllabus: GS I — Post-independence consolidation and reorganisation within the country.
paragraphs: Independent India's internal map did not match its languages. The Constitution's original scheme grouped states into four categories — Part A, B, C and D — inherited from provinces and princely unions, cutting across linguistic communities. Demands to redraw boundaries by language began immediately, and the government at first resisted, fearing that linguistic states would weaken national unity. Two early commissions, the Dhar Commission (1948) and the JVP Committee (1948-49), recommended reorganisation on administrative convenience rather than language, and their reports were shelved by popular demand.

The turning point was Andhra. Potti Sriramulu, a Gandhian activist, fasted for a separate Telugu-speaking state and died on 15 December 1952 after 56 days; the protests that followed forced the government to create Andhra State in October 1953, the first state formed on a linguistic basis, carved out of Madras. The States Reorganisation Commission, appointed in 1953 under Justice Fazl Ali with K. M. Panikkar and H. N. Kunzru as members, then recommended a broader linguistic reorganisation, accepting language as the main basis while weighing administrative and economic factors.

The States Reorganisation Act, enacted on 31 August 1956 and in force from 1 November 1956, redrew the map into 14 states and 6 union territories, abolishing the Part A-D classification through the 7th Constitutional Amendment. Andhra Pradesh united Telugu areas; Kerala united Malayalam areas; Mysore, later Karnataka, united Kannada areas; and Bombay remained a bilingual state of Marathi and Gujarati speakers, a compromise that lasted only until 1960, when it split into Maharashtra and Gujarat. Punjab, with its mix of Punjabi, Hindi and Pahari speakers, was reorganised later, in 1966, into Punjab, Haryana and Himachal Pradesh.

Linguistic reorganisation is often judged a success: it gave large language communities a state of their own, made administration accessible in the local language, and, contrary to early fears, strengthened rather than weakened the Union, because linguistic identity found expression within the federation instead of against it. But it did not end boundary disputes or demands for new states — Telangana, created in 2014 from Andhra Pradesh, is the most recent — and it left linguistic minorities inside every state, a problem the Constitution addresses through safeguards for linguistic minorities and official language provisions.
takeaways: Andhra State (October 1953), after Potti Sriramulu's death in December 1952, was the first linguistic state.
The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 (in force 1 November 1956), created 14 states and 6 union territories.
Bombay split into Maharashtra and Gujarat in 1960; Punjab was reorganised in 1966; Telangana followed in 2014.
relevance: Linguistic states show how the federation absorbed identity demands instead of being broken by them.
