It did, however, stay the operation of the five-year practising requirement until rules are framed for how it is to be verified, and it stayed the provision allowing a government officer to decide whether waqf property encroached on government land. It also capped non-Muslim membership at four in the Central Waqf Council and three in State Waqf Boards.

The order was interim, not final. Its observations were prima facie, meaning they were provisional views pending a full hearing, and the Court left petitioners free to press other grounds. The case therefore illustrates an important distinction for civil studies readers: an interim order can freeze or adjust the most contested parts of a law while leaving the rest in operation, without deciding the law's ultimate validity.
takeaways: Parliament passed the Waqf (Amendment) Act in April 2025, amending the 1995 Act on registration, management, and board composition.
On 15 September 2025 the Supreme Court refused a wholesale stay but stayed the five-year practising requirement and the officer-led inquiry into government land.
The interim order capped non-Muslim membership of the Central Council at four and of State Boards at three, pending a final hearing.
relevance: Interim orders show how courts balance a legislature's authority against claims of rights, without deciding a case before it is fully heard.
question: When should a court stay part of a law before a final hearing, and when should it let the law operate in full?

title: Caste enumeration returns to the Census: the 2025 decision
syllabus: GS II — Indian Constitution; separation of powers, dispute redressal mechanisms and institutions; government policies and interventions; statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies.
paragraphs: Since Independence, India's Census has systematically counted Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, but it has not counted caste for other communities as part of the Census itself. The last full caste count of the whole population was in 1931, before Independence. In 2011, caste information was collected separately through the Socio-Economic and Caste Census, rather than as part of the Census, and that exercise later drew criticism over the usability of its data.

On 30 April 2025, the Cabinet Committee on Political Affairs decided that caste enumeration would be included in the forthcoming Census, Census 2027. The decision reversed the government's earlier position and met a long-standing demand from several political parties and social groups, who argued that policy on backwardness, welfare, and representation cannot be properly assessed without current caste data.

Census 2027 is planned as India's first digital Census, conducted in two phases: house listing and housing, followed by population enumeration. The reference date for most of the country is 1 March 2027, with earlier reference dates for snow-bound and other non-synchronous areas. Caste enumeration is to form part of the population enumeration phase, and the government has described the exercise as a major preparatory undertaking, with training, a pre-test, and administrative arrangements across states and districts.

The decision does not by itself change reservation policy. Any change to reservation percentages, to the categories covered, or to the 50 per cent ceiling discussed in the Indra Sawhney case would still require a separate legal or constitutional step, and the data would need to be collected, cleaned, and published before it could be used in that debate. Critics of caste enumeration have raised concerns about privacy, about how caste identity is recorded when there is no single agreed list, and about whether counting caste entrenches the very divisions policy seeks to reduce.

Supporters respond that caste already shapes access to education, work, and public services, and that refusing to count it leaves policy to guesswork. For civil studies readers, the key point is methodological as much as political: the value of the exercise will depend on how the question is asked, how responses are coded, and how transparently the results are released.
takeaways: On 30 April 2025 the Cabinet Committee on Political Affairs decided to include caste enumeration in Census 2027.
Since Independence, the Census has systematically counted only Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes; the last full caste count was in 1931.
Caste data alone does not change reservation law; any change to quotas or ceilings would need a separate legal step.
relevance: Census design shapes every later debate on welfare, representation, and social justice, because policy can only respond to what has been measured.
question: Does counting caste help correct disadvantage, or does it risk reinforcing caste identity in public life?

title: Demolitions and due process: the Supreme Court's 2024 guidelines
syllabus: GS II — Indian Constitution; separation of powers, dispute redressal mechanisms and institutions; government policies and interventions; statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies.
paragraphs: In several states in the early 2020s, houses and shops belonging to people accused of crimes, or to their families, were demolished by municipal or development authorities, sometimes shortly after an alleged offence or a communal incident. Critics described this pattern as bulldozer justice, arguing that demolition was being used as punishment without a trial. Authorities generally replied that the structures were unauthorised or encroachments, and that action was taken under municipal law.

The Supreme Court took up the issue in a suo motu matter concerning directions for demolition of structures. On 13 November 2024, a Bench of Justices B. R. Gavai and K. V. Viswanathan held that demolishing a person's home merely because that person is accused, or even convicted, of a crime, without following due process, is unconstitutional. The Court stressed the presumption of innocence, the right to shelter, and Article 300A of the Constitution, which provides that no person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law.

The judgment laid down pan-India guidelines. Authorities must give at least 15 days' notice to the owner or occupier before demolition, with an opportunity to respond, and a further 15 days after a final order before execution, so that the person can remove the structure or challenge the order. Demolition must be videographed, inspection and demolition reports must be prepared, and a digital portal was to be set up within three months to display notices and orders.

The guidelines do not apply to unauthorised structures in public places such as roads, footpaths, railway lines, and water bodies, or where a court has already ordered demolition. The Court also said that if only one structure among similarly placed structures is demolished, that selectivity may indicate a punitive motive rather than bona fide enforcement. Officials who violate the guidelines face contempt proceedings and prosecution, and affected persons are entitled to compensation.

Reporting since the judgment has suggested uneven implementation, with further demolitions challenged in courts and compensation ordered in at least one Prayagraj case. The guidelines therefore remain a useful test case: a clear judicial rule is only as strong as the local administration that must follow it, and as the courts and citizens who insist on it.
takeaways: On 13 November 2024 the Supreme Court held that demolition as punishment, without due process, is unconstitutional.
Its guidelines require at least 15 days' notice, a hearing, a further 15 days after a final order, videography, and written reports.
The guidelines do not cover unauthorised structures in public places or demolitions already ordered by a court.
relevance: Demolition cases link property rights, criminal justice, and administrative fairness: punishment must follow a trial, not precede it.
question: How can courts ensure that local officials follow national guidelines when no one is watching a particular demolition?

title: Online money games banned: the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025
syllabus: GS II — Indian Constitution; separation of powers, dispute redressal mechanisms and institutions; government policies and interventions; statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies.
paragraphs: Before 2025, online games involving money in India were regulated by a patchwork of state laws and court rulings. Courts had, in several cases, distinguished games of skill, such as rummy and fantasy sports as then operated, from games of chance, and that distinction shaped what states could prohibit. The result was uncertainty for players, companies, payment providers, and state governments, and a fast-growing market for real-money games advertised heavily during sporting seasons.

Parliament changed that framework in August 2025. The Lok Sabha passed the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Bill on 20 August 2025, the Rajya Sabha followed, and the President assented on 22 August 2025, enacting the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025. The Act prohibits offering, operating, facilitating, advertising, and promoting online money games, defined as games played by paying fees or staking money or other stakes in expectation of winning, whether the game is based on skill, chance, or both.

The Act deliberately removes the skill-versus-chance distinction for money games. Offering an online money game can attract imprisonment of up to three years, a fine of up to one crore rupees, or both, while advertising such games can attract up to two years' imprisonment and a fine of up to fifty lakh rupees. Banks and payment providers that process transactions for banned services also face penalties. At the same time, the Act seeks to promote e-sports and online social games, which do not involve staking money or an expectation of winning money, and provides for an authority to regulate the sector.

The Act was not brought into force immediately. After months in which its commencement was awaited, the government announced in April 2026 that the Act and its Rules would come into force on 1 May 2026. Challenges to the Act were transferred to the Supreme Court, where petitioners argued that a blanket ban violates Articles 14, 19(1)(g), and 21 of the Constitution, while the government defended the ban on grounds including addiction, financial harm, fraud, and money laundering.

For civil studies readers, the Act is a case study in how Parliament can override a judicial distinction by statute, and in how a ban is only the first step. Enforcement, the treatment of offshore operators, and the line between a social game and a money game will determine how far the law changes behaviour in practice.
takeaways: Parliament passed the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act in August 2025, with Presidential assent on 22 August 2025.
The Act bans online money games whether based on skill, chance, or both, and penalises offering and advertising them.
The Act and its Rules came into force on 1 May 2026, while constitutional challenges remained pending in the Supreme Court.
relevance: A statute can replace a court-made distinction, but enforcement and definition still decide whether a ban works in a digital market.
question: Is a blanket ban on all online money games proportionate, or should skill-based games be regulated rather than prohibited?

title: Three new criminal codes: BNS, BNSS, and BSA from 1 July 2024
syllabus: GS II — Indian Constitution; separation of powers, dispute redressal mechanisms and institutions; government policies and interventions; statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies.
paragraphs: For more than a century and a half, India's criminal justice system ran on three colonial-era statutes: the Indian Penal Code of 1860, the Code of Criminal Procedure of 1973, and the Indian Evidence Act of 1872. Parliament replaced all three in December 2023, and the new codes came into force on 1 July 2024, except for Section 106(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, which was held back. The change affects every first information report, charge sheet, trial, and judgment for offences committed on or after that date.

The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, replaces the Indian Penal Code and defines offences and punishments. It has 358 sections, compared with 511 in the old Code. It introduces community service as a punishment for certain minor offences, creates distinct offences for organised crime and terrorism, and provides a specific offence of mob lynching, where a group of five or more persons acting together commits murder on grounds including race, caste, community, sex, place of birth, language, or personal belief. It drops the old sedition offence as such, while providing for offences against the sovereignty and integrity of India.

The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, replaces the Code of Criminal Procedure and governs procedure: information to the police, arrest, investigation, bail, trial, and appeal. It has 531 sections. It formalises electronic and zero first information reports, so that a report can be filed at any police station regardless of jurisdiction and then transferred, and it requires audio-video recording of search and seizure. It also sets timelines for investigation and trial, and requires forensic investigation for offences punishable with seven years or more.

The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, replaces the Indian Evidence Act and governs what evidence a court may admit and how it is proved. It has 170 sections. It gives clearer statutory recognition to electronic and digital records, reflecting how much evidence today exists on phones, computers, and servers rather than on paper alone.

The transition is not retroactive. Offences committed before 1 July 2024 continue to be governed by the old codes for substantive liability, while offences on or after that date fall under the new codes. For students and practitioners, the practical lesson is that section numbers have changed: cheating, formerly Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code, is now Section 318 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, and murder, formerly Section 302, is now Section 103. Knowing the old number is no longer enough.
takeaways: From 1 July 2024, the BNS, BNSS, and BSA replaced the Indian Penal Code, the Code of Criminal Procedure, and the Indian Evidence Act.
The BNS has 358 sections, the BNSS 531, and the BSA 170, with new provisions on organised crime, mob lynching, and electronic evidence.
Offences before 1 July 2024 remain under the old codes; offences on or after that date fall under the new codes.
relevance: Replacing procedure and evidence law changes how every criminal case is investigated, proved, and decided, not just how offences are named.
question: Does renaming and restructuring criminal law change outcomes, or does it mainly change the labels lawyers must learn?

title: India's data protection law moves from statute to rules: the DPDP Act
syllabus: GS II — Indian Constitution; separation of powers, dispute redressal mechanisms and institutions; government policies and interventions; statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies.
paragraphs: India had no comprehensive, standalone data protection statute until the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which received Presidential assent on 11 August 2023. Before it, data protection rested mainly on provisions of the Information Technology Act, 2000, and the Sensitive Personal Data or Information Rules, 2011. The 2023 Act was designed to govern the processing of digital personal data, balancing the rights of individuals with the need for lawful processing by businesses and the state.

The Act uses two central terms. A data fiduciary is the person or organisation that determines the purpose and means of processing personal data, while a data principal is the individual to whom the data relates. The Act gives data principals rights including access to information about processing, correction and erasure of their data, and withdrawal of consent. It also requires fiduciaries to give clear notice, obtain consent where required, protect data, and notify breaches to the Data Protection Board of India and to affected principals.

The Act itself did not bring the whole regime into force at once. Its commencement was to be notified in stages, and detailed rules were needed to make it workable. On 3 January 2025, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published the Draft Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, for public consultation. The draft covered consent notices, consent managers, parental consent for children's data, data breach notification, and the establishment and working of the Data Protection Board.

After consultation, the government notified the final Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, in November 2025, formally setting the implementation framework in motion. The Rules adopt a staggered commencement: some provisions, including those establishing the Board, take effect immediately, while other obligations for fiduciaries phase in over 12 to 18 months. That phasing matters, because a law that looks complete on paper can still take more than a year to bite in practice.

Critics have raised questions about exemptions for the state, about cross-border transfer conditions set by the government, and about whether individuals will in practice be able to exercise rights against large platforms. Supporters argue that a single national framework, with a dedicated Board and significant penalties, is a step forward from the earlier patchwork. Either way, the DPDP story shows why civil studies readers should track both the Act and its rules: the rules decide how a right is actually claimed.
takeaways: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, received assent on 11 August 2023 and is India's first comprehensive data protection statute.
Draft Rules were published on 3 January 2025, and final Rules were notified in November 2025 with staggered commencement.
The Act gives data principals rights of access, correction, erasure, and withdrawal of consent, enforced through the Data Protection Board of India.
relevance: Data protection law only becomes real when rules, a regulator, and workable complaint routes exist alongside the statute.
question: Should the state enjoy broad exemptions from a data protection law it enforces against private companies?

title: Stray dogs, public safety, and animal welfare: the Supreme Court's 2025 orders
syllabus: GS II — Indian Constitution; separation of powers, dispute redressal mechanisms and institutions; government policies and interventions; statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies.
paragraphs: In July 2025, the Supreme Court took suo motu cognisance of the stray dog problem in Delhi, after reports of children and others being attacked, including a report of a young girl's death following a rabid dog attack. The case, titled In Re: City Hounded by Strays, Kids Pay Price, raised a direct conflict: the safety of people, especially children and the elderly, on the one hand, and the welfare of stray animals and the existing legal framework for their control on the other.

On 11 August 2025, a two-judge Bench of Justices J. B. Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan directed municipal authorities in Delhi, Ghaziabad, Noida, Faridabad, and Gurugram to pick up stray dogs from all localities and relocate them to designated shelters, and not to release them back onto the streets even after sterilisation and immunisation. The order also called for shelters to be created and reported within eight weeks, and for action against those who obstructed the drive.

The order drew immediate criticism, including from animal welfare groups, on the ground that it conflicted with the Animal Birth Control Rules, 2023. Rule 11(19) of those Rules requires that stray dogs, once sterilised, dewormed, and immunised, be released back into the same area from which they were picked up, with exceptions for rabid or aggressive dogs. Critics also argued that shelters on the scale required did not exist, and that mass relocation without sterilisation would not reduce the population in the long term.

The matter was then placed before a three-judge Bench of Justices Vikram Nath, Sandeep Mehta, and N. V. Anjaria. On 22 August 2025, that Bench modified the earlier directions, holding that a complete prohibition on release was too harsh and potentially impossible to comply with. It directed that dogs that have been sterilised, dewormed, and vaccinated must be released back into the same area, while rabid dogs and dogs displaying aggressive behaviour must be kept in separate shelters and not released. It also expanded the scope of the case beyond Delhi and the National Capital Region to all states and union territories.

The sequence is instructive. Within eleven days, the same Court moved from removal to capture, sterilise, vaccinate, and release, with exceptions for dangerous animals. The final position therefore rests less on a single dramatic order than on the unglamorous work of municipal sterilisation, vaccination, feeding points, and record-keeping that the Animal Birth Control Rules already required.
takeaways: On 11 August 2025 the Supreme Court ordered stray dogs in Delhi and nearby cities to be rounded up and kept in shelters without release.
On 22 August 2025 a three-judge Bench modified that order, directing release after sterilisation, deworming, and vaccination, except for rabid or aggressive dogs.
The Animal Birth Control Rules, 2023, already required release into the same locality, which was the main legal tension in the case.
relevance: When public safety and animal welfare collide, courts must weigh an urgent order against an existing rulebook and the capacity to implement either.
question: Should feeding and sterilisation be treated as a municipal service, like waste collection, rather than as charity?

title: President's Rule in Manipur: from February 2025 to an elected government
syllabus: GS II — Indian Constitution; separation of powers, dispute redressal mechanisms and institutions; government policies and interventions; statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies.
paragraphs: Manipur has been in crisis since ethnic violence between Meitei and Kuki-Zo communities erupted in May 2023, following a dispute linked to a demand for Scheduled Tribe status for Meiteis and a Manipur High Court direction on the issue. The violence displaced large numbers of people, and central security forces were deployed, but political normalcy did not return. The state government, led by Chief Minister N. Biren Singh, faced sustained criticism over its handling of the conflict.

On 9 February 2025, Biren Singh resigned as Chief Minister. The immediate constitutional problem was practical: the Assembly's budget session was due, and under Article 174, the gap between two sessions of a legislature cannot exceed six months. The last session had been held in August 2024, so a session had to be convened by February 2025, yet no consensus Chief Ministerial candidate emerged to form a government that could face the House.

On 13 February 2025, President Droupadi Murmu imposed President's Rule in Manipur under Article 356, on the Governor's report that the state government could not be carried on in accordance with the Constitution. The Assembly was placed under suspended animation, not dissolved, which meant its members remained in place but the House did not function, while the state came under the direct administration of the Centre through the Governor, Ajay Kumar Bhalla, who had taken office in January 2025.

President's Rule was initially imposed for six months and was extended for a further six months in August 2025, after parliamentary approval, as required for an extension beyond the initial period. Article 356 proclamations must be laid before Parliament and lapse after two months unless approved, and in total, President's Rule in a state cannot ordinarily continue beyond three years without further constitutional steps. Manipur's case thus became the most recent use of Article 356 since Puducherry in 2021, and the eleventh imposition in Manipur's history, according to contemporary reporting.

On 4 February 2026, President's Rule was revoked, and Yumnam Khemchand Singh, leader of the Bharatiya Janata Party legislature party, was sworn in as Chief Minister, restoring an elected government after almost a year of central rule. The restoration of a government, however, is not the same as the restoration of peace, and the underlying questions of displacement, security, and reconciliation in Manipur remained open at the time of writing.
takeaways: President's Rule was imposed in Manipur on 13 February 2025 under Article 356, after Chief Minister N. Biren Singh resigned on 9 February 2025.
The Assembly was placed under suspended animation, not dissolved, and President's Rule was extended for a further six months in August 2025.
President's Rule was revoked on 4 February 2026, when Yumnam Khemchand Singh was sworn in as Chief Minister.
relevance: Article 356 is meant as a last resort for a breakdown of constitutional machinery, but its use always raises the question of whether central rule helps or hinders reconciliation.
question: When, if ever, should the Centre replace an elected state government rather than wait for a new one to emerge?

title: One-third of seats for women: the Women's Reservation Act, 2023
syllabus: GS II — Indian Constitution; separation of powers, dispute redressal mechanisms and institutions; government policies and interventions; statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies.
paragraphs: Women have long been under-represented in India's legislatures relative to their share of the population, even though women already hold a large share of seats in panchayats, where reservation has operated for decades. The demand for reservation in Parliament and state assemblies dates back to the 1990s, with Bills introduced and lapsing across several Lok Sabhas. In September 2023, Parliament finally passed the measure, in a special session held in the new Parliament building.

The Constitution (One Hundred and Sixth Amendment) Act, 2023, popularly called the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, was introduced as the Constitution (One Hundred and Twenty-Eighth Amendment) Bill on 19 September 2023 and received the President's assent on 28 September 2023. It inserts Articles 330A and 332A, reserving one-third of seats filled by direct election in the Lok Sabha and in state legislative assemblies, and in the Delhi Assembly, for women. One-third of the seats already reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes are also to be reserved for women from those categories.

The reservation is not immediate. Article 334A provides that it will come into effect only after an exercise of delimitation is undertaken following the publication of the relevant figures of the first Census conducted after the Act comes into force. In practice, that means the Census must first be completed, its figures published, and constituencies redrawn, before the Election Commission can notify which specific seats will be reserved for women in a given election. The reservation is initially valid for 15 years, extendable by a law passed by Parliament.

The delay has been the main criticism. Supporters of the Act argue that linking reservation to delimitation is necessary, because reserved seats must be identified on the basis of current population and constituency boundaries, and because the Act also sits alongside the wider question of how many seats each state should have. Critics argue that a law passed in 2023, whose effect depends on a Census and delimitation that may take years, postpones a reform that could have been applied to the next general election.

The specific seats to be reserved had not been notified in the material checked for this note. The Act therefore remains, for now, a statute whose promise is clear but whose electoral effect is still to be tested. Its study value lies in that gap between enactment and implementation, which is common to many constitutional reforms.
takeaways: The Constitution (One Hundred and Sixth Amendment) Act, 2023, reserves one-third of directly elected seats in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies for women.
The Act received Presidential assent on 28 September 2023 and inserts Articles 330A and 332A, with a 15-year initial period.
Reservation takes effect only after delimitation following the first Census after the Act comes into force.
relevance: Linking a reform to Census and delimitation can make it technically workable, but it can also delay it for a full electoral cycle or more.
question: Should women's reservation have applied from the next election on existing boundaries, even if that meant an imperfect allocation of seats?

title: The 2024 Lok Sabha election: a majority for the alliance, not for one party
syllabus: GS II — Salient features of the Representation of People's Act; appointment to various Constitutional posts, powers, functions and responsibilities of various Constitutional Bodies.
paragraphs: India's 2024 general election was held in seven phases between 19 April and 1 June 2024, to elect all 543 members of the 18th Lok Sabha. About 970 million people were eligible to vote, making it the largest democratic exercise ever held. Counting took place on 4 June 2024, and the result surprised many observers who had expected a larger majority for the ruling party.

The Bharatiya Janata Party won 240 seats, down from 303 in 2019, and short of the 272 needed for a majority on its own. The BJP-led National Democratic Alliance, however, won 293 seats, enough to form the government. Its two largest allies were the Telugu Desam Party, with 16 seats, and the Janata Dal (United), with 12 seats, and their support became essential in a way it had not been in the previous two Lok Sabhas, when the BJP had a majority alone.

The opposition Indian National Developmental Inclusive Alliance won 234 seats in total. The Congress, its largest party, improved from 52 seats in 2019 to 99 seats, while the Samajwadi Party won 37 seats, the Trinamool Congress 29, and the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam 22. The result gave the opposition a substantially larger presence in the House, and a stronger claim to the role of a check on the government, than it had held since 2014.

Narendra Modi was sworn in as Prime Minister for a third consecutive term on 9 June 2024, leading a coalition government for the first time in his tenure as Prime Minister. The shift from single-party majority to coalition majority changed the politics of the Lok Sabha, even though the Prime Minister and the governing alliance remained the same. Allies gained leverage over policy, appointments, and the legislative agenda, and the government could no longer assume that its Bills would pass without negotiation.

For civil studies readers, 2024 is a reminder that vote share and seat share are different things, and that a national result is the sum of state contests. The BJP remained by far the largest single party, with more seats than the next several parties combined, yet the arithmetic of 240 out of 543 meant that coalition management, not just parliamentary arithmetic, became the central skill of government.
takeaways: The BJP won 240 of 543 Lok Sabha seats in 2024, down from 303 in 2019, and short of the 272 majority mark.
The BJP-led NDA won 293 seats, with the Telugu Desam Party (16) and Janata Dal (United) (12) as its largest allies.
The Congress rose from 52 to 99 seats, and the INDIA bloc won 234 seats in total.
relevance: Coalition arithmetic changes how a government legislates, even when the same Prime Minister remains in office.
question: Does a coalition government produce better scrutiny, or does it mainly slow down decision-making?

title: Haryana 2024: a third term on a narrow vote margin
syllabus: GS II — Salient features of the Representation of People's Act; appointment to various Constitutional posts, powers, functions and responsibilities of various Constitutional Bodies.
paragraphs: Haryana voted in a single phase on 5 October 2024 to elect all 90 members of its Legislative Assembly, and counting took place on 8 October 2024. Exit polls had widely predicted a Congress victory, and the early trends on counting day appeared to support that expectation. By the end of counting, however, the result had reversed, and the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party had retained power.

The BJP won 48 seats, crossing the majority mark of 46, while the Congress won 37 seats. The Indian National Lok Dal won two seats and independents won three. The BJP's victory gave it a third consecutive term in Haryana, a first for any party in the state's history. Chief Minister Nayab Singh Saini, who had taken office earlier in 2024, continued as Chief Minister.

What made the result striking was how close the vote was. The BJP secured 39.94 per cent of the vote and the Congress 39.09 per cent, a gap of less than one percentage point, yet that translated into an 11-seat gap in the Assembly. That difference is a normal feature of first-past-the-post elections, in which a party can win many seats narrowly and lose others narrowly, but it also explains why the result felt unexpected to observers who had focused on vote share or on exit polls.

The Congress, which had complained during counting about a slowdown in the publication of trends on the Election Commission's website, did not succeed in overturning the result, and the Commission rejected the suggestion that the counting process itself was flawed. The episode is a useful reminder that a complaint about the speed of reporting is not the same as evidence about the validity of votes counted, and that the two should be assessed separately.

Haryana 2024 also matters for what it did not do. It did not produce a hung Assembly, it did not require post-poll bargaining for a majority, and it did not break the pattern of the BJP's state-level organisation converting a narrow vote lead into a workable majority. For students of elections, it is a clean example of how first-past-the-post can amplify a small vote advantage.
takeaways: The BJP won 48 of 90 seats in Haryana in 2024, and the Congress won 37, with counting on 8 October 2024.
The vote shares were close, 39.94 per cent for the BJP and 39.09 per cent for the Congress, yet the seat gap was 11.
The BJP's win gave it a third consecutive term in Haryana, the first time any party had done so.
relevance: First-past-the-post can turn a vote lead of under one point into a clear Assembly majority.
question: Should a state election that is this close in votes produce a clearer check on the winning party?

title: Jammu and Kashmir votes again: the 2024 Assembly election
syllabus: GS II — Salient features of the Representation of People's Act; appointment to various Constitutional posts, powers, functions and responsibilities of various Constitutional Bodies.
paragraphs: Jammu and Kashmir had not held an Assembly election for a decade when it voted in three phases on 18 and 25 September and 1 October 2024. The election was the first since the abrogation of Article 370 in August 2019, which had ended the former state's special status, and since the reorganisation of the state into two union territories, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh. The Supreme Court had directed that Assembly elections be held, and the election was therefore watched as a test of whether electoral politics could resume in the union territory.

The National Conference-Congress alliance won 48 of the 90 seats, crossing the majority mark of 46. The National Conference itself won 42 seats and the Congress six, while the Bharatiya Janata Party won 29 seats, all from the Jammu region, the Peoples Democratic Party won three, and independents and smaller parties shared the remainder. Omar Abdullah, who had won both Budgam and Ganderbal, became Chief Minister, taking oath on 16 October 2024.

The geography of the result mattered. The National Conference's strength was concentrated in the Kashmir Valley, while the BJP's strength was concentrated in Jammu, producing an Assembly that reflected the union territory's regional divide. The result also showed the limits of reading a single election as a verdict on a single issue: voters in different regions weighed statehood, development, security, and local governance differently, and the alliance's victory did not settle the statehood question.

That question remained open after the election. Omar Abdullah and his government pressed for the restoration of statehood, while the union territory continued to operate with a Lieutenant Governor holding significant powers, particularly over police and public order, under the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019. The division of powers between an elected Chief Minister and a Lieutenant Governor therefore became a continuing feature of governance in Jammu and Kashmir, not a question resolved by polling day.

The election's significance is thus twofold. It restored an elected Assembly after a decade, which is itself a democratic milestone, and it left the constitutional future of the union territory unresolved, to be decided by Parliament and by the courts rather than by one Assembly result alone.
takeaways: Jammu and Kashmir voted in September-October 2024, its first Assembly election in a decade and its first since the abrogation of Article 370.
The National Conference-Congress alliance won 48 of 90 seats; the National Conference won 42, the Congress six, and the BJP 29.
Omar Abdullah became Chief Minister on 16 October 2024, while the demand for restoration of statehood remained open.
relevance: An election can restore an Assembly without settling the constitutional status of the territory it governs.
question: Can an elected government govern effectively when a Lieutenant Governor retains key powers?

title: Maharashtra 2024: a landslide that reversed the Lok Sabha pattern
syllabus: GS II — Salient features of the Representation of People's Act; appointment to various Constitutional posts, powers, functions and responsibilities of various Constitutional Bodies.
paragraphs: Maharashtra voted in a single phase on 20 November 2024 for all 288 seats in its Legislative Assembly, and counting took place on 23 November 2024. The election was a direct contest between two alliances, each of which had split from the other in recent years. The ruling Mahayuti alliance comprised the Bharatiya Janata Party, the Shiv Sena faction led by Eknath Shinde, and the Nationalist Congress Party faction led by Ajit Pawar. The opposition Maha Vikas Aghadi comprised the Congress, the Shiv Sena faction led by Uddhav Thackeray, and the Nationalist Congress Party faction led by Sharad Pawar.

The Mahayuti won a landslide. The BJP emerged as the single largest party with 132 seats, its best-ever result in the state, ahead of 122 in 2014 and 105 in 2019. Its allies won 57 seats for the Shinde Shiv Sena and 41 for the Ajit Pawar Nationalist Congress Party. The Maha Vikas Aghadi, by contrast, won only 46 seats among its three main parties: 20 for the Thackeray Shiv Sena, 16 for the Congress, and 10 for the Sharad Pawar Nationalist Congress Party.

The result was striking because it reversed the pattern of the 2024 Lok Sabha election in the same state, held only months earlier, in which the Maha Vikas Aghadi had won 30 of Maharashtra's 48 parliamentary seats. The Assembly result therefore showed that voters do not simply repeat a national verdict in a state election, and that state-level issues, candidate selection, alliance management, and campaign organisation can produce a very different outcome in a short period.

Devendra Fadnavis became Chief Minister, leading a Mahayuti government with a comfortable majority. The scale of the victory also changed the internal balance of the ruling alliance, giving the BJP a dominant position within it, while the opposition faced the longer task of rebuilding after a defeat that left it with less than a sixth of the Assembly.

For civil studies readers, Maharashtra 2024 is a warning against reading too much into a single election. A party or alliance that looks dominant in one election can look vulnerable in the next, and a state election fought on state issues can diverge sharply from a national election fought on national issues, even when the same voters cast both ballots within months.
takeaways: The BJP won 132 of 288 seats in Maharashtra in 2024, its best-ever state result, with allies winning 57 and 41 seats.
The Maha Vikas Aghadi's three main parties won 20, 16, and 10 seats respectively, a sharp reversal from the 2024 Lok Sabha result in the state.
Devendra Fadnavis became Chief Minister of a Mahayuti government with a comfortable majority.
relevance: State and national elections can diverge sharply, even within months, when voters judge different issues and different candidates.
question: Why do voters sometimes choose one alliance nationally and the opposite alliance in their state?

title: Jharkhand 2024: an incumbent alliance holds on
syllabus: GS II — Salient features of the Representation of People's Act; appointment to various Constitutional posts, powers, functions and responsibilities of various Constitutional Bodies.
paragraphs: Jharkhand voted in two phases on 13 and 20 November 2024 for all 81 seats in its Legislative Assembly, with counting in November 2024 alongside Maharashtra. The contest was between the incumbent Mahagathbandhan, led by the Jharkhand Mukti Morcha, and the National Democratic Alliance, led by the Bharatiya Janata Party. The election was watched closely because incumbents in several Hindi-belt states had struggled to retain power, and because Jharkhand's politics turns on tribal identity, welfare delivery, and land and mining questions as much as on national issues.

The Mahagathbandhan won 56 seats, a clear majority in an 81-member House where 41 seats are needed to govern. The Jharkhand Mukti Morcha itself won 34 seats, its best-ever result, while the Congress won 16, the Rashtriya Janata Dal four, and the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist) Liberation two. The BJP won 21 seats, and the NDA as a whole won 24, well short of a majority despite the BJP securing the largest single-party vote share, at 33.18 per cent.

Hemant Soren, the Jharkhand Mukti Morcha leader, continued as Chief Minister. His return to office was notable because he had resigned earlier in 2024 after his arrest by the Enforcement Directorate in a land case, and had returned as Chief Minister after being granted bail. The election result therefore also functioned as a public judgment on a period in which the state's politics had been dominated by investigation, arrest, and legal proceedings, as well as by governance.

The result contrasted with Maharashtra, counted in the same week, where the incumbent alliance won by a landslide, and with Haryana, where the incumbent party also retained power. Taken together, the three results in late 2024 suggested that there was no single national swing, and that state-level leadership, welfare schemes, and tribal and regional identity continued to shape outcomes in ways that national narratives alone could not explain.

Jharkhand also illustrated a familiar feature of Indian elections: the largest vote share does not always produce the largest seat share. The BJP's vote, though the largest for a single party, was spread across the state, while the Mahagathbandhan's combined vote translated into a larger seat total. That is not an anomaly; it is how first-past-the-post works.
takeaways: The Mahagathbandhan won 56 of 81 seats in Jharkhand in 2024, with the Jharkhand Mukti Morcha winning 34 and the Congress 16.
The BJP won 21 seats despite securing the largest single-party vote share, at 33.18 per cent.
Hemant Soren continued as Chief Minister after an election fought against a background of investigation and legal proceedings.
relevance: Seat share follows where votes are concentrated, not just how many votes a party wins in total.
question: Should a party with the largest vote share but fewer seats be seen as the real winner?

title: Delhi 2025: the BJP returns to power after 27 years
syllabus: GS II — Salient features of the Representation of People's Act; appointment to various Constitutional posts, powers, functions and responsibilities of various Constitutional Bodies.
paragraphs: Delhi voted on 5 February 2025 to elect all 70 members of its Legislative Assembly, and counting took place on 8 February 2025. The election ended a decade of Aam Aadmi Party government in the capital and returned the Bharatiya Janata Party to power in Delhi for the first time since 1998, a gap of 27 years. The result was therefore historic in Delhi's own terms, even though it involved only 70 seats.

The BJP won 48 seats and the Aam Aadmi Party won 22, while the Congress won none, for the third consecutive Delhi Assembly election. The vote shares were closer than the seats suggested: the BJP secured 47.15 per cent of the vote and the AAP secured 43.57 per cent. The gap in votes was only a few percentage points, but the gap in seats was 26, another illustration of first-past-the-post amplification.

Several prominent AAP leaders lost, including former Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal, who lost the New Delhi seat to the BJP's Parvesh Verma, and former Deputy Chief Minister Manish Sisodia. The outgoing Chief Minister, Atishi, retained her Kalkaji seat. Rekha Gupta, the BJP legislator from Shalimar Bagh, was sworn in as Chief Minister on 20 February 2025.

The campaign had centred on governance in the capital, including air quality, water, roads, and the working of Delhi's unique constitutional arrangement, under which the elected government shares power with the Lieutenant Governor and the Centre controls police, land, and public order. The AAP had built its appeal on schools, health clinics, and subsidised services, while the BJP campaigned on corruption allegations against AAP leaders and on the promise of double-engine government, meaning the same party in power in Delhi and at the Centre.

Delhi's result also mattered nationally, because it removed the AAP's only state government outside Punjab and weakened its claim to be a national alternative. For civil studies readers, Delhi shows how a capital's election can be both a local verdict on services and a national signal about a party's trajectory.
takeaways: The BJP won 48 of 70 seats in Delhi in 2025, and the AAP won 22, while the Congress won none.
Voting was held on 5 February 2025 and counting on 8 February 2025; Rekha Gupta was sworn in as Chief Minister on 20 February 2025.
The vote gap was only a few percentage points, but the seat gap was 26, illustrating first-past-the-post amplification.
relevance: A capital election can be a local verdict on services and, at the same time, a national signal about a party.
question: Does Delhi's shared-power arrangement make it harder for voters to judge who is responsible for services?

title: Who chooses the Chief Election Commissioner? The 2025 appointment
syllabus: GS II — Salient features of the Representation of People's Act; appointment to various Constitutional posts, powers, functions and responsibilities of various Constitutional Bodies.
paragraphs: Article 324 of the Constitution vests the superintendence, direction, and control of elections in the Election Commission of India, headed by the Chief Election Commissioner and such other Election Commissioners as the President may fix. For decades, the appointment process was not spelled out in detail in the Constitution, and in practice the government of the day appointed Commissioners. That arrangement was challenged in the Supreme Court, which in March 2023 directed that appointments be made by a committee comprising the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition, and the Chief Justice of India, until Parliament legislated.

Parliament did legislate, in December 2023, with the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023. The Act replaced the Chief Justice on the selection committee with a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the Prime Minister, so that the committee consists of the Prime Minister as chair, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, and a Union Minister. A search committee led by the Law Minister first shortlists candidates, and the President formally appoints the person selected.

The first Chief Election Commissioner appointed under the new Act took office in February 2025. Gyanesh Kumar, a retired Indian Administrative Service officer of the 1988 Kerala cadre who had served as an Election Commissioner since March 2024, took charge as the 26th Chief Election Commissioner on 19 February 2025, succeeding Rajiv Kumar, who demitted office on 18 February 2025. The selection meeting on 17 February 2025 was attended by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah as the nominated Minister, and Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi, who recorded a dissent note urging that the appointment wait until the Supreme Court decided challenges to the 2023 Act.

The change matters because the Election Commission's independence is judged not only by what it does during an election, but by how its members are chosen. Supporters of the 2023 Act argue that Parliament is entitled to design the appointment process, and that the presence of the Leader of the Opposition provides a check. Critics argue that replacing the Chief Justice with a Minister gives the government two of the three votes on the committee, and that this weakens the independence the Supreme Court had sought to protect in 2023.

Challenges to the 2023 Act were already pending when the appointment was made, and the appointment process itself remained a subject of political debate. The case is therefore unfinished, and readers should distinguish between the law as enacted and the law as it may finally be upheld or modified by the Court.
takeaways: Gyanesh Kumar took charge as the 26th Chief Election Commissioner on 19 February 2025, the first appointed under the 2023 Act.
The 2023 Act's selection committee comprises the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition, and a Union Minister nominated by the Prime Minister.
The Supreme Court's March 2023 direction had included the Chief Justice of India on the committee, until Parliament legislated.
relevance: How an election watchdog is appointed shapes trust in it, even before a single vote is cast.
question: Should the Chief Justice, a Minister, or neither sit on the committee that chooses election commissioners?

title: The Vice-Presidential election of 2025: an indirect election in plain view
syllabus: GS II — Salient features of the Representation of People's Act; appointment to various Constitutional posts, powers, functions and responsibilities of various Constitutional Bodies.
paragraphs: The Vice President of India is not chosen by direct popular vote. Under Article 66, the Vice President is elected by members of an electoral college consisting of members of both Houses of Parliament, voting by proportional representation through the single transferable vote, with secret ballot. The Vice President is also the ex officio Chairperson of the Rajya Sabha, so the election matters for the conduct of the upper House as well as for succession to the Presidency.

The 2025 election was necessitated by the resignation of Jagdeep Dhankhar on 21 July 2025, citing health reasons. His term would otherwise have run until August 2027, so the election was held to fill a mid-term vacancy, not at the end of a full term. The National Democratic Alliance nominated C. P. Radhakrishnan, then Governor of Maharashtra, while the opposition INDIA bloc nominated former Supreme Court judge B. Sudershan Reddy.

Voting took place on 9 September 2025. Of 781 eligible members of Parliament, 767 cast votes, a turnout of about 98.2 per cent. Fifteen votes were declared invalid, and 13 members abstained, including members of the Biju Janata Dal, the Bharat Rashtra Samithi, the Shiromani Akali Dal, and one independent. Radhakrishnan secured 452 first-preference votes and Reddy secured 300, a margin of 152 votes, and Radhakrishnan was declared elected as the 15th Vice President of India.

The result broadly tracked the strength of the two sides in Parliament, but not exactly. The opposition had claimed support from 315 members, yet its candidate polled 300 first-preference votes, a shortfall that prompted discussion of cross-voting and invalid votes. That discussion is a normal feature of secret-ballot indirect elections, in which party discipline cannot be enforced in the same way as in an open vote in the House.

The election is a useful teaching case because it shows the difference between a direct election, in which voters choose a representative, and an indirect election, in which representatives choose an office-holder. The outcome was decided by fewer than 800 voters, yet it filled the second-highest constitutional office in the country and determined who would chair the Rajya Sabha.
takeaways: The Vice President is elected by members of both Houses of Parliament under Article 66, and serves as ex officio Chairperson of the Rajya Sabha.
The 2025 election followed Jagdeep Dhankhar's resignation on 21 July 2025; voting was held on 9 September 2025.
C. P. Radhakrishnan won 452 first-preference votes against B. Sudershan Reddy's 300, with 15 invalid votes and 13 abstentions.
relevance: Indirect elections concentrate power in a small electoral college, which makes turnout, validity, and discipline unusually visible.
question: Is it democratic for fewer than 800 parliamentarians to choose the Vice President?

title: Bihar 2025: a landslide for the NDA after a contested roll revision
syllabus: GS II — Salient features of the Representation of People's Act; appointment to various Constitutional posts, powers, functions and responsibilities of various Constitutional Bodies.
paragraphs: Bihar voted in two phases in November 2025 for all 243 seats in its Legislative Assembly, and counting took place on 14 November 2025. The election was the first Assembly election in the country to be held after a Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, which had been ordered in Bihar in June 2025 and had become a major political controversy. The opposition argued that the revision risked excluding eligible voters, while the Election Commission maintained that it was necessary to clean rolls of dead, shifted, and duplicate entries.

The result was a landslide for the ruling National Democratic Alliance, which won 202 seats in the 243-member House, well above the majority mark of 122. The Bharatiya Janata Party emerged as the single largest party with 89 seats, followed by the Janata Dal (United) with 85 seats and the Lok Janshakti Party (Ram Vilas) with 19 seats. The opposition Mahagathbandhan won 35 seats in total, with the Rashtriya Janata Dal winning 25 and the Congress six.

The scale of the victory surprised many observers, not only because of its size, but because the Janata Dal (United), which had won only 43 seats in 2020, nearly doubled its tally to 85, while the Rashtriya Janata Dal fell from 75 seats in 2020 to 25. The new entrant Jan Suraaj, led by Prashant Kishor, failed to win a seat. Chief Minister Nitish Kumar, whose party had been written off by some commentators before polling, remained at the centre of Bihar politics after the result.

Turnout was also notable. Bihar recorded an overall turnout of 66.91 per cent, reported as the highest in 74 years, with women outvoting men in both phases. That figure complicates any simple story about the election: a high turnout, a contested roll revision, and a landslide for the incumbent alliance all occurred in the same election, and different observers drew different conclusions from that combination.

The opposition, including Congress leader Udit Raj, attributed its defeat in part to the Special Intensive Revision and to the Election Commission, while the ruling alliance presented the result as an endorsement of its governance and welfare delivery. For civil studies readers, Bihar 2025 is a case in which the same result can support competing explanations, and in which the evidence for each explanation must be examined separately from the result itself.
takeaways: The NDA won 202 of 243 seats in Bihar in 2025, with the BJP winning 89, the Janata Dal (United) 85, and the Lok Janshakti Party (Ram Vilas) 19.
The Mahagathbandhan won 35 seats, with the Rashtriya Janata Dal falling from 75 seats in 2020 to 25.
Turnout was 66.91 per cent, reported as the highest in 74 years, with women outvoting men in both phases.
relevance: A landslide after a contested roll revision invites competing explanations, and the result alone cannot settle which one is right.
question: How should an election result be judged when the roll revision that preceded it is itself disputed?

title: Five assemblies in one spring: the 2026 election schedule
syllabus: GS II — Salient features of the Representation of People's Act; appointment to various Constitutional posts, powers, functions and responsibilities of various Constitutional Bodies.
paragraphs: Assembly elections are due when a House completes its five-year term, unless it is dissolved earlier. In early 2026, five Houses were approaching the end of their terms at the same time: West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Assam, and the union territory of Puducherry. All five had last voted in 2021, and all five were due to vote again in the spring of 2026, making that round one of the largest state election exercises between general elections.

On 15 March 2026, the Election Commission announced the schedule. Polling was set for 9 April in Assam, Kerala, and Puducherry, for 23 April in Tamil Nadu, and in two phases, on 23 and 29 April, in West Bengal. Counting for all five Houses was scheduled for 4 May 2026. The terms of the outgoing Houses expired on different dates: West Bengal on 7 May, Tamil Nadu on 10 May, Assam on 20 May, Kerala on 23 May, and Puducherry on 15 June, so the schedule was designed to complete the process before those dates.

The scale was substantial. The five Houses together comprised 824 seats: 294 in West Bengal, 234 in Tamil Nadu, 140 in Kerala, 126 in Assam, and 30 in Puducherry. The electorate was reported at about 17.4 crore voters. The Commission also announced Model Code of Conduct directions and the deployment of flying squads and observers, as it does for every major election round, to monitor expenditure, inducement, and violations of the code.

The political stakes differed by state. West Bengal was a contest between the ruling Trinamool Congress and the BJP, with the Left and Congress also in the field. Tamil Nadu pitted the ruling Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam alliance against the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam alliance. Kerala, which has historically alternated between the Left Democratic Front and the United Democratic Front, was watched for whether that pattern would hold. Assam and Puducherry were contests in which the ruling National Democratic Alliance sought to retain power.

This note covers the schedule, not the results, which were due on 4 May 2026 and should be read separately. Its teaching value is in the logistics: a single Commission, working to five different term-end dates, must sequence polling, counting, and government formation so that no state is left without a House when its term expires, and so that the Model Code does not run longer than necessary.
takeaways: The Election Commission announced the 2026 schedule on 15 March 2026, with polling in April and counting on 4 May 2026.
The five Houses totalled 824 seats, with an electorate reported at about 17.4 crore voters.
Terms expired between 7 May and 15 June 2026, which set the deadline for completing the process in each state.
relevance: Staggering polls across five Houses is a logistical exercise as much as a political one, governed by term-end dates.
question: Should elections in several states be held together to save time and money, or does that nationalise what should be state contests?

title: Budget 2025-26: no income tax up to 12 lakh rupees under the new regime
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilisation of resources, growth, development and employment; Government Budgeting.
paragraphs: The Union Budget is the government's annual statement of revenue and expenditure, presented to Parliament under Article 112 of the Constitution. On 1 February 2025, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman presented the Union Budget for 2025-26, with its headline measure aimed at middle-income taxpayers: a restructuring of personal income tax under the new regime, which had become the default regime for most individual taxpayers.

Under the revised structure, no income tax is payable on annual income up to 12 lakh rupees under the new regime, through a combination of revised slabs and an increased rebate under Section 87A of the Income-tax Act. For salaried taxpayers, the standard deduction of 75,000 rupees takes the effective threshold to 12.75 lakh rupees, provided the income is of the kind covered by the rebate and other conditions are met. Income taxed at special rates, such as certain capital gains, is not covered by the rebate in the same way, and the threshold is therefore not a blanket exemption for every kind of income.

The revised slabs themselves were also restructured. Income up to 4 lakh rupees is taxed at nil, income from 4 to 8 lakh rupees at 5 per cent, from 8 to 12 lakh rupees at 10 per cent, from 12 to 16 lakh rupees at 15 per cent, from 16 to 20 lakh rupees at 20 per cent, from 20 to 24 lakh rupees at 25 per cent, and above 24 lakh rupees at 30 per cent, with the rebate then bringing the liability to zero for eligible taxpayers up to the threshold.

The government presented the change as a way to leave more disposable income with households, boost consumption, and encourage adoption of the new regime, which offers fewer deductions than the old regime but lower rates. Critics noted that the benefit is concentrated among taxpayers in the middle of the income distribution, that it does not directly help people below the tax threshold, and that its effect on consumption would depend on whether households spent the saving or used it to repay debt or save.

For civil studies readers, the Budget is a reminder that a single headline number, 12 lakh rupees, conceals a mechanism. The number is the product of slabs, a rebate, and a standard deduction, each with its own conditions, and understanding the mechanism is necessary to judge who actually benefits and by how much.
takeaways: Budget 2025-26, presented on 1 February 2025, made income up to 12 lakh rupees tax-free under the new regime through slabs and a Section 87A rebate.
For salaried taxpayers, a 75,000-rupee standard deduction takes the effective threshold to 12.75 lakh rupees.
The rebate does not cover income taxed at special rates, so the threshold is not a blanket exemption for all income.
relevance: A headline tax threshold is the product of slabs, a rebate, and deductions, each with its own conditions.
question: Should tax relief be targeted at middle-income earners, or should it reach people who pay no income tax at all?

title: GST 2.0: two main rates from 22 September 2025
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilisation of resources, growth, development and employment; Government Budgeting.
paragraphs: The Goods and Services Tax, introduced in July 2017, replaced a maze of central and state indirect taxes with a single national tax, administered through the GST Council, in which the Centre and the states sit together. For eight years, GST operated with four main slabs: 5, 12, 18, and 28 per cent, plus compensation cess on certain goods. The multiplicity of slabs was a frequent complaint from businesses, which argued that classification disputes and inverted duty structures, where inputs are taxed higher than outputs, added cost and litigation.

On 3 September 2025, the GST Council, at its 56th meeting chaired by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, approved a major rationalisation, widely called GST 2.0. From 22 September 2025, most goods and services were taxed at two main rates, 5 per cent, called the merit rate, and 18 per cent, called the standard rate, with a 40 per cent demerit rate for a short list of luxury and sin goods. The 12 and 28 per cent slabs ceased to exist as general categories, and a number of staples, including ultra-high temperature milk, paneer, and certain breads, became exempt.

The changes also affected services and insurance. Life and health insurance premiums, previously taxed at 18 per cent, became exempt from GST, and a range of services, including gyms, salons, and yoga services, moved from 18 per cent to 5 per cent. Packaged foods, soaps, shampoos, toothpaste, bicycles, and many household goods moved to 5 per cent. Tobacco products were treated separately, with their rate changes deferred, reflecting the revenue and public health considerations that apply to that sector.

The government presented the reform as a next-generation GST reform aimed at simplifying compliance, reducing classification disputes, and passing on benefits to consumers, especially for essentials and health-related spending. Businesses welcomed the simpler structure but noted that the transition required repricing, updating software, and managing input tax credit, particularly where an output rate fell below the input rate. States, which share GST revenue, watched collections closely, since a rate cut that boosts consumption may or may not compensate for the lower rate on each sale.

GST 2.0 is therefore not just a tax cut. It is a redesign of the rate structure that will be judged over several quarters, by whether it simplifies compliance, whether price reductions reach consumers, and whether revenue remains stable enough to fund state and central spending.
takeaways: The GST Council approved GST 2.0 at its 56th meeting on 3 September 2025, effective 22 September 2025.
The four slabs of 5, 12, 18, and 28 per cent were replaced by two main rates, 5 and 18 per cent, plus a 40 per cent demerit rate.
Life and health insurance premiums became GST-exempt, and many everyday goods and services moved to 5 per cent.
relevance: Simplifying a tax structure changes compliance, pricing, and revenue together, not just the rate on a single product.
question: Should essentials be taxed at all, or does a low rate on everything keep the system simpler?

title: The RBI cuts the repo rate to 5.5 per cent in 2025
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilisation of resources, growth, development and employment; Government Budgeting.
paragraphs: The repo rate is the rate at which the Reserve Bank of India lends money to commercial banks, usually against government securities, under the liquidity adjustment facility. It is the RBI's main policy rate, set by the Monetary Policy Committee, which is required to keep consumer price inflation at 4 per cent, within a band of 2 percentage points on either side, while supporting growth. When the repo rate falls, banks' borrowing costs fall, and in time, lending and deposit rates tend to follow, though transmission is rarely immediate or complete.

At the start of 2025, the repo rate stood at 6.50 per cent, where it had been since early 2023. The Monetary Policy Committee, chaired by Governor Sanjay Malhotra, cut the rate by 25 basis points in February 2025, to 6.25 per cent, and by a further 25 basis points in April 2025, to 6.00 per cent, while shifting its stance from neutral to accommodative, signalling a priority for supporting growth. In June 2025, it cut by a larger 50 basis points, to 5.50 per cent, taking the cumulative cut since February to 100 basis points.

The June decision was accompanied by two other steps. The Committee shifted its stance back from accommodative to neutral, signalling that, having front-loaded support, it saw limited space for further cuts without new information. It also announced a 100-basis-point cut in the cash reserve ratio, from 4 per cent to 3 per cent, to be implemented in four equal tranches between September and November 2025, injecting durable liquidity estimated at 2.5 lakh crore rupees into the banking system.

The cuts were made possible by easing inflation. Consumer price inflation had moderated from levels above the tolerance band in late 2024 to about 3.16 per cent in April 2025, driven by falling food prices, and the RBI revised its inflation forecast for the year down. The Committee kept its growth projection broadly unchanged, while noting global uncertainties, including tariffs and trade tensions, which could affect exports and growth in the second half of the year.

In August and October 2025, the Committee held the repo rate unchanged at 5.50 per cent, citing tariff uncertainties and the need to assess the effect of cuts already made. The 2025 easing cycle therefore illustrates a central bank's balancing act: cut too slowly, and growth suffers; cut too fast, and inflation or financial stability may suffer, and the stance language matters as much as the rate itself.
takeaways: The RBI cut the repo rate from 6.50 per cent to 5.50 per cent in 2025, through cuts of 25 points in February, 25 in April, and 50 in June.
In June 2025 the Committee also cut the cash reserve ratio from 4 per cent to 3 per cent, phased between September and November 2025.
The repo rate was then held at 5.50 per cent in August and October 2025, with the stance shifted back to neutral.
relevance: A policy rate cut works through banks, liquidity, and expectations, not by directly setting the interest rate a borrower pays.
question: Should a central bank cut rates aggressively when inflation falls, or preserve room for a future shock?

title: Growth of 6.5 per cent in 2024-25: reading the GDP estimates
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilisation of resources, growth, development and employment; Government Budgeting.
paragraphs: Gross domestic product is the total value of goods and services produced in an economy in a given period, and its growth rate is the most widely quoted summary of economic performance. In India, GDP estimates are compiled by the National Statistics Office, under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, using a benchmark-indicator method that extrapolates from indicators such as industrial production, agricultural output, and services data. Estimates are revised several times as fuller data arrive, so an early figure is always provisional.

On 30 May 2025, the National Statistics Office released provisional estimates for 2024-25. Real GDP, measured at constant 2011-12 prices, was estimated to have grown by 6.5 per cent in 2024-25, to 187.97 lakh crore rupees, against 176.51 lakh crore rupees in 2023-24. Nominal GDP, measured at current prices, grew by 9.8 per cent, to 330.68 lakh crore rupees. Growth in the fourth quarter, January to March 2025, was stronger, at 7.4 per cent in real terms, the fastest quarterly rate of the year.

The 6.5 per cent figure was slightly below the Reserve Bank's earlier forecast of 6.6 per cent, and below the 8.2 per cent growth recorded in 2023-24 on revised estimates. Contemporary reporting described it as a four-year low, which is accurate as a description of the annual rate, but it should not be read as a recession: the economy was still expanding at a pace faster than most large economies, and the quarterly pattern showed momentum improving towards the end of the year.

For civil studies readers, the important distinction is between real and nominal growth. Real growth adjusts for price changes and shows how much more was actually produced, while nominal growth includes price increases. A nominal rate of 9.8 per cent alongside a real rate of 6.5 per cent implies that prices contributed about 3.3 percentage points to the nominal increase, though the exact deflator depends on the composition of output.

The provisional nature of the figures also matters. Provisional estimates are based on partial data and are routinely revised in first and second revised estimates. A responsible reading therefore treats 6.5 per cent as the best estimate available in May 2025, not as a final, unchangeable fact, and checks later revisions before drawing strong conclusions about the year's performance.
takeaways: The National Statistics Office's provisional estimates, released on 30 May 2025, put real GDP growth in 2024-25 at 6.5 per cent.
Real GDP reached 187.97 lakh crore rupees, while nominal GDP grew by 9.8 per cent to 330.68 lakh crore rupees.
Fourth-quarter real growth was 7.4 per cent, the fastest quarterly rate of the year, but the annual figure was below 2023-24.
relevance: Provisional GDP figures are the best early estimate, not a final verdict, and they are routinely revised.
question: Is a single annual growth rate a good summary of an economy, or does it hide who actually benefited?

title: The 50 per cent United States tariff on India in 2025
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilisation of resources, growth, development and employment; Government Budgeting.
paragraphs: Trade between India and the United States is among India's most important external economic relationships, with the United States as one of India's largest export markets. In 2025, that relationship was strained by two separate tariff actions. The first, announced in April 2025, imposed a 25 per cent reciprocal tariff on Indian goods. The second, imposed as a penalty for India's purchases of Russian oil, added a further 25 per cent, taking the total additional tariff to 50 per cent for many goods.

On 6 August 2025, United States President Donald Trump signed an executive order titled Addressing Threats to the United States by the Government of the Russian Federation, imposing an additional 25 per cent ad valorem duty on certain imports from India, on the ground that India was directly or indirectly importing Russian oil. The additional duty took effect on 27 August 2025, with exceptions for goods already in transit and for certain categories, including pharmaceuticals, energy products, critical minerals, and many electronics and semiconductors.

The sectors most exposed, according to contemporary reporting, included textiles and clothing, gems and jewellery, shrimp and marine products, leather and footwear, chemicals, and electrical and mechanical machinery. Those are labour-intensive sectors in which Indian exporters compete on price, and in which a 50 per cent tariff can quickly make an order unviable. Exporters reported cancelled or deferred orders, pressure to absorb part of the tariff, and a search for alternative markets, while the Indian government argued that India's energy purchases were driven by the need for affordable supplies and by national interest.

The tariff episode also illustrated how trade policy can be used as a foreign policy tool. The additional duty was not presented as a response to India's own trade barriers alone, but as a penalty for a third-country relationship, namely India's energy trade with Russia. That linkage drew criticism in India, where commentators noted that other buyers of Russian oil, including China and Turkey, did not face the same additional penalty at that time, while the United States argued that its measures were aimed at reducing Russia's revenue from the war in Ukraine.

In February 2026, after further negotiations, the United States and India agreed to reduce the tariff, with the reciprocal tariff falling from 25 per cent to 18 per cent and the additional Russian-oil penalty withdrawn, according to contemporary reporting, after India committed to curbing Russian oil purchases and expanding energy and defence cooperation. The 50 per cent rate therefore lasted about six months, but its effect on exporters, supply chains, and trade negotiations continued beyond that period.
takeaways: A 25 per cent reciprocal tariff in April 2025 was followed by an additional 25 per cent on 6 August 2025, effective 27 August 2025, taking the total to 50 per cent.
The additional duty was imposed on the ground of India's direct or indirect importation of Russian oil, with exemptions for pharmaceuticals, energy, and many electronics.
In February 2026 the tariff was reported to have been reduced, with the reciprocal rate falling to 18 per cent and the additional penalty withdrawn.
relevance: Tariffs can be used as foreign policy leverage, not only as protection for domestic producers, and that changes how their costs should be judged.
question: Should energy security justify purchases that invite tariffs, or should trade access take priority?

title: India and the United Kingdom sign a trade agreement in July 2025
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilisation of resources, growth, development and employment; Government Budgeting.
paragraphs: India and the United Kingdom began negotiations for a free trade agreement in January 2022, after the United Kingdom's departure from the European Union, building on an Enhanced Trade Partnership launched in 2021. After 14 rounds of negotiations over nearly three and a half years, the two sides concluded the agreement on 6 May 2025 and signed it on 24 July 2025, during Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to London. The agreement is formally called the India-United Kingdom Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, or CETA.

Under the agreement, the United Kingdom eliminates duties on about 99 per cent of Indian exports, covering textiles, leather, engineering goods, marine products, gems and jewellery, and other labour-intensive sectors. India, in turn, reduces or eliminates tariffs on about 90 per cent of tariff lines for British goods, with 85 per cent becoming fully duty-free over ten years. The average tariff on British goods imported into India was expected to fall from about 15 per cent to about 3 per cent once staging was complete.

Two headline cuts illustrate the bargain. Tariffs on Scotch whisky and gin fall from 150 per cent to 75 per cent when the agreement takes effect, and then to 40 per cent over ten years. Tariffs on British cars, previously up to 110 per cent, fall to 10 per cent under a quota system, phased over several years. From day one, India also removes tariffs on about 64 per cent of British products, including salmon, lamb, aircraft parts, machinery, and electronics.

The agreement covers more than goods. It includes chapters on services, digital trade, financial services, intellectual property, innovation, sustainability, and government procurement, totalling 30 chapters. It also includes provisions on business mobility, which were a key Indian interest, and on rules of origin, which determine whether a good qualifies for preferential treatment and which are administered in India through Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs rules.

Critics noted that tariff cuts are phased, that quotas limit the immediate benefit for cars, and that the agreement's long-run gains depend on implementation, including the treatment of steel, which became a sticking point in 2026 as the United Kingdom introduced safeguard measures.
