Supporters argued that the agreement's value lies less in any single tariff cut than in the signal it sends: that India is willing to open its market in a negotiated, reciprocal way, while protecting sensitive sectors such as dairy and certain agricultural products.
takeaways: India and the United Kingdom concluded their Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement on 6 May 2025 and signed it on 24 July 2025.
The United Kingdom eliminates duties on about 99 per cent of Indian exports, while India reduces tariffs on about 90 per cent of tariff lines.
Scotch whisky duties fall from 150 per cent to 75 per cent initially and then to 40 per cent over ten years; car duties fall to 10 per cent under a quota.
relevance: A trade agreement is a phased bargain, not an instant price cut, and quotas and staging decide how quickly benefits arrive.
question: Should India open sensitive sectors such as dairy to trade deals, or protect them even at the cost of a smaller agreement?

title: The rupee's slide to record lows in late 2025
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilisation of resources, growth, development and employment; Government Budgeting.
paragraphs: The exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another, and for India the most watched rate is rupees per United States dollar. India does not fix the rupee at a particular level. The Reserve Bank of India intervenes in the foreign exchange market from time to time, selling dollars and buying rupees to reduce volatility, but it does not defend a specific rate, and the rupee's value is ultimately set by supply and demand for dollars, including trade flows, investment flows, and expectations.

In late 2025, the rupee fell to a series of record lows. In November 2025, it depreciated by about 0.8 per cent in the month and closed at a record low of 89.46 rupees per dollar on 28 November, after breaching 89 rupees for the first time in the same month. On 21 November, it had closed at 89.49 rupees per dollar, after intraday trading between 88.60 and 89.67. The trigger, according to market reporting, included a widening trade deficit, foreign portfolio outflows, uncertainty over a trade deal with the United States, and expectations about United States interest rates.

The slide continued into December. On 1 December 2025, the rupee fell to 89.76 rupees per dollar, and on 3 December it breached 90 rupees for the first time, closing at a fresh all-time low of 90.19 rupees per dollar, after intraday trading up to 90.30. For the calendar year to that point, the rupee had depreciated by about 5 per cent against the dollar, even though India's growth remained strong and inflation had eased, a combination that puzzled some observers.

Several factors were cited for the weakness. India's merchandise trade deficit widened to 41.68 billion dollars in October 2025, from 32.15 billion dollars in September, increasing demand for dollars to pay for imports. Foreign investors sold Indian equities, with net equity outflows for the year reported at more than 16 billion dollars by early December. Importers, anticipating further depreciation, bought dollars in advance, and the lack of visibility on a United States trade deal added to uncertainty. The Reserve Bank intervened at times, but, according to market reporting, restrained its intervention rather than spending reserves to hold a particular level.

A weaker rupee has mixed effects. It makes imports, especially crude oil, more expensive in rupee terms, which can feed into inflation, but it makes Indian exports cheaper in dollar terms, which can help exporters, provided tariffs and demand do not offset the benefit. For households, the most visible effect is on the cost of imported goods, travel, and education abroad, while for the government, it affects the rupee cost of external debt and of oil imports.
takeaways: The rupee closed at a record low of 89.49 rupees per dollar on 21 November 2025 and 89.46 on 28 November, after breaching 89 for the first time.
On 3 December 2025 it breached 90 rupees for the first time, closing at 90.19 rupees per dollar.
India's merchandise trade deficit widened to 41.68 billion dollars in October 2025, from 32.15 billion dollars in September.
relevance: A currency can weaken even when growth is strong, because trade, investment flows, and expectations also set its price.
question: Should the Reserve Bank spend reserves to defend a particular rupee level, or let the market find its level?

title: UPI crosses 20 billion transactions in a month
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilisation of resources, growth, development and employment; Government Budgeting.
paragraphs: The Unified Payments Interface, or UPI, is a real-time payment system developed by the National Payments Corporation of India, which allows instant transfer of money between bank accounts using a mobile phone. Launched in 2016, UPI allows a user to pay a merchant, a friend, or a service provider by scanning a code or entering an identifier, without needing to share bank account details, and it operates around the clock, including on holidays.

In August 2025, UPI crossed 20 billion transactions in a single month for the first time. The platform recorded 20.01 billion transactions in August, up from 19.47 billion in July, with a total value of 24.85 lakh crore rupees, slightly lower than July's 25.08 lakh crore rupees. The average daily volume was 645 million transactions, with an average daily value of about 80,177 crore rupees, and on some days daily volume crossed 700 million. The milestone was announced by the Department of Financial Services and the National Payments Corporation of India.

Year-on-year growth was strong. Transaction volume was about 33 to 34 per cent higher than in August 2024, when about 14.9 billion transactions were recorded, while value was about 21 to 24 per cent higher, depending on the precise comparison used in different reports. The platform had 684 banks live on it in July and August 2025, giving it a reach that spans large public and private banks as well as smaller banks and payment providers.

The milestone matters for three reasons. First, it shows the scale of India's digital payment infrastructure, which now handles more transactions in a month than many countries' payment systems handle in a year. Second, it shows how a public infrastructure, built by a non-profit company owned by banks and the Reserve Bank, can support a competitive market of apps and providers on top of it. Third, it raises questions about fraud, failed transactions, and digital exclusion, since a system used by hundreds of millions of people must also work for people with limited connectivity, literacy, or access to a smartphone.

UPI's growth has also attracted international interest, with several countries exploring similar instant payment systems or linking to UPI for cross-border payments. That interest, however, should not obscure the domestic challenge: maintaining reliability, security, and low cost at a scale of 20 billion transactions a month, while ensuring that the benefits reach small merchants and rural users as well as urban smartphone users.
takeaways: UPI recorded 20.01 billion transactions in August 2025, for the first time crossing 20 billion in a month, with a value of 24.85 lakh crore rupees.
UPI was launched by the National Payments Corporation of India in 2016 and had 684 banks live on it in August 2025.
Average daily volume in August 2025 was 645 million transactions, with an average daily value of about 80,177 crore rupees.
relevance: A public payment infrastructure can support a competitive market, but scale also creates new risks around fraud and exclusion.
question: Should instant payments be free for users, or should someone pay for the infrastructure that makes them possible?

title: Fourth largest? Why India's ranking claim changed in 2025
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilisation of resources, growth, development and employment; Government Budgeting.
paragraphs: In May 2025, NITI Aayog Chief Executive Officer B. V. R. Subrahmanyam told a press briefing, after the 10th Governing Council meeting, that India had become the world's fourth-largest economy. His words were widely reported: we are the fourth largest economy as I speak. We are a 4 trillion dollar economy as I speak, and this is not my data. This is IMF data. India today is larger than Japan. Until 2024, India had been the world's fifth-largest economy, behind the United States, China, Germany, and Japan.

The claim rested on a projection, not on final data. The International Monetary Fund's World Economic Outlook of April 2025 projected India's nominal gross domestic product at 4,187 billion dollars for 2025, just ahead of Japan's 4,186 billion dollars, a margin of about one billion dollars on economies of more than four trillion dollars each. A margin that small can be reversed by a small change in growth, prices, or exchange rates, and it was not a measured, final ranking.

By October 2025, the IMF's updated outlook had reversed the order. Japan was projected at 4,280 billion dollars and India at 4,125 billion dollars, putting Japan back in fourth place and India in fifth. The change reflected, among other factors, a weaker rupee, which reduces India's dollar-denominated GDP, and stronger-than-expected performance in Japan, including yen appreciation. Contemporary analysis noted that India's nominal growth in the April to June quarter had been lower than projected, while Japan's real growth and currency had performed better.

The episode is a useful lesson in how to read rankings. A ranking based on nominal GDP in current United States dollars is sensitive to exchange rates, so a country can rise or fall in the ranking without any change in what its people actually produce. A ranking based on purchasing power parity, which adjusts for price differences, gives a different order, and a ranking based on GDP per person, which divides output by population, gives a very different picture again, with India far lower than fourth.

The government's year-end economic review, reported in December 2025, again described India as having overtaken Japan, with GDP valued at 4.18 trillion dollars, and said the ranking would be confirmed in 2026 once final annual data were released. As of 1 November 2026, readers should therefore treat fourth largest as a contested claim based on projections and on the choice of measure, not as a settled fact, and should check which vintage of IMF data and which measure, nominal or purchasing power parity, a particular claim uses.
takeaways: In May 2025 the NITI Aayog CEO said India had become the fourth-largest economy, citing IMF data, with India at 4,187 billion dollars and Japan at 4,186 billion in the April 2025 outlook.
The IMF's October 2025 outlook reversed the order, putting Japan at 4,280 billion dollars and India at 4,125 billion dollars.
Nominal GDP rankings in dollars are sensitive to exchange rates, so a small currency move can reverse a ranking based on a one-billion-dollar margin.
relevance: A ranking that depends on a one-billion-dollar margin on a four-trillion-dollar economy is a projection, not a settled fact.
question: Should India celebrate a size ranking, or focus on income per person and living standards?

title: Retail inflation falls to 0.25 per cent in October 2025
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilisation of resources, growth, development and employment; Government Budgeting.
paragraphs: Retail inflation, measured by the Consumer Price Index, tracks how much more, or less, a representative basket of goods and services costs compared with a year earlier. The Reserve Bank of India is required to keep consumer price inflation at 4 per cent, within a band of 2 percentage points on either side, so the monthly inflation print is one of the most watched numbers in Indian economic policy. It affects interest rate decisions, household budgets, and wage negotiations.

In October 2025, retail inflation fell to 0.25 per cent year-on-year, the lowest in the current Consumer Price Index series, which began in 2015 with 2012 as the base year. The figure was down 119 basis points from September 2025, whose print was revised to 1.44 per cent, and it followed a steady moderation through 2025. Food inflation, measured by the Consumer Food Price Index, fell to minus 5.02 per cent, meaning food items were on average 5 per cent cheaper than a year earlier, with vegetables, pulses, spices, cereals, and eggs all contributing to the decline.

Three factors explained the low print, according to the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation. First, a favourable base effect: inflation a year earlier, in October 2024, had been 6.2 per cent, so even a normal price level in October 2025 looked low by comparison. Second, sustained falls in food prices, driven by better supply and moderating global prices. Third, the full month's impact of GST rate cuts that took effect on 22 September 2025, which reduced prices in transport and communication, clothing and footwear, health, and other categories.

The headline figure, however, concealed a different story underneath. Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and fuel prices, was about 4.33 per cent in October, up slightly from September, driven in part by gold and silver prices, with gold inflation reported at about 57.8 per cent. Excluding gold, core inflation was lower, at about 2.6 per cent, according to contemporary reporting. Rural inflation fell to minus 0.25 per cent, while urban inflation was 0.88 per cent, and Kerala recorded the highest state inflation, at 8.56 per cent, driven by food and gold prices.

In November 2025, headline inflation rose again, to 0.71 per cent, as food deflation eased to minus 3.91 per cent and vegetable, egg, meat, fish, spice, and fuel prices rose. The October low was therefore a trough, not a new normal, and it illustrates why a single month's inflation figure should not be read in isolation. A low headline rate driven by food and a base effect can coexist with firmer core inflation, and both matter for policy.
takeaways: Retail inflation fell to 0.25 per cent in October 2025, the lowest in the current CPI series, down from a revised 1.44 per cent in September.
Food inflation fell to minus 5.02 per cent in October, driven by lower vegetable, pulse, and cereal prices and by GST cuts from 22 September 2025.
Core inflation was about 4.33 per cent in October, with gold inflation at about 57.8 per cent, and headline inflation rose to 0.71 per cent in November.
relevance: A headline inflation low driven by food and a base effect can hide firmer prices elsewhere in the basket.
question: Should monetary policy respond to a headline rate, or to core inflation that excludes food and fuel?

title: The India–United States trade deal of 2026: from 50 per cent tariffs to the edge of agreement
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy — growth, development and employment; effects of liberalisation on the economy (trade).
paragraphs: For most of 2025, India faced the steepest American tariffs of any major trading partner. After trade talks collapsed in August 2025, the United States imposed duties of up to 50 per cent on most Indian goods: a 25 per cent reciprocal tariff plus a further 25 per cent penalty linked to India's purchases of Russian oil. The duties hit labour-intensive exports such as textiles, gems and jewellery, and seafood, and they became the single largest shock to India's export economy in years.

The logjam began to break in February 2026, when the two sides agreed a framework for a first-phase deal. Under it, Washington cut the reciprocal tariff on Indian goods from 25 per cent to 18 per cent and removed the additional 25 per cent Russian-oil duty. In return, India committed to eliminate or reduce tariffs on American industrial goods and a range of farm products, including tree nuts, fruit, soybean oil, wine and spirits. The framework did not, however, settle the deal: it left the detailed text, and the question of how Indian exporters would compare with competitors, to further negotiation.

By October 2026 the first tranche was, in the words of Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal, going through its final contours and legal drafting. Goyal said India would finalise it only once it secured a competitive advantage over peer exporters such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Indonesia. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar described the talks as nearing a landing point, while United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on 2 October that a deal was not imminent. United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio, visiting Mumbai on 20 October, said the two sides were very close, with only a small number of items left. Dairy access for American producers is reported to be the biggest remaining obstacle.

Two complications hung over the endgame. President Donald Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which could authorise tariffs of up to 100 per cent on buyers of Russian oil, but then waived those tariffs for such buyers. Meanwhile the underlying trade kept growing: India's goods exports to the United States rose to 42.79 billion dollars in April–August 2026, from 40.39 billion dollars a year earlier, and India recorded a trade surplus of nearly 34 billion dollars with the United States in the financial year 2025–26. As of 1 November 2026, no signed final text had been published, so the 18 per cent framework rate and the unfinished negotiation remained the facts on the ground.
takeaways: The United States cut its tariff on most Indian goods from 50 per cent to 18 per cent under a February 2026 framework, removing the Russian-oil penalty duty.
India's stated condition for signing is a tariff advantage over competing exporters such as Vietnam, Bangladesh and Indonesia, with dairy access the reported sticking point.
As of 1 November 2026 the first tranche was in legal drafting but not signed, so exporters still faced an unfinished negotiation.
relevance: Trade negotiations show how tariffs, energy policy and domestic farm politics interact: a deal is not just a tariff number, but a bargain across sectors.
question: Should India accept a deal that gives it the same tariff as Vietnam, or hold out for a lower rate — and what does each choice cost farmers, exporters and consumers?

title: The India–European Union free trade agreement: concluded after nearly two decades
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy — growth, development and employment; effects of liberalisation on the economy (trade).
paragraphs: On 27 January 2026, at the 16th India–European Union Summit in New Delhi, India and the European Union concluded negotiations on a free trade agreement that had been in the works, on and off, since 2007. Talks began that year as a broad-based trade and investment agreement, stalled in 2013, and were relaunched in 2022 alongside parallel negotiations on investment protection and geographical indications. The conclusion was described by India's Commerce Ministry as the mother of all deals: the two sides together cover almost two billion people and roughly a quarter of global gross domestic product.

The headline terms are asymmetric by design. India will eliminate or reduce tariffs on 96.6 per cent of European Union exports by value, while the European Union will reciprocate on 99.5 per cent of Indian goods, according to figures reported from the agreement. The European Commission projects about 4.7 billion dollars in annual duty savings, and has said bilateral exports could double by 2032. The European Union will phase out tariffs on most Indian goods over seven years, while India's reductions stretch over ten years. Bilateral trade in goods already stood at 136.54 billion dollars in 2024–25, making the European Union one of India's largest trading partners.

Two hard issues shaped the negotiation. One was the European Union's carbon border adjustment mechanism, which puts a carbon price on imports of emissions-intensive goods and which Indian exporters feared would blunt their tariff gains. The other was agriculture and automobiles, where both sides protected sensitive sectors: India kept protections for dairy and several farm products, while the European Union guarded its own farm interests. Services, digital trade, intellectual property and supply-chain diversification are also covered, reflecting a modern agreement rather than a simple tariff-cutting pact.

Conclusion is not the same as entry into force. The text still requires legal vetting, signature and ratification on the European side, including approval by the Council of the European Union and consent from the European Parliament, and completion of India's domestic procedures. Reporting in 2026 put entry into force in early 2027. At the same January summit the two sides also signed a Security and Defence Partnership covering maritime security, cyber issues, counter-terrorism, space and defence industry cooperation, signalling that the trade deal sits inside a wider strategic partnership.
takeaways: Negotiations begun in 2007, stalled in 2013 and relaunched in 2022 were concluded on 27 January 2026 at the 16th India–EU Summit.
India will cut tariffs on 96.6 per cent of EU exports by value; the EU will reciprocate on 99.5 per cent of Indian goods, with EU tariff phase-out over seven years and India's over ten.
The deal is concluded but not yet in force: signature and ratification are still required, with entry into force expected in early 2027.
relevance: Big trade deals link economics to strategy: the same summit produced a security partnership, and ratification politics can matter as much as the negotiated text.
question: Does a deal that gives India broad tariff access but leaves carbon border charges and farm protections in place count as a breakthrough, or as a managed compromise?

title: The India–United Kingdom trade deal enters into force
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy — growth, development and employment; effects of liberalisation on the economy (trade).
paragraphs: On 15 July 2026, the India–United Kingdom Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, generally called CETA, entered into force. It had been signed on 24 July 2025 in London by Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal and the then British Business and Trade Secretary Jonathan Reynolds, in the presence of Prime Ministers Narendra Modi and Keir Starmer, after negotiations launched in 2022. It is India's most comprehensive agreement with a G7 economy and, as the British government put it, the United Kingdom's most economically significant bilateral trade deal since leaving the European Union.

The goods terms are front-loaded in India's favour. From entry into force, 99 per cent of Indian goods entering the United Kingdom are duty-free or face reduced tariffs, removing duties that previously reached up to 70 per cent on processed foods, 21.5 per cent on marine products, 18 per cent on engineering goods and auto components, 16 per cent on leather and footwear, 12 per cent on textiles and clothing, and 8 per cent on chemicals and pharmaceuticals. On the Indian side, 64 per cent of British tariff lines became tariff-free immediately, rising to 85 per cent over ten years. Total United Kingdom–India trade was worth 48 billion pounds in 2025.

Alongside the trade agreement, a Double Contributions Convention on social security entered into force the same day. It ensures that employees moving between the two countries, and their employers, pay social security contributions in only one country at a time for up to five years, a provision aimed at Indian professionals on temporary assignments in Britain. The agreement's thirty chapters also cover services, investment, government procurement, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, technical barriers to trade, digital trade and intellectual property, though the House of Commons Library noted that its services provisions are relatively limited and that Indian tariff cuts are phased in over years while Indian exporters gained immediate access in many lines.

The British government estimates the deal will increase bilateral trade by 25.5 billion pounds a year in the long term and raise United Kingdom GDP by 0.13 per cent, or 4.8 billion pounds — modelling projections, not guaranteed outcomes. For India, the early test is practical rather than statistical: whether exporters, especially small firms, register for origin declarations, meet rules of origin, and convert duty-free access into orders. Preferential tariffs are claimed on the basis of an origin declaration by a registered exporter, so paperwork, not just tariff schedules, decides who benefits.
takeaways: Signed on 24 July 2025, the India–UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement entered into force on 15 July 2026.
99 per cent of Indian goods entering the UK are duty-free or reduced-tariff, while 64 per cent of UK tariff lines became tariff-free in India immediately, rising to 85 per cent over ten years.
A Double Contributions Convention also took effect, exempting temporarily posted workers from dual social security contributions for up to five years.
relevance: A signed deal only helps firms that can use it: rules of origin, registration and standards decide whether tariff cuts become real orders.
question: Why would a deal give one side immediate access and phase in the other's cuts over ten years — and is that asymmetry fair, or simply the price of agreement?

title: One year of the India–EFTA deal: investment promises meet export reality
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy — growth, development and employment; effects of liberalisation on the economy (trade).
paragraphs: The India–European Free Trade Association Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement, known as TEPA, completed its first year in force on 1 October 2026. Signed on 10 March 2024 after sixteen years of intermittent negotiations, it is India's first free trade agreement with a bloc of developed European economies: Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland. It has fourteen chapters covering goods, services, investment promotion, intellectual property, government procurement and sustainable development.

TEPA's distinctive feature is not its tariff schedule but its investment pledge. The EFTA states aim to increase foreign direct investment into India by 50 billion dollars within ten years of entry into force and a further 50 billion dollars in the following five years, and to facilitate the creation of one million jobs within fifteen years, with an investment facilitation mechanism to monitor delivery. It is the first time an Indian trade agreement has linked market access to an investment and jobs target of this kind, turning the usual question — who cuts tariffs? — into a second question: does the promised capital actually arrive?

On tariffs, the EFTA states' commitments cover 92.2 per cent of their tariff lines, accounting for 99.6 per cent of India's exports, with full coverage of non-agricultural products. India's commitments cover 82.7 per cent of tariff lines, accounting for 95.3 per cent of EFTA exports. Sensitive sectors such as dairy, gold, coal and soya remain largely untouched on the Indian side. Early evidence cited at the first anniversary was encouraging for Norway: bilateral goods trade between India and Norway grew by 9 per cent and Norwegian exports to India by 34 per cent in the first nine months of TEPA, with tariffs on frozen whole Norwegian salmon falling to zero from day one.

The first anniversary was marked in New Delhi by the second India–EFTA Prosperity Summit in 2026, where Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal urged exporters, industry associations and state governments to make greater use of the agreement. That message is the honest measure of TEPA's first year: the legal architecture and the investment pledge are in place, but utilisation — firms actually claiming preferences and investors actually committing capital — will decide whether the deal becomes a growth story or a well-drafted promise.
takeaways: TEPA, signed on 10 March 2024, entered into force on 1 October 2025 and completed its first year in October 2026.
It is India's first trade deal to link market access to an investment pledge: 100 billion dollars over fifteen years and one million jobs.
EFTA covers 92.2 per cent of tariff lines (99.6 per cent of India's exports); India covers 82.7 per cent of lines, with dairy, gold, coal and soya largely protected.
relevance: Linking trade to investment targets is a new experiment: it tests whether agreements can be judged by capital and jobs delivered, not just tariffs cut.
question: Should future Indian trade deals copy TEPA's investment pledge — and what happens to market access if the investment target is missed?

title: The India–New Zealand free trade agreement: nine months from launch to signature
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy — growth, development and employment; effects of liberalisation on the economy (trade).
paragraphs: On 20 October 2026, the India–New Zealand Free Trade Agreement entered into force, completing one of the fastest trade negotiations India has ever concluded. Negotiations were launched on 16 March 2025 by Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal and New Zealand Trade and Investment Minister Todd McClay, substantively concluded on 22 December 2025 after five formal rounds, signed in New Delhi on 27 April 2026, and ratified by both countries by 21 September 2026. The New Zealand Parliament passed the implementing legislation on 16 September 2026 by 93 votes to 29.

The market-access bargain is deliberately lopsided. New Zealand removed duties on every tariff line for Indian exports from day one, eliminating tariffs of up to 10 per cent on textiles, clothing, leather, footwear, ceramics, carpets, automobiles and auto components. India, in return, will cut or remove duties on about 70 per cent of its tariff lines, covering 95 per cent of bilateral trade by value; about 57 per cent of New Zealand's exports to India enter duty-free immediately, including sheepmeat, wool, coal and most forestry products, with a second round of tariff cuts following on 1 January 2027. India kept protections for dairy and several agricultural products, the politically sensitive core of the negotiation.

Beyond goods, the agreement carries a New Zealand commitment to facilitate 20 billion dollars of investment into India over fifteen years, access for Indian service providers across about 118 sectors and sub-sectors, and new temporary-entry routes for Indian workers and students. The two prime ministers have set an aspirational target of doubling bilateral trade in goods and services to 7 billion New Zealand dollars by 2030. The starting point is modest: in 2025–26 India exported 566.51 million dollars of goods to New Zealand and imported 589.1 million dollars, and total bilateral trade is around 1.3 billion dollars.

Speed was possible because the stakes were small and the politics were aligned: New Zealand wanted agricultural and forestry access, India wanted a demonstration that it could close a modern agreement quickly and give its exporters, especially small firms, a new market. The harder test begins now, as the Commerce Ministry itself has acknowledged: converting zero-duty access into orders requires meeting New Zealand standards, finding distributors, and competing on price and delivery with suppliers that already enjoy preferential access there.
takeaways: Negotiations launched in March 2025 were concluded in December 2025, signed on 27 April 2026 and entered into force on 20 October 2026.
New Zealand removed duties on 100 per cent of Indian tariff lines from day one; India cut duties on about 70 per cent of lines covering 95 per cent of trade value, protecting dairy.
New Zealand also committed to facilitate 20 billion dollars of investment into India over fifteen years, with a goal of doubling bilateral trade by 2030.
relevance: Small deals can be strategic: they test negotiating machinery, create precedents on services and investment, and give exporters a low-risk new market.
question: Is a fast, small deal with a 1.3-billion-dollar partner worth more as a template for bigger negotiations, or as trade in its own right?

title: India–Australia: the interim deal works, the comprehensive deal waits
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy — growth, development and employment; effects of liberalisation on the economy (trade).
paragraphs: India and Australia already trade under a deal, but not yet the deal both governments say they want. The Economic Cooperation and Trade Agreement, ECTA, signed in April 2022 and in force since 29 December 2022, was deliberately an interim, early-harvest agreement: it gave most Indian goods duty-free entry to Australia and cheaper access for Australian lentils, wool, sheepmeat and wine into India, while leaving services, investment, digital trade and government procurement for a fuller Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement, CECA, that has been under negotiation, with interruptions, since 2011.

The results of the interim deal are visible in the trade data. India's exports to Australia nearly doubled after ECTA came into force, rising to 7.28 billion dollars in 2025–26 from 4 billion dollars in 2020–21, and bilateral trade stood at 21.09 billion dollars in 2025–26. At the third India–Australia Annual Summit in Melbourne on 8–10 July 2026, Prime Ministers Narendra Modi and Anthony Albanese reaffirmed their commitment to an ambitious, balanced and mutually beneficial CECA and agreed to fast-track negotiations, alongside work on a standalone Bilateral Investment Treaty. No deadline was set, and CECA was not signed at the summit.

The Melbourne summit did produce one long-awaited step: an Administrative Arrangement operationalising the civil nuclear cooperation agreement signed in 2014 and in force since November 2015, opening the way for commercial uranium arrangements between Australian miners and Indian utilities. The summit also discussed critical minerals, renewable energy, technology, agritech, education and defence cooperation, including an Australia–India Defence Innovation Corridor. Reports from the summit's CEO Forum described a roadmap to lift two-way trade to 100 billion dollars by 2030, a target Australia's Trade Minister Don Farrell had earlier framed as reaching 100 billion dollars by the end of the decade.

The pattern is familiar in trade diplomacy: an early-harvest deal delivers measurable gains and political momentum, but the comprehensive deal stalls on the hardest issues — agricultural access, services liberalisation and investment protection. For students of negotiation, the India–Australia story is a case study in sequencing: lock in what is possible early, keep the comprehensive ambition alive, and accept that the last fifth of a trade negotiation often takes longer than the first four-fifths.
takeaways: ECTA, in force since 29 December 2022, was an interim deal; the fuller CECA, negotiated since 2011, remains unsigned.
India's exports to Australia rose from 4 billion dollars in 2020–21 to 7.28 billion dollars in 2025–26; bilateral trade was 21.09 billion dollars.
At the July 2026 Melbourne summit the leaders agreed to fast-track CECA and operationalised the 2014 civil nuclear agreement, but set no CECA deadline.
relevance: Early-harvest deals show how negotiators sequence ambition: bank the easy gains first, then bargain over the sensitive sectors that remain.
question: Does an interim deal help or hinder a comprehensive one — does it build trust, or does it remove the urgency to finish?

title: The ASEAN trade review: fixing a deficit that widened for fifteen years
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy — growth, development and employment; effects of liberalisation on the economy (trade).
paragraphs: India's oldest major regional trade pact is also its most lopsided. The ASEAN–India Trade in Goods Agreement, AITIGA, was signed in 2009 and implemented from 2010, and in the years since, India's trade deficit with the ten-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations has widened from about 7 billion dollars in 2010 to 51.55 billion dollars in 2025–26. Bilateral trade reached 128.38 billion dollars in 2025–26, with ASEAN accounting for 10.55 per cent of India's total global trade, so the relationship is far too large to walk away from — but, in India's argument, too unbalanced to leave unchanged.

That is why the two sides are reviewing the agreement. ASEAN agreed to a review after India raised concerns about the deficit, but agreeing on the terms of the review has proved difficult, and hopes that it would conclude at the ASEAN–India Summit in October 2025 were not met. At the 15th AITIGA Joint Committee meeting in Jakarta from 6 to 9 October 2026, co-chaired by Additional Secretary Nitin Kumar Yadav of India's Department of Commerce and Malaysia's Deputy Secretary-General Mastura Ahmad Mustafa, the committee directed its eight sub-committees to expedite pending chapters with firm, time-bound deliverables. Three sub-committees — on legal and institutional issues, national treatment and market access, and rules of origin — met alongside the committee. The next Joint Committee meeting is scheduled in India in January 2027.

India's asks in the review are specific. It wants to correct tariff asymmetries and remove non-tariff barriers that limit its exports, and it wants stronger rules of origin to prevent what it describes as circumvention: Chinese goods allegedly routed through ASEAN countries to claim preferential tariffs. ASEAN members, for their part, have pressed for deeper tariff cuts from India. The Department of Commerce has sought industry feedback on products where tariffs could be reduced without harming domestic manufacturers, favouring lines where India is a net exporter.

The AITIGA review is a test of a wider question in Indian trade policy: whether agreements signed in an earlier era, when India was more defensive about opening its market, can be rebalanced without unravelling them. The review's slow pace — years of talks, a missed 2025 deadline, and a January 2027 meeting as the next milestone — shows how hard it is to renegotiate a deal with ten partners who have different interests, even when all sides accept, as the Jakarta statement did, that the outcome should be balanced, constructive and forward-looking.
takeaways: AITIGA, signed in 2009 and in force from 2010, coincided with India's ASEAN deficit widening from about 7 billion dollars to 51.55 billion dollars by 2025–26.
The 15th Joint Committee met in Jakarta on 6–9 October 2026, directing eight sub-committees to set time-bound deliverables; the next meeting is in India in January 2027.
India seeks corrected tariff asymmetries, fewer non-tariff barriers and tighter rules of origin; ASEAN seeks deeper tariff cuts from India.
relevance: Renegotiating a trade deal is harder than signing one: ten partners, entrenched export interests and rules-of-origin politics all slow a review down.
question: If tariff cuts under the original deal widened the deficit, should India demand rebalancing first — or accept that deficits also reflect competitiveness, not just treaty terms?

title: The Gulf corridor: from a 100-billion-dollar milestone to a 200-billion-dollar target
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy — growth, development and employment; effects of liberalisation on the economy (trade).
paragraphs: India's fastest-growing major trade corridor runs west, across the Arabian Sea. The India–United Arab Emirates Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, CEPA, signed on 18 February 2022 and in force since 1 May 2022, has driven bilateral trade past 100 billion dollars ahead of schedule: trade reached 101.24 billion dollars in the financial year 2025–26, crossing the 100-billion mark for the second consecutive year, with non-oil trade accounting for nearly two-thirds of the total. India's exports to the UAE are led by gems and jewellery at 8.68 billion dollars, followed by engineering goods, petroleum products, electronic goods, chemicals, garments and agricultural products.

In January 2026, during the UAE President's visit to India, the two sides set a new target: doubling bilateral trade to 200 billion dollars by 2032, alongside a long-term liquefied natural gas supply deal and deeper cooperation in defence, space and emerging technologies. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to the UAE on 15 May 2026 produced further agreements covering energy, defence, shipbuilding, artificial intelligence infrastructure and investments of up to 5 billion dollars. The corridor has also moved beyond hydrocarbons: non-oil trade grew by nearly 20 per cent in one year to about 65 billion dollars, and the two governments have set a goal of 100 billion dollars in non-oil, non-precious-metal trade by 2030.

The Gulf story now extends beyond the UAE. India and Oman signed a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement on 18 December 2025, under which Oman has committed to eliminating duties on 98.08 per cent of its tariff lines, covering a reported 99.38 per cent of India's current exports to Oman by value. The UAE model — a fast, comprehensive agreement followed by investment, energy and technology cooperation — is being repeated as a template for the wider Gulf Cooperation Council region, with which India's total trade reached 178.56 billion dollars in 2024–25, about 15.42 per cent of India's global trade.

One structural fact tempers the success story. India's trade deficit with the UAE remained high, at 26.8 billion dollars in 2024–25, because crude oil imports are relatively price-inelastic: India buys energy it cannot easily replace, while its exports must compete for every order. The Gulf corridor therefore illustrates both the promise and the limit of trade agreements. They can accelerate non-oil trade, investment and strategic cooperation, but they cannot by themselves remove a deficit rooted in energy dependence.
takeaways: The India–UAE CEPA (in force 1 May 2022) took bilateral trade to 101.24 billion dollars in 2025–26, the second year above 100 billion dollars.
In January 2026 the two sides set a target of 200 billion dollars in trade by 2032, with non-oil trade already near two-thirds of the total.
India and Oman signed a CEPA on 18 December 2025, with Oman eliminating duties on a reported 98.08 per cent of tariff lines.
relevance: Trade corridors show that agreements work best in sequence: a trade pact, then energy, investment and technology deals that deepen the same relationship.
question: Can a trade corridor built on energy imports ever be balanced — or should India judge the Gulf partnership by investment and non-oil trade instead of the deficit?

title: Indian textiles under American tariffs: a labour-intensive sector takes the hit
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy — growth, development and employment; effects of liberalisation on the economy (trade).
paragraphs: Few sectors felt the 2025–26 American tariff shock as directly as textiles and apparel. The United States is the single largest market for India's textile and apparel exporters, and from 27 August 2025 to 7 February 2026 Indian exporters faced a combined 50 per cent American tariff: 25 per cent reciprocal duty plus a 25 per cent penalty linked to Russian oil purchases. On 7 February 2026 the penalty duty was removed by executive order, giving partial relief, but exporters still faced a higher reciprocal duty than competitors — 25 per cent against 20 per cent for Bangladesh and Vietnam, according to industry analysis at the time — and were compelled to absorb much of the burden by offering discounts of 15 to 18 per cent to American retailers.

The trade data shows the strain. Ready-made garment exports rose 2.4 per cent to 12 billion dollars in April–December 2025, helped by demand from Japan, Saudi Arabia and Italy, but shipments to the United States fell 3 per cent to 3.6 billion dollars. In April–August 2026, textile exports grew 6.94 per cent while apparel exports fell 9.10 per cent, leaving total textile and apparel exports marginally lower by 0.24 per cent year-on-year. Credit rating agency ICRA had earlier revised its outlook for export-oriented apparel firms to negative for 2025–26, projecting a revenue decline of 6 to 9 per cent and a fall in operating margins from 10 per cent in 2024–25 to about 7.5 per cent.

A second American measure added a different kind of pressure in 2026. From 24 July 2026, the United States imposed Section 301 tariffs linked to forced-labour import prohibitions on covered imports from 60 economies. India was set at 10 per cent after adopting a forced-labour import prohibition, while Vietnam was set at about 12 per cent, according to a September 2026 industry report; four textile-producing competitors — Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia and Malaysia — were included in a tariff-rate quota mechanism tied to their imports of American cotton and textile inputs, from which India was excluded. Industry estimates cited in that reporting suggested compliance costs could reduce exporter margins by 8 to 10 per cent.

The Confederation of Indian Textile Industry warned in September 2026 that further American tariffs under the newly signed Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act would be very difficult for the micro, small and medium enterprise-dominated sector to absorb. The episode illustrates a structural point: labour-intensive export sectors are the most exposed to tariff wars, because their margins are thin, their buyers can switch suppliers quickly, and their workers — in clusters such as Tirupur, Panipat and Solapur — feel the adjustment first.
takeaways: From 27 August 2025 to 7 February 2026 Indian textiles faced a combined 50 per cent US tariff; the penalty half was then removed, leaving a higher reciprocal duty than competitors faced.
Garment exports to the US fell 3 per cent to 3.6 billion dollars in April–December 2025, and apparel exports fell 9.10 per cent in April–August 2026.
From July 2026, Section 301 forced-labour tariffs added compliance costs, with India at a reported 10 per cent and excluded from a quota mechanism offered to four competitors.
relevance: Tariff wars are not abstract: they land hardest on thin-margin, labour-intensive sectors, where discounts and lost orders translate quickly into jobs.
question: If tariff relief depends on American law rather than a signed deal, how should exporters and policymakers plan — diversify markets, or wait for Washington?

title: Record exports in a fractured trading system
syllabus: GS III — Indian Economy — growth, development and employment; effects of liberalisation on the economy (trade).
paragraphs: India closed the financial year 2025–26 with a headline that survived a year of tariff turmoil: total exports of goods and services reached a record 863.11 billion dollars, up 4.6 per cent from 825.26 billion dollars in 2024–25, according to Commerce Ministry figures. Merchandise exports grew only 0.93 per cent to 441.78 billion dollars, held back by disrupted shipping and uncertain demand, while services exports grew 8.71 per cent to a lifetime high of 421.32 billion dollars, reflecting sustained global demand for Indian information technology, business and professional services. Total imports, however, rose faster, to 979.65 billion dollars, widening the overall trade deficit.

The export performance was helped, the government told Parliament in July 2026, by expanding market access under India's free trade agreements. Among FTA partners, merchandise exports were highest to ASEAN countries at 38.42 billion dollars, followed by the UAE at 37.36 billion dollars, SAFTA countries at 25.77 billion dollars, the United Kingdom at 13.44 billion dollars and Singapore at 11.86 billion dollars. The pattern shows the dual engine of Indian trade: services, where India runs a large surplus, and merchandise, where growth is slower and more exposed to tariffs, shipping disruption and geopolitical shocks.

The global picture in 2026 was unexpectedly resilient. In its Global Trade Outlook update of 8 October 2026, the World Trade Organization raised its forecast for world merchandise trade volume growth to 3.9 per cent in 2026, up from 1.9 per cent in its March baseline, and to 4.1 per cent in 2027. The upgrade was driven by an artificial-intelligence investment boom: trade in AI-enabling goods such as semiconductors and servers jumped 67 per cent year-on-year in the first half of 2026 and accounted for 47 per cent of global merchandise trade growth. Asia was expected to lead, with exports rising 9.9 per cent, while the WTO downgraded its services trade forecast to 3.3 per cent for 2026 because the Middle East conflict raised aviation fuel costs and disrupted transport and travel.

The lesson of 2026 for trade policy is that resilience and vulnerability can coexist. Supply chains adapted to war and tariffs faster than forecasters expected, and AI investment created a powerful new driver of goods trade. At the same time, the gains were uneven: services trade slowed, West Asian exports were forecast to contract 17.2 per cent, and the WTO warned that higher fuel and fertiliser costs from the Strait of Hormuz disruption, the war in Ukraine and any slowdown in AI investment remained live risks to the outlook.
takeaways: India's total exports hit a record 863.11 billion dollars in 2025–26: merchandise 441.78 billion dollars (+0.93 per cent), services 421.32 billion dollars (+8.71 per cent).
The WTO raised its 2026 world merchandise trade growth forecast to 3.9 per cent in October 2026, from 1.9 per cent in March, driven by AI-related goods trade.
Trade in AI-enabling goods rose 67 per cent in early 2026 and made up 47 per cent of merchandise trade growth, while services trade was downgraded to 3.3 per cent.
relevance: Aggregate records can hide a split story: services surging while goods crawl, and global growth driven by one sector, AI hardware, rather than broad demand.
question: When one technology boom drives nearly half of world trade growth, is the trading system resilient — or newly concentrated and fragile?

title: The 2026 Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz crisis
syllabus: GS II — India and its neighbourhood — relations; bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements; important international institutions, agencies and fora.
paragraphs: On 28 February 2026, the United States and Israel launched an air war against Iran, following the failure of nuclear negotiations in Geneva and a shorter twelve-day air conflict in 2025. Iran retaliated with attacks on Israel and American military installations across the region, and its Revolutionary Guard Corps moved to close the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman through which about a quarter of the world's seaborne oil trade and a fifth of its liquefied natural gas passed before the war. Merchant ships were boarded and attacked, sea mines were laid, and shipping through the strait was largely blocked.

The United States responded with a naval blockade of Iranian ports from 13 April to 29 May 2026 and an aerial campaign against Iranian targets along the strait. A ceasefire was reached on 8 April, according to reporting on the conflict, but it did not reopen the strait or end the standoff: by late October 2026 the United States was moving additional naval forces and marines towards the region, two carrier strike groups were already in the wider theatre with a third on the way, and Gulf states were reported to have been briefed on the possibility of American strikes after the United States midterm elections on 3 November. Iran, meanwhile, warned that any fresh attack would risk a much wider regional war, and Iranian representatives met Qatari mediators in Doha on 31 October.

The economic shock travelled far beyond the Gulf. Oil prices rose above 100 dollars a barrel, and the average price of petrol in the United States reached 4.30 dollars a gallon by late October 2026, up from less than 3 dollars before the war began — the highest in four years, according to the American Automobile Association. The World Trade Organization cited the Middle East conflict, higher energy prices and disruption to transport routes as a key risk to its trade outlook, downgrading its services trade forecast and warning of higher fuel and fertiliser costs. For India, which imports most of its crude oil by sea, the crisis underlined the vulnerability of energy supply routes it does not control.

The war also exposed the limits of military superiority at sea. Despite the United States possessing the world's most formidable navy, it had not, by November 2026, fully reopened the strait to normal shipping, and tanker incidents continued to be reported in late October. The episode is a textbook case of geographic coercion: a coastal state using mines, missiles, drones and the regulation of authorised routes to impose costs on far stronger adversaries, and a reminder that control of a chokepoint can matter as much as victory in battle.
takeaways: The US–Israeli air war on Iran began on 28 February 2026; Iran responded by largely blocking the Strait of Hormuz, a route for about a quarter of seaborne oil trade.
A ceasefire in April did not end the standoff: the strait stayed contested, the US blockaded Iranian ports, and escalation risks remained live in late October 2026.
The shock raised global oil prices above 100 dollars a barrel and US petrol to 4.30 dollars a gallon, with knock-on effects on trade, transport and fertiliser costs.
relevance: Chokepoints are a core concept in geopolitics: whoever can close a strait can raise costs for the whole world economy without winning a war.
question: Does a blockade of a global waterway strengthen the blockading state's bargaining power, or does it unite the world against it?

title: Ukraine in 2026: fighting continues while talks resume
syllabus: GS II — India and its neighbourhood — relations; bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements; important international institutions, agencies and fora.
paragraphs: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, begun in February 2022, entered its fifth year in 2026 as a grinding war of attrition in which both sides repeatedly struck each other's energy infrastructure. There was no general ceasefire in force as of late October 2026. Ukraine's General Staff reported 269 combat clashes in a single day on 20 October, including heavy fighting on the Kostiantynivka and Pokrovsk fronts, and Russian strikes in late October left more than 500,000 Ukrainians without electricity, according to Ukraine's Energy Ministry. A localised ceasefire did begin on 27 October around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, to allow aid deliveries and evacuations, but both sides continued strikes elsewhere, including on Kyiv.

Diplomacy restarted in parallel. After United States envoy Steve Witkoff met President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on 21 October, Putin agreed in principle to resume United States–Russia–Ukraine trilateral talks after 10 November, possibly in Abu Dhabi, while insisting that the goal was a final peace agreement, not a short ceasefire. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he supported resuming talks and would accept a ceasefire freezing the current front line, and reiterated willingness for a complete or partial ceasefire, including moratoriums on energy strikes or in the Black Sea. Kremlin officials, however, continued to reject ceasefire proposals, with spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying continued talks did not imply restrictions on military operations.

The gap between the two positions is the heart of the negotiation. Russia demands full control of the Donbas region and opposes Ukraine joining NATO, and has revived its long-standing demand that NATO roll back its post-1997 enlargement. Ukraine will not cede Ukrainian-held Donbas territory such as Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, and wants strong security guarantees. An energy ceasefire announced by President Donald Trump on 11 October failed to hold: Zelenskyy said Ukraine refrained from striking Russian energy targets for three days, then resumed, citing continued Russian strikes.

For students of conflict resolution, Ukraine in 2026 illustrates the difference between a ceasefire, a freeze and a settlement. A local humanitarian pause, an energy moratorium and a final peace agreement are three different things, and the parties' disagreement is not only about territory but about sequencing: whether fighting stops first and terms follow, or terms are agreed first and fighting stops only then.
takeaways: No general ceasefire was in force in late October 2026, though a local humanitarian pause began around Oleshky on 27 October.
Putin agreed in principle to resume US–Russia–Ukraine trilateral talks after 10 November, possibly in Abu Dhabi, seeking a final agreement rather than a short ceasefire.
The core gap remains territory and security: Russia demands all of Donbas and opposes NATO membership; Ukraine accepts a front-line freeze but not ceding held territory.
relevance: Peace processes have stages — humanitarian pauses, partial moratoriums, freezes, settlements — and confusing one for another is a common analytical error.
question: Should mediators push for a ceasefire first even if the final terms are unresolved, or does a ceasefire without terms simply freeze an unjust outcome?

title: Gaza one year after the peace plan: ceasefire without reconstruction
syllabus: GS II — India and its neighbourhood — relations; bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements; important international institutions, agencies and fora.
paragraphs: The Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict, a twenty-point plan brokered by the United States, came into effect on 10 October 2025, bringing a ceasefire, the release of Israeli captives and Palestinian prisoners, and a promise of reconstruction, humanitarian access, Israeli withdrawal to agreed lines, a transitional Palestinian administration and an International Stabilization Force. One year on, October 2026 assessments describe implementation as largely stalled. The American Friends Service Committee's report card of 13 October 2026 found that Israel had complied in full with only one of the twenty points — the release of 250 Palestinian prisoners and 1,700 detained Palestinians — while the United States had failed to deliver on its commitments, and assessed that Israel had killed at least 1,460 Palestinians in Gaza since the ceasefire began, bringing the total killed to more than 75,000.

Some institutional steps did occur. The National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, the technocratic body meant to run Gaza's municipal and public services, was formed in January 2026, and Hamas relinquished control to it on 6 July. A roadmap published in July 2026 set out a phased path to a second phase, including verification by an International Verification Committee, deployment of the International Stabilization Force to separate Israeli forces from committee-controlled areas, and eventual disarmament arrangements under which only the committee would hold weapons. But the committee had not established itself inside Gaza, the force had not deployed as envisaged, and reconstruction had made little meaningful progress, leaving displaced families in temporary shelters and damaged buildings.

Humanitarian access remained far below the plan's own benchmark. The plan envisaged aid returning to previous levels of about 600 trucks a day; Israel was allowing an average of only 217 trucks a day, according to the October 2026 assessment, and the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification projected about 1.4 million Palestinians in Gaza facing hunger through at least December 2026. A 25-billion-dollar economic development and reconstruction plan presented by Jared Kushner at Davos in January 2026 was drawn up without consultation with Palestinians, according to the same assessment, and no action had followed.

The deadlock's core is sequencing. Israel has insisted that complete Hamas disarmament precede rehabilitation of the Strip; Hamas has refused to disarm completely without parallel Israeli steps, including withdrawal. The Board of Peace created to oversee implementation, endorsed by United Nations Security Council Resolution 2803 of 2025, has been criticised for sidelining the Palestinian Authority and the United Nations Relief and Works Agency. Gaza in 2026 is thus a case study in the gap between signing a plan and implementing one — and in how a ceasefire that stops major offensives can coexist with continued killing, blocked aid and unbuilt homes.
takeaways: The twenty-point Gaza plan took effect on 10 October 2025; one year on, an October 2026 report card found Israel in full compliance with only one point.
A technocratic administration was formed in January 2026 and Hamas handed control to it on 6 July, but it had not established itself inside Gaza and reconstruction barely began.
Aid averaged about 217 trucks a day against a plan benchmark of about 600, with about 1.4 million Palestinians projected to face hunger through December 2026.
relevance: Implementation is where peace plans succeed or fail: institutions, sequencing and verification matter as much as the signed text.
question: When disarmament and withdrawal are each conditioned on the other happening first, who should move first — and who can verify that they did?

title: The Trump–Xi summit of 2026: a truce extended, not a trade war ended
syllabus: GS II — India and its neighbourhood — relations; bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements; important international institutions, agencies and fora.
paragraphs: On 24 September 2026, Chinese President Xi Jinping made his first state visit to the United States since 2015, meeting President Donald Trump in Washington for a day of closed-door talks and a state dinner. The summit was the most closely watched diplomatic event of the year between the world's two largest economies, and its most important outcome was announced before the leaders even sat down: the existing United States–China trade truce, due to expire on 10 November 2026, would be extended by two months, to 10 January 2027. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the extension as Xi arrived, saying it would allow negotiations to continue, while stopping short of promising a broader agreement.

The summit produced a framework rather than a comprehensive deal. The two sides agreed to pursue lower tariffs on about 30 billion dollars of non-sensitive goods in each direction, to operationalise their Boards of Trade and Investment, and to establish a bilateral dialogue on superintelligence and artificial-intelligence-related incidents. China committed to importing at least 10 million tonnes of American coal annually in 2027 and 2028, and announced it would send two pandas to the Atlanta zoo, a traditional gesture of stable ties. The framework was significant, but it did not mean tariffs had disappeared: businesses still needed to establish which products qualified and when changes took effect.

The structural disputes remained untouched. Rare earths and critical-mineral supply, technology restrictions, Chinese purchases of American agricultural products, broader tariffs, and Taiwan all remained unresolved. On Taiwan, China reiterated calls for the United States to formally oppose Taiwan independence, while a proposed 14-billion-dollar American arms package for Taiwan was reported stalled in mid-October. On 16 October, China proposed expanding export controls on technologies related to artificial intelligence, biotechnology and solar power, adding a new point of tension to the technology relationship.

Analysts described the outcome as de-escalation, not a reset. The extension removed the threat of a renewed tariff spike before the year's end, carrying the truce through the United States midterm elections and the Christmas shopping season, but it was shorter than many market expectations, and the next checkpoints were already fixed: the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders' meeting in Shenzhen on 18–19 November 2026 and the G20 summit in Miami on 14–15 December 2026. The summit thus illustrates managed instability: two rivals using deadlines and extensions to keep competition from becoming confrontation, without resolving the competition itself.
takeaways: Xi Jinping's first US state visit since 2015, on 24 September 2026, extended the US–China trade truce from 10 November 2026 to 10 January 2027.
The summit agreed a framework: lower tariffs on about 30 billion dollars of goods each way, trade and investment boards, and an AI-incidents dialogue.
Rare earths, technology restrictions, farm purchases and Taiwan remained unresolved, with China proposing wider tech export controls in October.
relevance: Great-power rivalry is often managed through deadlines: truces, extensions and summit frameworks can stabilise relations without settling them.
question: Is a two-month truce extension a sign of strength — buying time to negotiate — or of weakness, because neither side can accept a lasting deal?

title: BRICS in New Delhi: India's chair year and the limits of consensus
syllabus: GS II — India and its neighbourhood — relations; bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements; important international institutions, agencies and fora.
paragraphs: India chaired BRICS in 2026 and hosted the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on 12–13 September 2026, under the theme Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability. The grouping now has eleven members — Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates — accounting, by the chair's account, for about 49 per cent of the world's population and 40 per cent of global GDP. The summit capped more than 400 BRICS meetings across 30 Indian cities, and adopted the New Delhi Declaration by consensus, despite divergence among members on West Asia, notably between Iran and the UAE.

The declaration's political messages were carefully balanced. Members condemned unilateral tariffs and sanctions, supported reform of the World Trade Organization and the United Nations Security Council, and called for maximum restraint in West Asia without attributing blame. On economics, the bloc again declined to endorse a common currency, favouring payment-system interoperability and local-currency settlement instead. Institutional outcomes included a BRICS Incubator Network, a Startup Innovation Fund, a Grain Exchange framework, a logistics and supply-chain cooperation framework, a digital public infrastructure repository, and a 2026–2030 Global Value Chain Action Plan. India also proposed a ten-point global governance reform roadmap based on representation, responsiveness and rule-making.

The summit's symbolism mattered as much as its text. Xi Jinping attended in person, his first visit to India since 2019, and Vladimir Putin also participated, demonstrating India's ability to engage multiple major powers simultaneously while facing American tariff pressure linked to its Russian crude imports. The Modi–Putin meeting set a bilateral trade target of 100 billion dollars by 2030, and the Modi–Xi meeting addressed border stabilisation and economic normalisation, though neither meeting resolved the underlying disputes. India used the summit to present BRICS as a platform for Global South representation and practical cooperation rather than an explicitly anti-Western bloc.

The limits were equally visible. BRICS has no permanent secretariat with dedicated expertise, funding and negotiating authority, and most of the summit's measures remain at the framework stage. The trade arithmetic also cuts against the rhetoric: India's deficit with BRICS partners widened to a reported 226 billion dollars in 2025–26, from 75 billion dollars in 2021, even as India targeted 200 billion dollars of exports to BRICS by 2030. The test of India's chair year, as analysts noted, is whether portals, frameworks and declarations turn into orders, settlements and reforms under China's chairmanship in 2027.
takeaways: India hosted the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on 12–13 September 2026, with eleven members, under the theme of resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability.
The New Delhi Declaration was adopted by consensus, condemning unilateral tariffs and sanctions and backing UN Security Council reform, but the bloc again declined a common currency.
Outcomes were largely institutional — incubators, funds, payment interoperability — while India's deficit with BRICS partners widened to a reported 226 billion dollars.
relevance: Multilateral summits produce declarations; their value lies in what gets implemented afterwards, and by whom.
question: Can a grouping that includes both Iran and the UAE, and both India and China, be more than a forum — or is consensus itself the achievement?

title: COP31 in Antalya: a climate summit with two captains
syllabus: GS II — India and its neighbourhood — relations; bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements; important international institutions, agencies and fora.
paragraphs: The 2026 United Nations climate summit, COP31, will be held in Antalya, Türkiye, in late 2026, under an arrangement without precedent in the history of the climate negotiations. Türkiye will host the conference and hold the COP presidency, while Australia will lead the negotiations as President of Negotiations, managing draft texts and guiding decision-making. A pre-COP meeting was held in a Pacific island country, honouring Australia's original bid to co-host the summit with Pacific island nations and to foreground the concerns of the world's most climate-vulnerable states.

The split presidency was the product of a diplomatic impasse. Australia announced its intention to host COP31 in 2022, proposing a Pacific co-hosting arrangement that would have made it the first United Nations climate summit held physically in Oceania. Türkiye also bid to host. The standoff persisted through the final week of COP30 in Belém, Brazil, in 2025, and risked pushing the 2026 meeting to Bonn, Germany, where the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change secretariat is based, with no agreed president. The compromise, struck at COP30, gave Türkiye the venue and Australia the negotiating gavel, with Australian Climate Minister Chris Bowen describing the outcome as preserving a leadership role even without the venue.

The substance awaiting Antalya was set at COP30. Countries agreed to mobilise 1.3 trillion dollars annually by 2035 for climate action, to double adaptation finance by 2025 and triple it by 2035, to launch a Global Implementation Accelerator and the Belém Mission to 1.5 degrees Celsius, and to operationalise the loss and damage fund. But more than 80 countries' push for explicit fossil-fuel phase-out language failed: the final text only referenced the COP28 UAE Consensus language of transitioning away from fossil fuels, and a draft roadmap was removed in the final hours. UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned that overshooting 1.5 degrees remained a real risk without deep, rapid emissions cuts.

Expectations for COP31 are deliberately modest. Analysts at the World Resources Institute noted that this year's summit is not expected to be defined by a landmark negotiated outcome; the focus is on overcoming practical barriers, backing pledges with finance and policy, and advancing the COP presidency's goal of meeting 35 per cent of energy needs with electricity by 2035. The ocean is a priority of the Action Agenda, and Pacific leaders at the pre-COP called for a stronger role for ocean solutions. Whether the ocean becomes a formal outcome or remains a theme, and whether the split presidency functions smoothly, will be the summit's real tests.
takeaways: COP31 is hosted by Türkiye in Antalya in late 2026, while Australia leads negotiations as President of Negotiations — a split agreed at COP30 after a hosting deadlock.
COP30 set finance goals of 1.3 trillion dollars a year by 2035, but failed to agree explicit fossil-fuel phase-out language.
COP31 is expected to focus on implementation — finance, electricity goals and ocean action — rather than a landmark new treaty.
relevance: Institutions improvise under deadlock: a split presidency shows how multilateral talks preserve momentum when no single host can be agreed.
question: Does judging a climate summit by implementation rather than new pledges lower ambition, or finally measure what matters?

title: The United Nations opens a global dialogue on AI governance
syllabus: GS II — India and its neighbourhood — relations; bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements; important international institutions, agencies and fora.
paragraphs: On 6–7 July 2026, the United Nations convened the first annual Global Dialogue on Artificial Intelligence Governance in Geneva, the first universal forum operating under a General Assembly mandate in which governments and other stakeholders can deliberate collectively on AI governance. Established by consensus through General Assembly Resolution 79/325 of August 2025, the dialogue brought together more than 4,200 participants from nearly 170 states, alongside international organisations, technology companies, civil society, academia and the technical community. It opened Geneva Digital Week and overlapped with the International Telecommunication Union's AI for Good Global Summit, held in Geneva from 7 to 10 July.

Secretary-General António Guterres opened the session with a warning: artificial intelligence is expanding faster than the legal rules designed to govern it. He renewed his call to prohibit lethal autonomous weapons systems that can make life-or-death decisions without meaningful human control, and proposed an AI Child Safety Pledge requiring developers to demonstrate that systems intended for children meet basic protections before release. The dialogue's sessions covered safety, equitable access, technical standards, capacity-building, interoperability and human rights, and the preliminary report of the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI was presented.

The central message from Geneva was that everyone agreed AI needs rules, and nobody agreed whose rules. The dialogue produced no treaty and no rulebook; a second session was scheduled for New York in May 2027. At the AI for Good Summit, the World Intellectual Property Organization's Assistant Director General Ken-Ichiro Natsume explained that member states had not yet reached agreement to begin treaty negotiations on AI and intellectual property, and discussions centred instead on three foundations: high-quality data, technological innovation and effective regulation. Private licensing agreements between AI developers and rights holders, speakers observed, were proliferating faster than legislation.

A parallel track showed a different model. On 29 September 2026, President Donald Trump and major American technology companies — Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI and Nvidia — signed a voluntary agreement in Washington on the safe and responsible development of advanced AI models, setting out four levels of oversight. Kazakhstan's President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev then proposed developing that Washington Model into an international treaty under UN auspices, with proposals to be presented at the G20 summit in Miami in December 2026. The contrast captures the state of AI governance in 2026: a universal dialogue that compares approaches, a voluntary corporate model, and a treaty proposal — but no binding global rules yet.
takeaways: The UN's first Global Dialogue on AI Governance met in Geneva on 6–7 July 2026, with over 4,200 participants from nearly 170 states, under Resolution 79/325.
It produced no treaty: WIPO confirmed no consensus to negotiate one, and a second session was set for New York in May 2027.
A voluntary Washington agreement of September 2026 was proposed by Kazakhstan as the basis for a future UN AI treaty.
relevance: Global governance often begins as dialogue: comparing national approaches can build the common ground that later treaties require — or stall indefinitely.
question: Should AI be governed by a binding treaty, voluntary corporate commitments, or national laws first — and who loses while the world decides?

title: Security Council reform in 2026: the case against 1945
syllabus: GS II — India and its neighbourhood — relations; bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements; important international institutions, agencies and fora.
paragraphs: On 22 October 2026, India's Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Ambassador Parvathaneni Harish, told the General Assembly that a Security Council which does not adequately represent the wider membership faces a deficit in legitimacy. The Council has fifteen members: five permanent members — China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States — who hold veto power over substantive resolutions, and ten members elected for two-year terms. Harish argued that authority derived from victory in a war more than eighty years ago cannot substitute for representation today, noting that about 2.5 million Indians served in the Second World War and about 90,000 died in military service.

India's practical demand was procedural rather than rhetorical: that the intergovernmental negotiations on reform proceed on the basis of a written text, so that countries debate and revise a shared document instead of allowing the process to remain open-ended. A written text would not settle the dispute over permanent seats or the veto, but it would force negotiators to work through their differences on representation and power. India wants the Council expanded in both the permanent and elected categories, and works with Brazil, Germany and Japan in the Group of Four, which supports new permanent seats and greater representation for regions that lack them.

The 81st General Assembly debate in September 2026 showed both the breadth of support and the depth of disagreement. Portugal's Prime Minister Luís Montenegro called for permanent seats for Africa, Brazil and India; Mauritius's Foreign Minister Dhananjay Ramful explicitly reiterated support for India's candidature; the Marshall Islands backed Japan and its G4 partners; Finland's President Alexander Stubb proposed at least two new permanent seats for Africa, two for Asia-Pacific and one for Latin America. Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov supported India and Brazil but opposed Germany and Japan, exposing a fault line inside the G4 itself. The Uniting for Consensus group, by contrast, opposes any new permanent members and favours expansion through elected or rotating seats.

Reform remains blocked by the Charter's own amendment rule: any change to the Council's membership requires approval by two-thirds of the General Assembly and ratification by two-thirds of UN members, including all five permanent members — each of which can veto the change that would dilute its own privilege. The Council's membership was last changed by an amendment adopted in 1963 and in force from 1965, which raised it from eleven to fifteen by adding four elected seats, without touching the five permanent seats.
